items.title: Field Notes: EtherRAT Distributed Through a Legitimate Intune Workflow
items.summary: Introduction The investigation began with a Microsoft Defender for Endpoint alert for suspicious screen capture activity involving PowerShell. Examining the process ancestry revealed a larger execution chain involving FbtRYX8x.exe , a renamed Node.js runtime communicating with several public Ethereum RPC providers. The observed behavior was consistent with EtherRAT , a Node.js-based backdoor previously documented by Atos Threat Research Center , The DFIR Report , and Malwarebytes . Further hunting identified the same malware on four managed endpoints, all of which had received a malicious MSI through Microsoft Intune. The deployment itself was not the result of an identified compromise of Intune. Instead, the customer had imported what appeared to be a legitimate Advanced IP Scanner installer into its existing software distribution workflow, inadvertently deploying the malware to multiple systems.

Introduction

The investigation began with a Microsoft Defender for Endpoint alert for suspicious screen capture activity involving PowerShell. Examining the process ancestry revealed a larger execution chain involving FbtRYX8x.exe, a renamed Node.js runtime communicating with several public Ethereum RPC providers. The observed behavior was consistent with EtherRAT, a Node.js-based backdoor previously documented by Atos Threat Research Center, The DFIR Report, and Malwarebytes.

Further hunting identified the same malware on four managed endpoints, all of which had received a malicious MSI through Microsoft Intune. The deployment itself was not the result of an identified compromise of Intune. Instead, the customer had imported what appeared to be a legitimate Advanced IP Scanner installer into its existing software distribution workflow, inadvertently deploying the malware to multiple systems.

items.title: Visual Studio Copilot and SSMS Remote Code Execution (CVE-2026-103572)
items.summary: A . is all you need! Today Microsoft shipped the patch for a vulnerability in Visual Studio Copilot that I reported in August. Microsoft classified it as Important severity Remote Code Execution vulnerability. At the root cause it allows Copilot in Visual Studio or SQL Server Management Studio to bypass a path validation check and write to its own settings and configuration files . This allows Copilot to escape containment restrictions and achieve arbitrary command execution.

items.title: Micropatches released for Windows DNS Server Remote Code Execution Vulnerability (CVE-2026-62878)
items.summary: August 2026 Windows Updates brought a patch for CVE-2026-62878, a remote code execution vulnerability in Windows DNS Server, allowing an attacker to remotely cause memory corruption on the DNS server without authentication or special privileges. According to Microsoft's advisory, such memory corruption could be used for arbitrary code execution. Subsequently, security researchers Nicolas Alejandro Malizia and Joaquín Grassi published their own proof of concept, which allowed us to reproduce the issue and create patches for legacy Windows systems. The Vulnerability This is a stack-based buffer overflow in Windows DNS Server, caused by flawed code processing a recursive query. Read Nicolas and Joaquín's analysis for more details. Microsoft's Patch Microsoft fixed this issue by limiting the query recursion nesting depth to 62, effectively preventing the overflow. Our Patch Our patch is logically identical to Microsoft's. Let's see our patch in action.

items.title: Part 2 – Cybersecurity journeys: What even is this job?
items.summary: If you’ve ever looked at a list of cybersecurity jobs and felt like none of them fit you, you might just be looking at a short list. Most career guides cover the same few roles, like the analyst watching alerts or the pen tester (penetration tester, someone hired to legally break into systems to find weaknesses) looking for a way in. Those jobs matter, but they’re a small slice of a field with room for a lot of different skills. The three people in this post do work you probably won’t find in those guides, and none of them started out qualified for it. What they had in common was a willingness to aim at something before they were ready and to build the skills on the way there. If you’ve ever talked yourself out of a role because you didn’t tick every box, their stories are worth a few minutes, because the move each of them made is one you can make too. In Part 1: I didn’t plan this , I shared how three people found their way into security from a warehouse floor, a marketing desk, and a teenager’s bedroom. This week is about where people end up after they’re inside. I’ve been in security for over a decade, and while putting this series together I kept running into work I hadn’t come across before: measuring the risk of a million applications at once, building detection tools from the customer service side of the house, and thinking seriously about how to secure infrastructure that’s being launched into orbit. The skill tree Jason Lane, Security Engineer When Jason Lane told me he plans his career like a Dungeons & Dragons character build, I assumed he was being metaphorical, but he meant it literally. “Think of it like a video game skill tree,” he said, and then walked me through the whole framework. You start by picturing your level 20 character, the version of yourself with the skills and the role you actually want, and then you work backward. At level 19, what choices get you to 20? At level 18, what needs to be true so you even have those options? You keep stepping back until you’re standing at level 1, looking at a path you built from the top down. For Jason, level 20 was vulnerability research (finding unknown security flaws in software before attackers do). At the time he was a systems administrator, keeping servers and networks running, which gave him a solid grasp of how systems fit together but little exposure to picking apart the applications on top of them. That gap, application security, was the next node on his tree, so he called an IT recruiter, laid out his plan, and was honest about where he stood. The recruiter found a credit card processing company that needed an application security engineer and was open to someone who wasn’t one yet. For Jason it was a paid apprenticeship in the exact skill he was after; for the company it was a motivated engineer who would grow into the role. He describes it as a deal where both sides got what they needed, and that framing matters: he wasn’t settling for less, he was trading a steeper learning curve for a faster path to where he wanted to be. He spent 4 years there taking applications apart to understand what made them breakable, and when he had learned what that role could teach him, he applied the same framework again. A friend offered to get him an interview at Google, and Jason’s honest reaction, that he wasn’t smart enough to work there, is the kind of self-doubt most of us recognize (also known as imposter syndrome). His friend didn’t buy it, the interviewers didn’t either, and they hired him. The lesson he took from it is one worth borrowing: the voice telling you that you don’t belong in the room is often wrong, and the way to quiet it is to put in the work until the skills speak for themselves. He went on to spend nearly 7 years doing Android vulnerability research, the kind of deep technical work most companies don’t have the budget for. That track record opened the door to Amazon. When the team that measures application risk interviewed him, the hiring manager’s pitch was simple: we could really use your vulnerability research experience. Years of tearing systems apart to find what made them breakable turned out to be the perfect background for judging which systems were most at risk. Today, Jason measures risk across roughly a million applications at Amazon, evaluating which ones would cause the most damage if compromised and which are most likely to be targeted, so the organization can focus on the most dangerous ones first. When his manager recently presented the team’s work to a new senior leader, the example he used was a project Jason had built from scratch. Jason’s name wasn’t on the slide, and he told me he didn’t need it to be, but you could hear the pride in his voice. When I asked what he’d tell someone with a big vision and no idea where to start, he said to get obsessively clear about where you’re going, because the gaps will show up on their own. He compared it to planning a 100-mile trip and realizing you aren’t wearing shoes; once you see it, you can’t unsee it. And if it turns out the dream is really a hobby, he’s at peace with that too. “If you can wait for Saturday, maybe you should just wait for Saturday. There’s nothing wrong with that.” —Jason Lane If you’ve been waiting for someone to hand you a career ladder, Jason’s approach offers another option: decide where you want to end up, and let that tell you what to learn next. Full circle Jason Goodman, Security Engineer Where Jason Lane planned his career from the finish line, Jason Goodman’s career has looked more like a pinball machine, bouncing through three security disciplines in about a year and picking up new skills along the way. The foundation was laid long before he knew it. Eight years ago, before Amazon acquired Ring, he was working in customer service, troubleshooting doorbells and helping customers with their accounts, and before that he sold computers at Best Buy. “That was the most tech I had,” he told me, grinning. What pointed him toward security was partly a nudge from his father-in-law, who worked in IT, and partly what he was seeing on the phones every day: the occasional account access that didn’t look right, the quiet signals that something might be off. Those patterns made him want to understand the systems behind them, so while he was still in customer service he went back to school for a cybersecurity degree. He didn’t wait until graduation to start building toward the move. He reached out to the manager of the internal threat team (the people who look for misuse of access from inside an organization) and asked a question anyone can ask: what could I do to keep progressing while I’m in school? That turned into stretch projects, and here is the part worth noticing, he earned the bigger ones by delivering the smaller ones first. His standout project was a fraud prevention dashboard that helped the team spot potential misuse of customer account access, a blind spot nobody had flagged. He had the credibility to be handed it because he’d already shown up for the low-stakes work, and it opened the door to his first security engineering role on that same team. From there he moved to an adversarial threat detection team (the people who watch for outside attackers trying to get in), which meant flipping his mindset overnight: instead of asking what someone on the inside could do with their existing access, he was now asking how someone on the outside would try to break in. A later move took him into application security, where the work shifted from responding after the fact to building security into processes from the ground up. “I’m in my third discipline in a year since transitioning out of customer service into security engineering.” —Jason Goodman What I find fascinating is how much carried over from one role to the next. The Splunk queries (Splunk is a tool for searching and analyzing large volumes of log data) he learned in customer service carried into internal threat work, the detection logic from insider investigations carried into adversarial detection, and now in application security he has come full circle, working alongside the same customer service teams he started with, except this time he’s helping build the security around them. Through all of it, he has leaned on four different mentors, and the way he found them is worth stealing. Finding one mentor who truly invests in you is hard; finding four is rare. Jason didn’t wait to be assigned anyone. He reached out to people whose work he admired, starting with that internal threat manager during school, asked specific questions, and stayed in touch over the years as he grew. Each mentor served a different purpose: one for navigating school, one for stretch projects, one for learning to think like an adversary, and one for getting grounded in application security. “I’ve always felt like I could take at least a little nugget from each one of them,” he said. Next on his list is offensive security, meaning pen testing and red teaming (simulating real attackers to test how well an organization defends itself). He figures starting on defense was the right call: learn what attackers do and how to stop them, then learn to think like one. If your current role feels unrelated to security, Jason’s story is a good reminder that the skills you’re building now may be exactly the ones your first security job needs. The analytical habit of noticing when something is off, the patience to explain a problem clearly, even the instincts you pick up from a completely different field all transfer. The trick is learning to name what you already have and point it at the work you want. The edge of the map Harshvardhan Chunawala, Solutions Architect, AWS Startups Harshvardhan Chunawala was still in high school when he started finding security flaws in real products and reporting them to the companies that built them. He had started out building websites and web applications, and after he understood how software was put together, he couldn’t stop wondering how it could be pulled apart. Rather than wait until he had a degree or a job to explore that, he began poking at real products on his own, and when he found a flaw he contacted the company and worked with them to fix it. Today he advises startup founders at AWS on security and volunteers his time to teach cloud and security courses to students, who often ask him where to start when entry-level work is being automated. His answer has changed over the years. Now that generative AI can answer the surface-level questions, he believes curiosity matters more than credentials, because the people who stand out are the ones who keep asking questions after the tool runs out of answers. “AI tools put everyone on the same starting line. Interest and passion has become the driving force.” —Harshvardhan Chunawala What surprised me most, though, was where his own curiosity took him. While studying at Carnegie Mellon University (CMU), he ended up working on space missions, including time as a mission operator for the Iris lunar rover (Iris and CMU’s next rover, MoonRanger, appear with him in the photo above). If you had asked me a few years ago whether security belonged anywhere near a rover on the Moon, I wouldn’t have known what to say, but Harshvardhan would have answered right away: anything that can be commanded remotely can be commanded by the wrong person. When I asked about the future of security, he took the conversation completely off the map. He talked about robots entering people’s homes and about data centers moving from land to underwater to space. A satellite has to be protected in orbit, where nobody can physically reach a compromised system, and on the ground, where the stations that command it are targets too. “So are cyber security specialists going to go under astronaut training?” he asked, grinning, and he was only half joking. He has already written a two-part guide to incident response for satellite operations on AWS , so for him, this corner of the map is already part of the job. If you’re drawn to an area that doesn’t look like a security job yet, Harshvardhan’s story is worth taking seriously: the move he keeps making is to follow a question past the point where the easy answers run out, into territory nobody has fully mapped. You don’t need a satellite to do that. Pick the corner of technology that genuinely fascinates you, start asking how it could be attacked and defended, and you might find you’re standing at the edge of a role that doesn’t have a name yet. The thread These three stories share one thread: the job you end up loving might be one you haven’t heard of yet. Jason Lane mapped his moves in advance, Jason Goodman carried his skills through three disciplines in a single year, and Harshvardhan is already helping AWS customers secure satellites and the ground systems that run them. None of them could answer “what do you do?” in a single sentence, and I suspect that’s true for a lot of people doing interesting work in this field. If you’re curious about the roles that exist beyond the ones you already know, here are a few places to start exploring: The NICE Workforce Framework for Cybersecurity lays out dozens of security work roles and the skills each one needs CyberSeek offers an interactive career pathway map showing how entry-level roles connect to advanced ones AWS Skill Builder has free security and cloud training you can start today CISA’s Cybersecurity Awareness Month page has more resources for this October In Part 3: The work behind the work, we pull back the curtain on what the day-to-day of security actually looks like compared to what people imagine. items.title: Reviews of the new Framework Laptop 12 are live
items.summary: Reviews are live on the new Framework Laptop 12 powered by Intel Core Series 3! We designed Framework Laptop 12 from the start to be a fun, colorful, portable, Linux-ready 2-in-1. With this generation, we focused on power efficiency, CPU performance, and improvements to quality of life with options for fingerprint reader and backlit keyboard. Reviewers confirmed we maintained what makes this form factor great while leveling up the overall experience: “If you’re tired of disposable electronics and want a portable device you can easily repair and upgrade for years to come, the Laptop 12 is an outstanding choice.” – Tom’s Guide “Overall this is a very nice Intel Wildcat Lake laptop option for Linux use with Framework's legendary upgrade-ability and friendly Linux support.” – Phoronix "If you like the MacBook Neo but you want to run Linux, and you care about repairability and upgradability, this is probably the laptop you want." – The Linux Experiment Shipments of the new Framework Laptop 12 start later this week. Pre-orders are still open , with the current available batch shipping in November. We’re targeting making new modules like the Fingerprint Reader available in the Framework Marketplace by the end of this year. Framework Laptop 12 continues to be our system with the highest percentage of Linux usage. Our Linux compatibility page is now up to date with the latest distro recommendations. Note that Core Series 3 and the BE213 Wi-Fi 7 module we used are both very new, so we recommend using a distro with kernel 7.1 or newer. We have a pre-built option that comes with a customized Fedora 44 KDE Plasma install with all the needed patches for full hardware support, and you can pick up that image to install onto a DIY Edition too. Whenever we launch a new generation of a product, we want to make sure you have a way to reuse any original modules after upgrading to new ones. To enable that, we partnered with Printables to run a design competition for 3D-printable cases to re-use the Framework Laptop 12 Mainboard. We saw some truly incredible and creative designs, and we’re excited to share the winners. First is a refined, minimal case by Pom. Second place goes to Rusty6285’s Portable Access Console , and third is Jankbu’s modular cyberdeck . We’re happy to see the Framework Laptop 12 ecosystem continue to grow, and all of the community efforts continue to make this our most loveable computer.

Shipments of the new Framework Laptop 12 start later this week. Pre-orders are still open, with the current available batch shipping in November. We’re targeting making new modules like the Fingerprint Reader available in the Framework Marketplace by the end of this year.

Framework Laptop 12 continues to be our system with the highest percentage of Linux usage. Our Linux compatibility page is now up to date with the latest distro recommendations. Note that Core Series 3 and the BE213 Wi-Fi 7 module we used are both very new, so we recommend using a distro with kernel 7.1 or newer. We have a pre-built option that comes with a customized Fedora 44 KDE Plasma install with all the needed patches for full hardware support, and you can pick up that image to install onto a DIY Edition too.

Whenever we launch a new generation of a product, we want to make sure you have a way to reuse any original modules after upgrading to new ones. To enable that, we partnered with Printables to run a design competition for 3D-printable cases to re-use the Framework Laptop 12 Mainboard. We saw some truly incredible and creative designs, and we’re excited to share the winners. First is a refined, minimal case by Pom. Second place goes to Rusty6285’s Portable Access Console, and third is Jankbu’s modular cyberdeck. We’re happy to see the Framework Laptop 12 ecosystem continue to grow, and all of the community efforts continue to make this our most loveable computer.

items.title: Microsoft Fixes 1,118 Vulnerabilities in October Patch Tuesday and Introduces New Risk Cohorts
items.summary: Microsoft’s October 2026 Patch Tuesday briefing outlines 1,118 vulnerabilities across 15 risk groups, alongside a new approach designed to help security teams review large update releases. Called risk cohorts, these groups bring together flaws that require similar questions about an organization’s systems, users, and exposure. Microsoft’s accompanying document maps individual CVEs to these shared areas of assessment. The goal is to reduce repeated work without removing the need to review each vulnerability. Instead of asking the same deployment questions hundreds of times, analysts can assess a common area once and use that information across several CVEs. Microsoft describes the approach as exploratory, not a replacement for its existing update guidance or individual vulnerability assessments. The release follows other large update cycles covered in Cybersecuritynews.com’s September 2026 Patch Tuesday report and August 2026 Patch Tuesday coverage . Those reports show the broad range of Microsoft products that enterprise teams must consider when planning security updates. Why Microsoft Is Exploring Risk Cohorts Traditional vulnerability review starts with each CVE. Analysts check its severity, affected products, attack requirements, and exploitation status. They then decide how quickly their organization needs to respond. That process remains necessary, but a large release can force teams to repeat many of the same checks. For example, several flaws may require analysts to establish whether untrusted files reach a Windows component. Others may depend on whether users with limited permissions can run code locally. Server vulnerabilities may require checking whether a particular role is installed and reachable. A risk cohort groups vulnerabilities around those shared questions. The flaws do not need to have the same root cause or CVSS score. Their connection is the assessment needed to understand exposure in the customer’s environment. Microsoft highlights that these provisional groups are not official vulnerability categories. They do not change patching instructions, determine urgency on their own, or replace checks for active exploitation, user interaction, attack paths, and product guidance. Windows and Office Dominate the Groups The largest listed cohort covers Windows filesystems, storage, and backup, with 136 CVEs. Its shared assessment focuses on features and backup paths that handle untrusted input, disk images, media, or workloads. Office document and mail clients follow with 135 CVEs, while Windows graphics, media, and content processing accounts for 131. Windows graphics, media and content processing 131 Which systems process untrusted content or allow untrusted local code to interact with graphics, media, or text services, and with what permissions? Office document and mail clients 135 Which Office applications and versions are installed, what untrusted content reaches them, and how are updates deployed? Windows core and kernel privilege boundaries 109 Can untrusted or lower-privileged code run on these Windows systems, and which kernel and privilege boundaries need protection? Windows installation, deployment and update services 103 Which installation, update, and deployment services are used, and can lower-privileged code interact with their privileged operations? Windows device, peripheral and print surfaces 76 Which hardware, driver, and print features are used, and can untrusted devices, content, or users reach them? Remote-access and RDP deployments 65 Which hosts operate as clients, gateways, or remote-access servers, and which access paths and identities are permitted? Windows authentication, credentials and cryptography 61 Which authentication, credential, and cryptographic features protect these hosts, and which local or network identities can reach them? Windows networking and protocol stack 53 Which protocol features and interfaces are enabled on exposed Windows systems, and which network segments can reach them? DNS, DHCP and network-address infrastructure 76 Which name and address services and clients are enabled, and can untrusted devices or identities interact with them? Virtualization, container and isolation hosts 45 Which virtualization, container, and isolation features are used, and where can untrusted guest, tenant, or workload code run? Directory, federation and certificate infrastructure 24 Which domain, federation, and certificate enrollment services are enabled and reachable, and what trust and identity permissions do they provide? Network file and resource sharing 39 Which SMB, NFS, WebDAV, and other sharing services and clients are enabled, reachable, and accessible to untrusted identities? Endpoint management and security controls 38 Which management agents, security agents, and control features are deployed, and who can affect their policies or privileged operations? Windows web, RPC and messaging services 27 Which web, RPC, and messaging services are enabled and reachable, and what service identities or trust boundaries are involved? items.title: Framework Laptop 13 Pro press reviews and previewing a 192GB Framework Desktop
items.summary: Reviews of Framework Laptop 13 Pro are now live, with shipments of Batch 1 pre-orders starting this week. Our goal with this generation was to build the “MacBook Pro for Linux users”, a robust, refined, high-performance notebook with great battery life that deeply respects your rights through software choice, longevity, and upgradeability. It’s awesome to see that reviewers agree we landed that! Check out the videos and articles from: "The new Framework Laptop 13 Pro is still just as upgradeable as prior laptop models but the hardware quality is now at the next level thanks to the new chassis manufacturing." – Phoronix "The Framework Pro 13 is peak laptop" – Linus Tech Tips "This is their best build yet. They're finally doing what people have been asking for, a premium modular laptop" – MKBHD "This laptop has exceeded my expectations in every way imaginable." – Level1Techs We’ve also started shipping the first Batches of Intel Core Ultra Series 3 Mainboards, the new Touchscreen display, and some of the new configurations of Framework Laptop 16. Personal computing and consumer electronics overall is in a tough place for the foreseeable future due to memory and silicon costs and availability. We have access to supply to continue production, but we faced major cost increases recently from our suppliers. Unfortunately, we expect this trend to continue over the next year. This makes upgradeability and product longevity more important than ever. You can pick up the memory you can get your hands on today with the ability to upgrade in the future when you need to. If you’re planning out a computer purchase, we recommend making it sooner than later, and to choose configurations based on availability of the memory and storage capacity you need. DDR5 pricing is currently lower than LPCAMM2, so if you need a lot of memory, we have the Ryzen AI 300 Series version of Framework Laptop 13 Pro available as well. We also have the non-Pro Framework Laptop 13 with Ryzen AI 300 Series in stock and refurbished versions of several configurations in the Framework Outlet as other paths to save money. Last week, we teased an upcoming 192GB configuration of Framework Desktop at AMD’s Advancing AI event that can run very large models like the 284B parameter DeepSeek-V4-Flash in a single box. If AI is consuming all the silicon in the world, we want to make sure that you can still own your AI compute and run open weights models fully under your control. In addition to bringing in the new Ryzen AI Max+ PRO 495 processor, it uses slightly faster 8533 MT/s memory, has an open-end x4 PCIe slot to make it easier to plug in 50Gbps NICs for clustering, and optionally comes with Linux pre-loaded. We’ll have more to share on this later this year, and you can sign up to get notified in the meantime . Here too, we expect memory costs to continue to increase, and we recommend picking up a 64GB or 128GB configuration now if the models you want to run can fit in those capacities. Finally, if you want to get hands-on with any of these products, we’ll be at a few events over the rest of this year. Come by and meet the team at: PAX West : 9/4 - 9/7, Seattle, WA, USA Open Source Summit Europe : 10/7 - 10/9, Prague, Czechia KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America : 11/9 - 11/12, Salt Lake City, UT, USA

items.title: 192GB Framework Desktop open for pre-order
items.summary: Today, we opened pre-orders for the new 192GB configuration of Framework Desktop with AMD’s new Ryzen AI Max+ PRO 495 processor, enabling much larger and more capable AI models to run locally, entirely under your control. This config has both slightly higher clock speeds on the CPU and GPU and runs the LPDDR5X memory at slightly faster 8,533MT/s speeds, both of which enable an increase in AI inference speed over the original Framework Desktop. You can pick up a DIY Edition , a pre-built version with Fedora pre-loaded, or the Mainboard on its own, with shipments starting in November. We’re opening just one batch to start using the memory inventory we have on hand. Pricing and timing for further batches will depend on memory cost and supply updates from our suppliers. The open-weights model landscape is evolving and advancing rapidly. Today, 192GB lets you run models like DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash Q2 and MiMo V2.6 Flash RL MXFP4. We’re collaborating with Donato Capitella, a software engineer and open source AI content creator on guides and videos for how to get the best results and performance out of your Framework Desktop. He published a video and blog post today specifically on models and inference engines to use with the new 192GB Framework Desktop. Digging deeper into the specifications, Ryzen AI Max+ PRO 495 has 16 Zen 5 CPU cores supporting multithreading, 40-core Radeon 8065S Graphics, and a 256-bit memory bus that enables 273GB/s memory bandwidth. In the Framework Desktop, we interface that to two M.2 SSD slots, a x4 PCIe slot, two USB-C ports that support USB4, two USB-A ports, two front Expansion Card slots, two DisplayPort 2.1 ports, an HDMI 2.1 port, a 3.5mm audio jack, 5Gbps Ethernet, and an RZ717 Wi-Fi 7 module. We changed the PCIe x4 slot to be open-ended on this config, which allows you to use physically larger x8 or x16 cards directly without a riser. That lets you use cards like an Intel E810 for RoCE (RDMA over Ethernet) for 50Gbps networking at ultra low latency, enabling tensor parallelism for linear speedup in inference as you add nodes. As before, the Mainboard is a standard Mini-ITX form factor, meaning you can install it into an existing Framework Desktop case, a RackMate half-width rack tray , or any ATX-compatible case. We’ve also introduced a number of firmware improvements with this launch. First, we’ve brought in an BIOS patch from AMD that increases USB4 point-to-point networking throughput from 9Gbps to around 30Gbps. This makes USB4 another great way to cluster together multiple Framework Desktops. Next, we created a much simpler user experience for disabling Secure Boot for those of you who plan to use Arch Linux, CachyOS, and other distros that don’t support it. We’ll be bringing these to all Framework Desktop models soon, and we’re porting the Secure Boot improvements to Framework Laptops too. Both the DIY Edition and pre-built configurations of the 192GB Framework Desktop come with a 120mm Noctua NF-A12x25 HS-PWM fan pre-installed. Like Framework Laptop 12 (Intel Core Series 3) that we recently launched, the pre-built configuration uses Fedora, making it easy to get started out of the box. This configuration comes with a 2TB SSD, giving you space to download and run large models. Note that the Framework Desktop with Ryzen AI Max+ PRO 495 is designed specifically for Linux, so neither the DIY Edition nor the pre-built versions have Windows options available. With the current memory environment, the 192GB system is a step up in cost over the 128GB Framework Desktop. We expect memory pricing for every capacity to continue to increase over the next six months, so our recommendation if you want to get into local AI inference is to pick up the memory capacity now that matches the models and workloads that you want to run. There are excellent models available across each capacity configuration we offer: 32GB, 64GB, 128GB, and now 192GB. Owning your compute is more important than ever. We’ll continue to do everything we can to empower you on this, no matter what is happening in the rest of the industry.

items.title: Critical FortiSandbox GUI Vulnerability Allows Remote Attackers to Bypass Authentication
items.summary: Fortinet disclosed a critical authentication-bypass vulnerability in the FortiSandbox graphical user interface that could let remote attackers access protected functions without valid credentials. Tracked as CVE-2026-107656, the flaw carries a reported CVSSv3 score of 9.6 and affects both FortiSandbox appliances and selected FortiSandbox PaaS releases. Published on October 13, 2026, the disclosure is tracked under Fortinet advisory FG-IR-26-185 . Fortinet lists the potential impact as execution of unauthorized code or commands. Its advisory marks known exploitation as “No,” meaning the disclosure does not establish that attackers have already used this vulnerability in real attacks. The weakness is classified as CWE-288, Authentication Bypass Using an Alternate Path or Channel. A remote attacker could send crafted HTTP requests to bypass GUI authentication. The supplied CVSS vector describes a network attack with low complexity, no required privileges, and no user interaction. The advisory does not provide specific request paths, an exploit payload, or a detailed attack chain. Those limits matter when assessing exposure. Security teams should not assume that this flaw shares the same exploit method as earlier FortiSandbox authentication bypass vulnerabilities , which involved different components and vulnerability classes. Affected Versions and Required Updates FortiSandbox versions 5.0.0 through 5.0.6 are affected and require an upgrade to 5.0.7 or later. Versions 4.4.0 through 4.4.9 require an upgrade to 4.4.10 or later. FortiSandbox 5.2 is not affected. For FortiSandbox PaaS, versions 5.0.0 through 5.0.6 require an upgrade to 5.0.7 or later. All PaaS 4.4 versions are affected, and Fortinet directs customers to migrate to a fixed release. PaaS 5.2 is not affected. No virtual patch is listed. Fortinet credits Adham El Karn of its Product Security team with discovering and reporting the issue internally. The company also acknowledges Jason McFadyen of TrendAI Research for responsible disclosure. A separate FortiSandbox sensitive data exposure vulnerability previously affected the web interface, but its fixes should not be treated as protection against this new flaw. items.title: TFG London Cyberattack Disrupts IT Systems Used by Phase Eight, Hobbs, and Whistles Brands
items.summary: TFG London has confirmed a cyberattack that disrupted IT systems supporting Phase Eight, Hobbs, and Whistles. South Africa’s The Foschini Group detected the incident on October 11, 2026, and disclosed it to shareholders on October 13. Several systems remained unavailable, although stores continued trading. According to the company’s shareholder announcement , Inside Story and White Stuff were not affected. TFG Africa and TFG Australia also remained unaffected because they operate on separate systems. The confirmed disruption is therefore limited to part of the group’s UK business, rather than its global operations. TFG London Cyberattack TFG activated its incident response and business continuity plans after discovering the attack. External cybersecurity specialists are helping contain the incident, and the company has informed relevant UK authorities. Its investigation is still examining whether personal or other sensitive information was compromised. Customers face disruption, even as stores remain open. Some website functions may be unavailable, and orders placed on or after October 11 could be delayed. Customers have been told not to resubmit those orders. Purchases placed before Sunday are expected to be processed and delivered normally. In customer communications, TFG London said a third-party provider handles payment processing. Based on its investigation so far, it has “no reason to believe that payment information is at risk.” However, the company has not ruled out exposure of other customer information and will directly notify people whose data was affected. TFG has not disclosed the attackers’ identity, their entry point, or whether ransomware was involved. It has also not provided a deadline for full system recovery. These gaps matter because system unavailability alone does not show whether attackers encrypted files, stole data, or caused another form of disruption. The separate systems used in Africa and Australia provide an important boundary to the reported impact. However, TFG has not published enough technical detail to establish which UK applications were affected or how access across the three brands was disrupted. TFG’s June financial results described an earlier cyber incident affecting a key online concession partner. That disruption was one of several pressures on its UK portfolio. Adjusted operating profit fell 65.4%, excluding brand impairment and acquisition costs. This figure should not be presented as the cost of October’s attack. Neither report links to TFG. For now, the central questions remain how they gained access, whether they stole information, and when affected services can safely return. items.title: Critical Docker Hub Flaw Lets Attackers Impersonate Users and Push Container Images
items.summary: Docker has disclosed a critical Docker Hub vulnerability that could let attackers impersonate other users and publish container images under trusted names. Tracked as CVE-2026-105445, the flaw affected personal access tokens transferred during account conversions. Docker resolved the issue on September 30, 2026, stating its investigation found no evidence of exploitation. This issue posed a software supply chain risk, as attackers could potentially alter images that developers relied on. Depending on the token’s permissions and the target user’s access, they could pull, push, or delete images in personal repositories and connected organizations. However, the flaw did not allow full account takeover. Docker Hub Vulnerability Docker Hub allows users to convert a personal account into an organization while keeping existing repository names. This helps teams preserve image references used by applications and build systems. During conversion, the user selects an existing Docker Hub account to become the organization’s owner. Starting August 26, 2024, this process also transferred the original account’s personal access tokens, known as PATs, to the selected owner. Docker changed the ownership record without changing or revoking the token secret. The new owner was neither asked to approve the transfer nor notified that it happened. An attacker could therefore create an account, generate a PAT, and convert that account into an organization while naming a victim as its owner. The attacker still knew the token secret, but Docker Hub now linked that token to the victim. Registry requests using it could authenticate as the target user. This was a failure in credential-ownership handling rather than a stolen-password attack. The token remained usable after its identity changed. Docker says the exposure window lasted from August 26, 2024, at 20:33 UTC until September 30, 2026, at approximately 19:10 UTC, when the production fix went live. Publishing an image under a legitimate repository name could expose downstream users to unexpected code. Cybersecurity News previously covered the Trivy supply chain attack involving compromised Docker images , illustrating why trusted publishing paths matter. That incident is separate from this vulnerability, which Docker found no evidence attackers exploited. The affected tokens did not provide access to the Docker Hub website. Attackers could not use this flaw to change a victim’s password, email address, or two-factor authentication settings. The impact stayed at the registry level and depended on the token’s scope and the user’s repository permissions. Researchers Peter Molnar and Krisztian Hozak of mptrdev.com reported the issue through Docker’s vulnerability disclosure program. According to Docker’s security advisory , the company reproduced it with internal test accounts and deployed a fix less than four hours after receiving the report. Docker reviewed every account conversion since the flaw appeared and checked registry authentication logs, usage data, and token records. Investigators examined approximately 304,000 image pushes made with transferred tokens. All went to repositories belonging to the converted organization or the new owner, with none reaching unrelated accounts. Docker also inspected higher-risk public images without running them. It found no malware, cryptominers, credential theft, persistence, or tampering. However, registry logs record token use rather than token existence. Docker therefore treated every transferred PAT as potentially affected, including tokens that never appeared in usage logs. Docker notified exposed users and organization owners on October 2. On October 8, it deactivated transferred tokens, except those owners requested to retain. Account conversion no longer transfers PATs. Docker is also adding owner consent, notifications, and records of token ownership changes. Docker says users who received no notification were not exposed and need no incident-specific action. It recommends revoking unfamiliar or unused PATs and using organization access tokens for organizational automation. Related container image scanning tools provide context for teams reviewing image security alongside credential controls. An EDR alert reveals an attack. But can it tell the

The affected tokens did not provide access to the Docker Hub website. Attackers could not use this flaw to change a victim’s password, email address, or two-factor authentication settings.

The impact stayed at the registry level and depended on the token’s scope and the user’s repository permissions. Researchers Peter Molnar and Krisztian Hozak of mptrdev.com reported the issue through Docker’s vulnerability disclosure program.

All went to repositories belonging to the converted organization or the new owner, with none reaching unrelated accounts. Docker also inspected higher-risk public images without running them. It found no malware, cryptominers, credential theft, persistence, or tampering.

items.title: CrowdStrike Joins Anthropic Defense Program to Advance AI-powered Defense for Critical Infrastructure
items.summary: CrowdStrike has joined Anthropic’s Critical Infrastructure Defense Program to help strengthen AI-powered cybersecurity across energy, water, manufacturing, and transportation systems. Announced on October 8, 2026, the partnership combines CrowdStrike’s experience protecting business and industrial networks with Anthropic’s advanced Claude models, technical support, and cybersecurity research. The initiative targets a difficult security challenge. Critical infrastructure often connects modern information technology, or IT, with older operational technology, or OT, that controls physical equipment. These industrial systems can remain in service for decades. Taking them offline for updates may interrupt essential services, leaving known security weaknesses unresolved for years. Anthropic Defense Program According to Anthropic’s announcement , the program brings Claude models, on-site engineers, and threat research to trusted security providers and equipment manufacturers. CrowdStrike is among 11 founding partners, alongside organizations including Dragos, Nozomi Networks, Rockwell Automation, Palo Alto Networks, Accenture, and Deloitte. The approach puts AI support in the hands of teams that already understand industrial environments. The program forms part of the broader Anthropic Cyber Mission , which also supports open-source software security. Anthropic says several partners are already using Claude to fix vulnerabilities and help customers address weaknesses. Its initial focus is learning which defensive methods work safely and effectively, rather than treating AI as a complete solution for industrial security. CrowdStrike will contribute security data, threat intelligence, and experience from its Falcon platform. In its partnership announcement , the company describes an opportunity to connect its knowledge of attacker behavior with Anthropic’s AI research. That context matters because defenders must understand a weakness within the wider network before they can choose a practical response. A key part of CrowdStrike’s contribution is Falcon for XIoT , which covers industrial and connected devices alongside IT assets. CrowdStrike says it helps discover unmanaged and older equipment, assess exposure without disruptive scanning, and detect threats moving between business and operational networks. Supported Windows and Linux hosts can help discover and monitor nearby unmanaged devices. The Falcon platform also combines endpoint, identity, cloud, threat intelligence, and OT security data. This shared view gives defenders more context when investigating suspicious activity across connected environments. The partnership builds on an existing relationship, with Anthropic’s Claude already available within CrowdStrike’s Charlotte AI security assistant. Participation in the program adds technical guidance and access to a community focused on critical infrastructure defense. The announcement also follows Anthropic’s expanded Cyber Verification Program , which gives eligible security professionals broader model access for approved work. However, finding weaknesses is only part of the challenge. Anthropic acknowledges that verifying findings and safely applying fixes remain difficult, especially when industrial equipment cannot stop. The collaboration’s value will depend on turning AI findings into safe, practical improvements. An EDR alert reveals an attack. But can it tell the
