items.title: Rewinding the exponential: How we keep hardware usage down
items.summary: More than 20% of the web sits behind Cloudflare’s network, and our team, the Data team, owns the data pipeline responsible for plumbing that data (and more) from our global network to applicable central data centers. The Cloudflare network is a globally distributed system supporting tens of thousands of servers. Data that power Cloudflare Logs , SQL API , observability , internal analytics, and more flow through this network and use our data pipeline to serve customers. In May of this year, we were providing data delivery at roughly two billion events per second. This includes customer traffic as well as data sent from internal teams. Year after year, we tackle the same problem — exponential traffic growth against linear hardware growth. We have to react to this increase in order to keep resource costs under control. Over the past five years, we’ve made various improvements to compensate for the data volume increase in comparison to hardware allocation, equivalent to deferring two and a half years of hardware expansion. This post details those changes: breaking up our monolithic data schema in 2022, adjusting compression in 2024, rearchitecting pipeline replication in spring 2026, decentralizing sampling in summer 2026, and introducing aggregations into the pipeline in fall 2026. Background Our pipeline starts with an internal service called Logfwdr, where we collect from highly distributed data sources (think: Workers, FL ). We then feed this data to a set of centralized receivers, which eventually push them onto our buffering system , Buftee. Consumers fetch data from Buftee and distribute data to their final destinations, like ClickHouse, which we rely on heavily . Unpacking the monolith In 2022, we dismantled our one and only schema. Previously, there was a single stream packed with every product's fields, forcing Cloudflare-internal consumers to ingest everything and demux or discard records via filters. At the time, most of Cloudflare’s data products were built on HTTP, Security and CDN metadata. In 2021, our message schema looked like this: Some fields here belonged under the same product, but some were completely irrelevant to each other. The hypothesis was that none of these teams require 100% of fields in the monolithic schema. In other words, we can create small messages for each product’s required fields. Although we were going to duplicate fields, some of them in every message, replacing this firehose with product-specific schemas actually reduced the backbone bandwidth usage by 35-40%, knocking out roughly a year’s worth of compressed traffic growth. Compression By 2024, as traffic steadily grew, we were tackling network congestion issues on a daily basis. To react to this, we changed our compression algorithm from LZ4 to zstd. We had already experimented with zstd compression before, but we noticed a higher CPU usage at the time. Therefore, we were careful to track the metrics to ensure the trade-off was worth it. Initially, we rolled this change out to a few servers. To our relief, we didn’t observe a noticeable difference in CPU usage. With more confidence, we gradually rolled out to our entire fleet, which also showed little impact to CPUs. In the end, there was nearly a 40% reduction in compressed traffic throughput. The uncompressed bytes remained at the same growth, meaning we could support more than 1.5x the amount of traffic with the same size pipe. Or another way to put it, the estimated growth-equivalent reductions put us at about 10 months prior. Now, in 2026, we attempted three strategies to reduce uncompressed bytes (and thus, compressed bytes). Load balancing To make analytics resilient against regional disasters, our systems require redundant data to be stored in multiple centralized regions (data subject to Customer Metadata Boundaries is stored strictly within its designated region). Historically, the simplest way to achieve disaster resilience was double-writing: Logfwdr transmitted two full copies of every non-regional analytics event — one to each centralized region. Each region then independently processed a complete copy through to ClickHouse. We also apply sampling in each region, an incredibly scalable technique that works for all volumes of data during any traffic conditions. We downsample high-volume traffic while rare events are preserved. This infrastructure was manageable when only a handful of streams used secondary regions. However, as we expanded disaster resilience across almost all analytics streams, Logfwdr traffic doubled across the board. Sending every event, twice, over wide-area transit was unsustainable against our exponential traffic growth. We had already tackled a similar challenge for Logpush . For Logpush, Logfwdr treats the centralized data centers as a unified, shared pool of receivers: each message is sent to only one region, failing over to another destination if a machine or facility is unreachable. That model had already proven its worth during large incidents, shifting traffic seamlessly from one location to another without human intervention. This automatic failover was possible because Logpush delivery is stateless, as customer destinations do not care which centralized data center pushes the logs. Analytics was trickier. Unlike stateless logs, ClickHouse clusters in both regions still need a full copy of non-regional data to allow instant, independent query failover. The breakthrough was decoupling pipeline transit from database redundancy: 1. Shared Ingest Pool: We adopted Logpush’s model to the analytics streams. Logfwdr dispatches each event exactly once across wide-area transit to whichever centralized receiver is available. 2. Late Replication from centralized regions: Instead of replicating traffic at source, replication happens as late as possible in the pipeline. Data lands in our distributed buffering layer, Buftee, and remote inserters stream cross-data-center copies downstream. 3. Resilient Failure Handling: If a centralized region goes down, Logfwdrs immediately routes all non-regional traffic to the surviving region. If the inter-data center connection blips, each cluster continues ingesting its local share without backpressure; remote inserters catch up from Buftee's retention buffer once the backbone recovers. For the datasets we migrated, the cutover eliminated approximately 43 GB/s of compressed transit traffic while adding only ~7 GB/s of cross-data-center replication on our pipeline. Two architectural factors explain this asymmetry: 1. Replication happens downstream of sampling : In the old model, Logfwdrs transmitted two copies of raw, unsampled events over wide-area transit. In the new model, Logfwdrs send a single copy to centralized receivers, which immediately apply sampling before buffering into Buftee, carrying only this already-compacted stream. 2. Better compression through uniform partitioning : Data at source is fragmented across thousands of individual servers. After centralization, streams are aggregated and partitioned into uniform batches over wider time windows. This structural uniformity allows compression algorithms to achieve dramatically higher compression ratios than Logfwdr transit batches ever could. Overall, this was a net reduction of 36 GB/s across wide-area networks. We rolled this out initially to two datasets, HTTP analytics and Ready-Analytics, our in-house one-click analytics product . We’ve been actively migrating more datasets to this load-balanced architecture since the spring. Sampling from the get-go Another strategy we employed was further expanding our sampling mechanism so that we pulled critical processing earlier into the pipeline. Sampling was already used in our centralized services, particularly the receivers, easing pressure on downstream systems. We can be more resource efficient if we send less data downstream (without sacrificing data quality). The solution here was to simply sample in Logfwdr, in addition to maintaining the sampling in centralized receivers. How the sampling algorithm works here, in short, is each dataset has a key that producer teams have chosen to index and sample the data. When sampling, we first shuffle the records for each key to eliminate bias . Then, for each group of records, we select a sample size equal to the square root of the total count of the records. The result is a representative sample, whether sampled once or twice. To produce estimates, we scale calculations against the sample rate. For example, if we sample 10 out of 100 records, the sample rate would be 10/100, and the unbiased estimate of the original count would be 10*10 = 100. To ensure this approach was working well, we compared the number of rows written to ClickHouse against the estimated sum for total count using a variety of keys across a variety of traffic footprints, so that “least seen” keys to “most seen” keys were captured across the spectrum. The result is that for keys with more data, the sample rate decreases. However, keys with less data were sampled comparably. Thus, we still kept a representative sample while delivering and storing fewer events. We’re not compromising the quality of data delivered, even when we deliver less in quantity. If we look at this more closely, using power laws, we can observe that the double-sampled (red) grows at roughly x 0.319 v. sampled-once/control (blue) at x 0.485 . Now, it will only store roughly 4x the number of rows. Concretely, a total of 11.6 million events is represented by 18k rows in ClickHouse as opposed to 79k. Double sampling attenuates storage of the “most seen” keys, while still retaining the same detail per event for “least seen” keys. We initially implemented this strategy against three of our top datasets. Every single one at least halved the amount of compressed data we were originally sending on the wire to centralized receivers. That’s 25GB/s altogether, or over 2PB/day. Aggregating Cloudflare offers several analytics datasets built on rollups: aggregates of the raw events computed at ingest time. This makes the opposite tradeoff to sampling: rather than answering any question approximately, we answer a fixed set of questions exactly, provided we choose the dimensions and metrics up front. For example, in the HTTP dataset, we measure the number of unique occurrences of IP addresses during a given minute rather than the individual IPs themselves. Another example is we sum the total number of GET, POST, PUT, etc. requests for a given domain, for that minute, grouped by the HTTP method. None of these computations actually necessitate waiting until the tail-end of the pipeline to start calculating. Historically, this aggregation occurred towards the end of the pipeline, inside the inserters which read from Buftee and insert into ClickHouse. Decentralizing this aggregation was an opportunity to spread out load and reduce the amount of data we centralize. Hence, we built an aggregation functionality that is utilized every step of the way, creating repeated opportunities to combine matching partial aggregates as data converges. Much like sampling, records are grouped by a key, which determines which records can be combined. We aggregate on each instance of Logfwdr. We aggregate again after the partially aggregated events reach the centralized receivers, which push these re-aggregated events onto dedicated partitioned buffers. Because these buffers bring together records from multiple receivers, we aggregate another time after they’ve been read in batches by the ClickHouse inserters. Finally, we aggregate in ClickHouse with aggregating table engines. The first dataset we rolled this out to was for the HTTP traffic. In just this one dataset alone, we dropped from 9+ GB/s to <2 GB/s in compressed bytes traffic. Even though this is currently the highest cardinality dataset, the aggregations on it still gave us an approximate 80% reduction on the wire. This aggregation feature is powerful for datasets that can collapse easily, especially for use cases like usage metrics where accuracy on the sums and counts is paramount. It also means we can offer producer teams another option to reduce resource usage besides sampling, which we did. Like Ready-Analytics, we created a generic in-house one-click aggregating analytics product, called Ready-Aggregates. As we continue to iterate on this new feature in the pipeline, we expect to see savings continue to mount. Impact The starkest proof of this exponential growth is how rapidly traffic growth consumes headroom. Take Ready-Analytics for example, where two of the three mechanisms, load balancing and sampling techniques, were applied. In mid-May, load balancing dropped traffic by 50%, plunging from ~26 GB/s to ~13 GB/s. Two months later, traffic had already started surging back up to ~20 GB/s. That’s about half of the reduction, erased by organic traffic growth. We then created even more headroom by reducing this dataset’s throughput rate to the single digits, ~8GB/, when sampling rolled out. Without both interventions, Ready-Analytics alone would have breached 60 GB/s by September. By processing less data in centralized data centers, we also save a significant amount of CPUs and memory. We’ve halved the amount of data we’d be processing in another half a decade’s time. More than 20% of the web sits behind Cloudflare’s network, and our team, the Data team, owns the data pipeline responsible for plumbing that data (and more) from our global network to applicable central data centers. The Cloudflare network is a globally distributed system supporting tens of thousands of servers. Data that power Cloudflare Logs, SQL API, observability, internal analytics, and more flow through this network and use our data pipeline to serve customers.

In May of this year, we were providing data delivery at roughly two billion events per second. This includes customer traffic as well as data sent from internal teams. Year after year, we tackle the same problem — exponential traffic growth against linear hardware growth. We have to react to this increase in order to keep resource costs under control. Over the past five years, we’ve made various improvements to compensate for the data volume increase in comparison to hardware allocation, equivalent to deferring two and a half years of hardware expansion. This post details those changes: breaking up our monolithic data schema in 2022, adjusting compression in 2024, rearchitecting pipeline replication in spring 2026, decentralizing sampling in summer 2026, and introducing aggregations into the pipeline in fall 2026.

Background

Our pipeline starts with an internal service called Logfwdr, where we collect from highly distributed data sources (think: Workers, FL). We then feed this data to a set of centralized receivers, which eventually push them onto our buffering system, Buftee. Consumers fetch data from Buftee and distribute data to their final destinations, like ClickHouse, which we rely on heavily.

Unpacking the monolith

In 2022, we dismantled our one and only schema. Previously, there was a single stream packed with every product's fields, forcing Cloudflare-internal consumers to ingest everything and demux or discard records via filters. At the time, most of Cloudflare’s data products were built on HTTP, Security and CDN metadata. In 2021, our message schema looked like this:

Some fields here belonged under the same product, but some were completely irrelevant to each other. The hypothesis was that none of these teams require 100% of fields in the monolithic schema. In other words, we can create small messages for each product’s required fields. Although we were going to duplicate fields, some of them in every message, replacing this firehose with product-specific schemas actually reduced the backbone bandwidth usage by 35-40%, knocking out roughly a year’s worth of compressed traffic growth.

Compression

By 2024, as traffic steadily grew, we were tackling network congestion issues on a daily basis. To react to this, we changed our compression algorithm from LZ4 to zstd. We had already experimented with zstd compression before, but we noticed a higher CPU usage at the time. Therefore, we were careful to track the metrics to ensure the trade-off was worth it.

Initially, we rolled this change out to a few servers. To our relief, we didn’t observe a noticeable difference in CPU usage.

With more confidence, we gradually rolled out to our entire fleet, which also showed little impact to CPUs. In the end, there was nearly a 40% reduction in compressed traffic throughput. The uncompressed bytes remained at the same growth, meaning we could support more than 1.5x the amount of traffic with the same size pipe. Or another way to put it, the estimated growth-equivalent reductions put us at about 10 months prior.

Now, in 2026, we attempted three strategies to reduce uncompressed bytes (and thus, compressed bytes).

Load balancing

To make analytics resilient against regional disasters, our systems require redundant data to be stored in multiple centralized regions (data subject to Customer Metadata Boundaries is stored strictly within its designated region). Historically, the simplest way to achieve disaster resilience was double-writing: Logfwdr transmitted two full copies of every non-regional analytics event — one to each centralized region. Each region then independently processed a complete copy through to ClickHouse. We also apply sampling in each region, an incredibly scalable technique that works for all volumes of data during any traffic conditions. We downsample high-volume traffic while rare events are preserved.

This infrastructure was manageable when only a handful of streams used secondary regions. However, as we expanded disaster resilience across almost all analytics streams, Logfwdr traffic doubled across the board. Sending every event, twice, over wide-area transit was unsustainable against our exponential traffic growth.

We had already tackled a similar challenge for Logpush. For Logpush, Logfwdr treats the centralized data centers as a unified, shared pool of receivers: each message is sent to only one region, failing over to another destination if a machine or facility is unreachable. That model had already proven its worth during large incidents, shifting traffic seamlessly from one location to another without human intervention. This automatic failover was possible because Logpush delivery is stateless, as customer destinations do not care which centralized data center pushes the logs.

Analytics was trickier. Unlike stateless logs, ClickHouse clusters in both regions still need a full copy of non-regional data to allow instant, independent query failover. The breakthrough was decoupling pipeline transit from database redundancy:

1. Shared Ingest Pool: We adopted Logpush’s model to the analytics streams. Logfwdr dispatches each event exactly once across wide-area transit to whichever centralized receiver is available.

2. Late Replication from centralized regions: Instead of replicating traffic at source, replication happens as late as possible in the pipeline. Data lands in our distributed buffering layer, Buftee, and remote inserters stream cross-data-center copies downstream.

3. Resilient Failure Handling: If a centralized region goes down, Logfwdrs immediately routes all non-regional traffic to the surviving region. If the inter-data center connection blips, each cluster continues ingesting its local share without backpressure; remote inserters catch up from Buftee's retention buffer once the backbone recovers.

For the datasets we migrated, the cutover eliminated approximately 43 GB/s of compressed transit traffic while adding only ~7 GB/s of cross-data-center replication on our pipeline. Two architectural factors explain this asymmetry:

1. Replication happens downstream of sampling: In the old model, Logfwdrs transmitted two copies of raw, unsampled events over wide-area transit. In the new model, Logfwdrs send a single copy to centralized receivers, which immediately apply sampling before buffering into Buftee, carrying only this already-compacted stream.

2. Better compression through uniform partitioning: Data at source is fragmented across thousands of individual servers. After centralization, streams are aggregated and partitioned into uniform batches over wider time windows. This structural uniformity allows compression algorithms to achieve dramatically higher compression ratios than Logfwdr transit batches ever could.

Overall, this was a net reduction of 36 GB/s across wide-area networks. We rolled this out initially to two datasets, HTTP analytics and Ready-Analytics, our in-house one-click analytics product.

We’ve been actively migrating more datasets to this load-balanced architecture since the spring.

Finally, we aggregate in ClickHouse with aggregating table engines.

The first dataset we rolled this out to was for the HTTP traffic. In just this one dataset alone, we dropped from 9+ GB/s to <2 GB/s in compressed bytes traffic. As we continue to iterate on this new feature in the pipeline, we expect to see savings continue to mount.

Impact

The starkest proof of this exponential growth is how rapidly traffic growth consumes headroom.

items.title: Danfoss Refrigeration Hack Update – 4,980 Hosts Found Exposed to Internet
items.summary: France accounts for more than half of the internet-facing hosts found in a Shodan search for Danfoss web pages, following a cyberattack that disrupted supermarket refrigeration systems . An update from International Cyber Digest on October 13 reports a total of 4,980 hosts identified, with 2,911 located in France and 517 in South Africa. These findings raise new concerns about exposed cooling controls; however, they do not confirm that every listed host has been hacked. According to Shodan, Germany ranks third with 171 results, followed by Portugal with 158 and the United States with 141. Poland, Belgium, Sweden, Spain, and the Netherlands also appear among the leading countries. France represents roughly 58% of the reported total. International Cyber Digest estimates that around eight in ten matching hosts are in Europe. Danfoss Refrigeration Hack Update The search looks for Danfoss references in web content, not proof that every result is a vulnerable refrigeration controller. A separate screenshot shows 4,551 results from a more filtered search. Neither image provides firmware versions, confirms successful attacks against individual hosts, or establishes how many supermarkets each controller serves. The exposure update follows attacks overnight between October 11 and October 12. Reports describe attackers remotely triggering defrost functions at French supermarkets, leaving chilled and frozen goods spoiled. Cybersecurity News previously covered the supermarket fridge attacks , including reports of temperatures reaching 50°C. Those temperature reports should not be treated as measurements from every affected store. France’s CERT-FR confirmed numerous compromises involving Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC devices in an October 12 alert . The agency instructed operators to disconnect the systems or filter access. Danfoss told news outlets that affected refrigeration management systems were running outdated firmware and repeated its advice to update supported equipment and replace legacy systems. International Cyber Digest also shared a claim that affected systems used the username admin and a password that changed daily to the current date. Published technical research supports a narrower explanation. UPDATE regarding the Danfoss refrigerators hack: More than half of the world's internet-facing systems are in France. Of 4,980 hosts with Danfoss on their web pages, 2,911 are French. South Africa is second with 517. Roughly 8 in 10 are in Europe, from Portugal to Sweden. https://t.co/ka1AzkNDBB pic.twitter.com/ogUwrTqlWi — International Cyber Digest (@IntCyberDigest) October 13, 2026 Claroty’s Team82 found a hidden, date-based authentication path in the AK-SM 800A platform that could bypass the configured administrator password. According to Team82, the controller generates a daily authentication code using its current date. Someone who reproduces the algorithm could generate an accepted code and obtain an administrative session. This is not the same as proving that the ordinary administrator password simply becomes the date. Investigators have not publicly established that this specific flaw enabled the supermarket attacks. The issue is tracked as CVE-2025-41450. CISA identifies affected AK-SM 8xxA versions as those earlier than R4.2, which addressed the authentication weakness. Its advisory also covers CVE-2025-41451, a command injection flaw in email alert settings, and CVE-2025-41452, a web server configuration weakness. Both affect versions before R4.3.1. Team82 explains that the command injection flaw could allow code execution after authentication. The configuration weakness could let an authenticated attacker alter web traffic handling or disrupt the management interface. These findings show possible attack paths, not a confirmed account of how the French incident unfolded. The AK-SM 800A manages multiple refrigeration devices through one web interface. Operators can adjust temperature limits, schedules, alarms, and user accounts. That central role makes exposed management access especially risky because changes can affect physical cooling operations, rather than only digital records. Similar concerns appear in Cybersecurity News coverage of internet-exposed cooling and power controllers . Operators should also remove direct internet exposure, separate control networks from business networks, and use protected remote access. Patching remains essential, but access restrictions are equally important while teams assess, repair, or replace affected equipment. Danfoss told news outlets that affected refrigeration management systems were running outdated firmware and repeated its advice to update supported equipment and replace legacy systems.

— International Cyber Digest (@IntCyberDigest) October 13, 2026

Claroty’s Team82 found a hidden, date-based authentication path in the AK-SM 800A platform that could bypass the configured administrator password.

According to Team82, the controller generates a daily authentication code using its current date. Someone who reproduces the algorithm could generate an accepted code and obtain an administrative session.

This is not the same as proving that the ordinary administrator password simply becomes the date. Investigators have not publicly established that this specific flaw enabled the supermarket attacks.

The issue is tracked as CVE-2025-41450. CISA identifies affected AK-SM 8xxA versions as those earlier than R4.2, which addressed the authentication weakness.

Its advisory also covers CVE-2025-41451, a command injection flaw in email alert settings, and CVE-2025-41452, a web server configuration weakness. Both affect versions before R4.3.1.

Operators should also remove direct internet exposure, separate control networks from business networks, and use protected remote access. Patching remains essential, but access restrictions are equally important while teams assess, repair, or replace affected equipment. For retailers, the immediate priority is restoring safe cooling without leaving the same access open.

CISA Warns of Hackers Exploiting Two Citrix NetScaler 0-Days to Execute Code Remotely
items.summary: Threat actors are actively exploiting two critical zero-day vulnerabilities in Citrix NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway appliances, allowing them to execute code remotely on exposed systems. The flaws, tracked as CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772 , received a CVSS v4 severity score of 9.5 out of 10 and have been added to the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. CISA confirmed that it received reports and partner intelligence showing global exploitation activity. Citrix released emergency updates after confirming that exploitation had occurred against unpatched, customer-managed NetScaler deployments. The affected products are often placed at the network edge to provide application delivery, load balancing, VPN access, and secure remote access. That position makes a compromised appliance highly valuable to threat actors because it can sit between internet users and internal company systems. CVE-2026-88771 is an improper input validation issue that can allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to run arbitrary commands on a vulnerable NetScaler ADC or Gateway. It affects all vulnerable deployments, including devices using the default configuration. No optional feature needs to be enabled for the flaw to be reachable, making it the broader of the two issues. Citrix said the vulnerability has a low attack complexity rating, meaning a threat actor does not need an account or user interaction to begin exploitation. The second flaw, CVE-2026-88772, is a memory overflow vulnerability that can lead to remote code execution or denial-of-service conditions. Unlike CVE-2026-88771, this issue requires Datagram Transport Layer Security, or DTLS, to be enabled. DTLS is enabled by default on NetScaler VPN virtual servers unless administrators have explicitly turned it off. This makes remote-access deployments a key area for security teams to review. Citrix has provided configuration checks that can help administrators determine whether DTLS is active on a NetScaler virtual server. Both zero-days were disclosed on September 27, 2026, alongside six other NetScaler flaws. Citrix confirmed that attackers were already exploiting the two remote code execution issues before it made fixes public. CISA Warns of Two Citrix NetScaler 0-Days Security teams should treat the release as an active incident response matter rather than a routine patching task. Cyber Security News previously reported on Citrix’s confirmation of the two NetScaler zero-days , including the risks facing internet-exposed ADC and Gateway appliances. The vendor’s security bulletin lists NetScaler ADC and Gateway 14.1 releases before 14.1-73.37 and 13.1 releases before 13.1-64.23 as vulnerable. NetScaler ADC 14.1-FIPS builds before 14.1-73.37 FIPS and 13.1-FIPS or NDcPP builds before 13.1-37.279 are also affected. Secure Private Access Hybrid customers using vulnerable NetScaler instances must upgrade those instances as well. Citrix-managed cloud services are not covered by this bulletin because Cloud Software Group applies updates to those services directly. Administrators should identify every customer-managed NetScaler ADC and Gateway system, especially appliances reachable from the public internet, and upgrade to the fixed releases as soon as operationally possible. Citrix recommends 14.1-73.37 or later for the 14.1 branch and 13.1-64.23 or later for the 13.1 branch. FIPS and NDcPP deployments need their matching patched releases. Organizations should also check whether CVE-2026-88772 applies by reviewing DTLS-enabled VPN and other virtual server settings. According to CISA , patching alone may not remove the risk where a device was already compromised. CISA has advised organizations to look for signs of compromise before applying updates and to send NetScaler logs to a central SIEM or log-retention platform, since local appliance logs can rotate quickly and overwrite evidence. CISA also published a Sigma detection rule resource to support threat hunting for suspicious NetScaler activity. Where compromise is suspected, organizations should first preserve evidence, including system snapshots, support bundles, memory data where appropriate, and remote syslog records. Citrix advises isolating the affected appliance, changing credentials and stored secrets, revoking certificates and private keys, investigating connected systems, and rebuilding from a known-good backup that predates the suspected compromise. Restored passwords, key-encryption keys, and SSL certificates should then be rotated. The situation has expanded beyond the initial two flaws. CISA updated its alert on October 9 to include CVE-2026-107406 and to stress prompt updates for CVE-2026-88771 through CVE-2026-88779. CVE-2026-88779, a separate actively exploited SAML-related NetScaler issue, can cause denial of service and may be used to force a reboot that helps execute code previously injected through exploitation of CVE-2026-88771. Cyber Security News also covered the actively exploited NetScaler SAML zero-day , which requires affected organizations to apply a newer set of NetScaler updates. For defenders, the immediate priority is clear: patch exposed NetScaler systems, preserve logs before making major changes, review authentication and administrative activity, and assume that a vulnerable internet-facing device may have been probed or compromised. Threat actors are actively exploiting two critical zero-day vulnerabilities in Citrix NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway appliances, allowing them to execute code remotely on exposed systems.

The flaws, tracked as CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772, received a CVSS v4 severity score of 9.5 out of 10 and have been added to the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

CISA confirmed that it received reports and partner intelligence showing global exploitation activity. Citrix released emergency updates after confirming that exploitation had occurred against unpatched, customer-managed NetScaler deployments. The affected products are often placed at the network edge to provide application delivery, load balancing, VPN access, and secure remote access.

That position makes a compromised appliance highly valuable to threat actors because it can sit between internet users and internal company systems.

CVE-2026-88771 is an improper input validation issue that can allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to run arbitrary commands on a vulnerable NetScaler ADC or Gateway.

It affects all vulnerable deployments, including devices using the default configuration. No optional feature needs to be enabled for the flaw to be reachable, making it the broader of the two issues. Citrix said the vulnerability has a low attack complexity rating, meaning a threat actor does not need an account or user interaction to begin exploitation.

The second flaw, CVE-2026-88772, is a memory overflow vulnerability that can lead to remote code execution or denial-of-service conditions. Unlike CVE-2026-88771, this issue requires Datagram Transport Layer Security, or DTLS, to be enabled.

DTLS is enabled by default on NetScaler VPN virtual servers unless administrators have explicitly turned it off. This makes remote-access deployments a key area for security teams to review.

Citrix has provided configuration checks that can help administrators determine whether DTLS is active on a NetScaler virtual server. Both zero-days were disclosed on September 27, 2026, alongside six other NetScaler flaws. Citrix confirmed that attackers were already exploiting the two remote code execution issues before it made fixes public.

CISA Warns of Two Citrix NetScaler 0-Days

Security teams should treat the release as an active incident response matter rather than a routine patching task. Cyber Security News previously reported on Citrix’s confirmation of the two NetScaler zero-days, including the risks facing internet-exposed ADC and Gateway appliances.

The vendor’s security bulletin lists NetScaler ADC and Gateway 14.1 releases before 14.1-73.37 and 13.1 releases before 13.1-64.23 as vulnerable. NetScaler ADC 14.1-FIPS builds before 14.1-73.37 FIPS and 13.1-FIPS or NDcPP builds before 13.1-37.279 are also affected.

Secure Private Access Hybrid customers using vulnerable NetScaler instances must upgrade those instances as well. Citrix-managed cloud services are not covered by this bulletin because Cloud Software Group applies updates to those services directly.

Administrators should identify every customer-managed NetScaler ADC and Gateway system, especially appliances reachable from the public internet, and upgrade to the fixed releases as soon as operationally possible.

Citrix recommends 14.1-73.37 or later for the 14.1 branch and 13.1-64.23 or later for the 13.1 branch. FIPS and NDcPP deployments need their matching patched releases. Organizations should also check whether CVE-2026-88772 applies by reviewing DTLS-enabled VPN and other virtual server settings.

According to CISA, patching alone may not remove the risk where a device was already compromised. CISA has advised organizations to look for signs of compromise before applying updates and to send NetScaler logs to a central SIEM or log-retention platform, since local appliance logs can rotate quickly and overwrite evidence. CISA also published a Sigma detection rule resource to support threat hunting for suspicious NetScaler activity.

Where compromise is suspected, organizations should first preserve evidence, including system snapshots, support bundles, memory data where appropriate, and remote syslog records.

Citrix advises isolating the affected appliance, changing credentials and stored secrets, revoking certificates and private keys, investigating connected systems, and rebuilding from a known-good backup that predates the suspected compromise.

Restored passwords, key-encryption keys, and SSL certificates should then be rotated. The situation has expanded beyond the initial two flaws. CISA updated its alert on October 9 to include CVE-2026-107406 and to stress prompt updates for CVE-2026-88771 through CVE-2026-88779.

CVE-2026-88779, a separate actively exploited SAML-related NetScaler issue, can cause denial of service and may be used to force a reboot that helps execute code previously injected through exploitation of CVE-2026-88771.

Cyber Security News also covered the actively exploited NetScaler SAML zero-day, which requires affected organizations to apply a newer set of NetScaler updates.

For defenders, the immediate priority is clear: patch exposed NetScaler systems, preserve logs before making major changes, review authentication and administrative activity, and assume that a vulnerable internet-facing device may have been probed or compromised.

An EDR alert reveals an attack. But can it tell the full story? Discover how to reconstruct the attack timeline.

items.title: Threat Intelligence Guide for US SOC Teams and CISOs: How to Choose the Right Solution
items.summary: Choosing an enterprise threat intelligence solution is about more than just data volume or integrations. The right provider should deliver relevant intelligence, fit existing workflows, and help security teams investigate threats faster. While SOCs may prioritize rapid investigation and enrichment at scale, MSSPs may focus more on multi-tenancy and customer separation. This enterprise threat intelligence buying guide covers the key criteria to consider, including intelligence quality, integrations, data privacy, scalability, and proof-of-concept testing. Start With Your Security Team’s Requirements The first step in threat intelligence vendor selection is understanding what your security team needs intelligence to accomplish, rather than comparing feature lists. Some organizations may prioritize faster alert investigation and enrichment, while others need intelligence for threat hunting, malware analysis, or proactive monitoring. MSSPs may also require strong customer separation and efficient multi-tenant workflows. Start by identifying the teams, workflows, and data involved, then define your threat intelligence requirements around factors such as intelligence freshness, investigation context, API capacity, integrations, privacy, automation, and access management. Clear requirements make it easier to focus on capabilities that directly support your security operation. Mirage2FA phishing kit detonated inside ANY.RUN’s Interactive Sandbox For teams that need both intelligence and hands-on analysis, it can also be useful to consider how threat intelligence connects with malware and phishing investigation. ANY.RUN’s Int eractive Sandbox provides an environment for analyzing threats in real time, with capabilities including interactive analysis, SOC-ready reporting, and integrations through API, SDK, and security standards. Its virtual machines start in under 10 seconds, with reports available in about 40 seconds. Look at Threat Intelligence Quality and Context The size of an intelligence database doesn’t necessarily determine its value. During evaluation, consider the quality and sources of the data, how quickly it becomes available, how indicators are validated, and how much context accompanies each result. This is especially important for threat intelligence aggregation. Combining multiple sources can improve coverage, but may also introduce outdated, duplicate, or conflicting data. Without effective filtering and context, more data can simply create more noise. Analysts often need more than a malicious or benign verdict. Details such as related domains, URLs, files, malware families, infrastructure, and historical activity can help determine an indicator’s relevance. Threat intelligence enrichment provides analysts with the context needed to assess threats and determine what to investigate next. For example, ANY.RUN’s Threat Intelligence Lookup (TI Lookup) lets analysts search indicators and event fields and investigate relationships between domains, IPs, URLs, hashes, files, TTPs, and other data. It delivers each result in about 2 seconds and connects threat intelligence with data from sandbox research sessions, giving analysts additional context for investigations. TI Lookup delivers real-time threat intelligence TI Lookup draws on threat intelligence contributed through investigations from 16,000 organizations and more than 700,000 analysts, providing additional context for investigations. It delivers fresh, up-to-date intelligence on the latest malware and phishing attacks, helping security teams stay informed about emerging threats and attack trends. Tap into threat intelligence from 16K+ organizations to stay ahead of emerging threats. Boost DR by 36% and cut MTTR by 21 mins per case. Integrate ANY.RUN In addition, Threat Intelligence Reports (TI Reports) can provide another layer of context by summarizing emerging threats, attack techniques, malware activity, and relevant indicators. When evaluating a provider, consider whether reports are timely, well-sourced, actionable, and easy for analysts to connect with ongoing investigations. US threat landscape insights in ANY.RUN’s TI Reports Prioritize Fresh Intelligence Threat intelligence can lose relevance over time, especially when used to identify active infrastructure or support automated detection. When evaluating a provider, consider how quickly new intelligence becomes available and how outdated indicators are identified, updated, or retired. Fresh data helps teams respond to current activity, while historical visibility allows analysts to investigate whether an indicator or related infrastructure has appeared before. The right balance depends on your use case. Real-time alert enrichment may require frequent updates, while threat hunting may place greater value on extensive historical context. Look for clear information on how intelligence is timestamped, validated, updated, and maintained, as these factors directly affect its value in investigations and detection workflows. ANY.RUN’s Threat Intelligence Feeds (TI Feeds) can support these requirements by providing live malicious IPs, domains, and URLs enriched with sandbox analysis. TI Feeds continuously update their data, with 99% of unique, high-confidence IOCs undergoing validation before being added. ANY.RUN TI Feeds help detect and block emerging threats Evaluate Correlation, Not Just Individual Indicators An indicator is often just the starting point of an investigation. Its real value increases when analysts can connect it to related infrastructure, files, malware, and other activity. Threat intelligence correlation helps uncover these relationships. For example, a suspicious domain may be linked to an IP address, URL, malicious file, or malware family, giving analysts a broader view of the threat rather than a single isolated data point. This goes beyond IOC management, which focuses on tracking, validating, and distributing indicators. For more complex investigations, analysts also need to understand how indicators are connected and what those relationships reveal about the activity behind them. When evaluating a solution, test common investigation scenarios and see how easily analysts can pivot between related intelligence. The goal is to determine whether the available context can reduce investigation time and manual research. Strengthen your SOC with ANY.RUN. Investigate threats faster, turn analysis into actionable intelligence, and streamline your response. Contact us Assess Integration Options Threat intelligence should fit into the security workflows your organization already uses. Enterprise teams may need intelligence to move between SIEM, SOAR, EDR/XDR, firewalls, case-management systems, and other security tools. Integration should therefore be part of the procurement process, not an afterthought. ANY.RUN solutions deliver measurable outcomes in threat detection and hunting ANY.RUN integrates with existing security environments through APIs, SDKs, and ready-made integrations, helping teams bring threat analysis and shared context into their established workflows. Beyond API availability, consider request limits, quotas, bulk operations, response times, authentication, SDK support, and automation capabilities, especially when handling thousands of enrichment requests daily. Consider STIX/TAXII Support STIX/TAXII support can simplify the exchange of structured threat intelligence between security systems and reduce custom integration work. TI Feeds support STIX/TAXII alongside API and SDK integrations, making it easier to incorporate intelligence into existing workflows. During a proof of concept, test whether the data arrives in the expected format, includes the required context, updates at the right frequency, and works reliably with your existing systems. Plan for Scale From the Beginning A service that works for a small security team may face different demands as usage expands. More analysts and automated enrichment can increase investigation volume and API requests, while MSSPs may need to support multiple customer environments at once. Consider user management, permissions, workspace separation, auditability, API capacity, and data volumes when assessing scalability. MSSPs should also look closely at multi-tenancy to ensure customer data remains properly separated. ANY.RUN’s MSSP offering supports high-volume workflows with automation, standardized reporting, API/SDK access, and capabilities designed for multiple customer environments. Interactive Sandbox, TI Lookup, and TI Feeds deliver 3x better SOC performance. Strengthen MSSP capabilities for better client results with ANY.RUN Scalability also means keeping the service manageable as more teams, analysts, and customers rely on it. Cut Tier 1 workload by up to 20%. Increase analyst capacity, streamline operations, and improve service performance. Boost MSSP efficiency Test the Analyst Experience Threat intelligence should help analysts investigate threats efficiently. Even extensive intelligence can be difficult to use if analysts have to navigate multiple disconnected workflows. During evaluation, pay attention to search, filtering, historical visibility, pivoting, and how easily analysts can move between related indicators. A practical test is to give analysts a familiar investigation scenario involving a suspicious domain, IP, URL, or file hash. See how quickly they can determine its relevance, identify related activity, and gather enough context to decide what to investigate next. Interactive Sandbox can also support hands-on malware and phishing analysis, allowing analysts to interact with threats in live virtual environments and access findings such as IOCs and TTPs. For enterprise SOCs, 95% of SOC teams speed up threat investigations, while 94% of users achieve faster triage. Determine the Need for Dark Web Monitoring Dark web monitoring can help organizations identify leaked credentials, exposed corporate information, or brand-related threats. Rather than treating it as a must-have feature, assess whether it addresses a specific security requirement. Consider source coverage, validation, detection speed, and how easily analysts can act on the findings. Use Real Data in the Proof of Concept A proof of concept should reflect real security workflows, not just provider demonstrations. Use representative historical alerts, including malicious, benign, and ambiguous cases. Measure outcomes such as investigation time, enrichment quality, false-positive reduction, manual effort, search performance, and API reliability. If automated enrichment is planned, test realistic request volumes to identify potential limitations before deployment. Review the Total Cost of Ownership The cost of a threat intelligence service extends beyond the subscription. Integration, maintenance, training, analyst time, infrastructure, and API usage can all add to the total. Review API limits and additional usage costs, and consider whether the service adds meaningful coverage or context to your existing intelligence sources. For example, TI Feeds help identify up to 58% more threats overall and offer a 21-minute reduction in MTTR per case. When assessing ROI, teams can compare metrics such as these with their own baseline investigation time, detection coverage, and analyst workload. Turn Requirements into a Practical Decision Once requirements and testing are complete, assess how well each offering fits your security workflows. Consider intelligence quality, freshness, enrichment, correlation, integration, automation, privacy, scalability, usability, and cost. The priorities will vary by organization and use case. An MSSP may focus more on multi-tenancy and API capacity, while an enterprise SOC may prioritize investigation speed and contextual enrichment. A threat intelligence procurement guide should help teams base their decision on requirements, testing, and measurable operational outcomes. Conclusion Choosing an enterprise threat intelligence offering starts with understanding your security requirements and use cases. Assess intelligence quality, freshness, context, enrichment, integrations, privacy, scalability, and automation, then validate those criteria with real-world testing. The goal is to turn threat intelligence into useful context that helps security teams investigate threats faster and reduce unnecessary work.

items.title: LiteLLM flaws let low-privileged users hijack AI gateway and steal provider keys
items.summary: Check Point Research has disclosed two high-risk vulnerabilities in LiteLLM, the open-source gateway that sits between enterprise applications and AI providers such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Google. The flaws could allow a user with minimal privileges to take full control of the gateway, read sensitive files, execute arbitrary code and harvest the API keys an organisation uses to access its AI providers. LiteLLM is downloaded around 97 million times a month and has more than 59,000 stars on GitHub. Both issues, tracked as CVE-2026-35029 and CVE-2026-59823 , are fixed in version 1.83.9. One endpoint, three attack paths The more serious flaw, CVE-2026-35029, is a missing authorisation check on LiteLLM’s /config/update endpoint, which controls the proxy’s runtime configuration. Unlike other administrative endpoints, it did not verify that the caller held the PROXY_ADMIN role. Compounding this, any user who logs in through the LiteLLM dashboard is issued a session token tied to a special “litellm-dashboard” team, and those tokens are checked against a looser list of permitted UI routes. That list includes “/config”. Because the check uses simple prefix matching, requests to /config/update were allowed for any logged-in user, whatever their role. Testing against LiteLLM version 1.77.7, the researchers showed the flaw could be used to: Read arbitrary files , by injecting an environment variable that sets the path of the dashboard logo and pointing it at sensitive files such as /etc/passwd Take over the built-in admin account , by overwriting the UI_USERNAME and UI_PASSWORD variables and logging in with attacker-chosen credentials Execute remote code , by registering a “pass-through endpoint” that loads a Python module from an attacker-controlled S3 or GCS bucket, which LiteLLM then downloads and runs Stealing keys without touching the provider The second flaw, CVE-2026-59823, is a server-side request forgery (SSRF) issue in LiteLLM’s “Clientside LLM Credentials” feature. By passing a user_config parameter to the /chat/completions endpoint, an authenticated user could create a router pointing at their own server. Requests, along with the provider API keys attached to them, would then be sent to the attacker rather than to the AI provider. Check Point notes that this code path sidestepped restrictions LiteLLM already placed on client-supplied api_base and api_key parameters. The researchers also found that password hashes were exposed to low-privileged users and were stored without salting, using a single hash iteration. These issues duplicated an existing advisory, GHSA-69×8-hrgq-fjj8. Old bugs, bigger blast radius Check Point is clear that none of these are new classes of “AI” vulnerability. Missing authorisation checks, SSRF and unsafe dynamic module loading are all well understood. What raises the stakes is where they sit. An LLM gateway stores provider keys, manages user permissions and routes every prompt and response, making it a single point of compromise for an organisation’s AI estate. And because LiteLLM is embedded in many other AI platforms and internal tools, some organisations may be running it without realising. “The industry’s focus has largely been on securing AI models, but this research highlights an equally important reality: AI infrastructure is becoming a new critical layer of enterprise security,” said Mateo Rojas-Carulla, Head of Research, AI Agent Security at Check Point Software Technologies. “As organisations increasingly rely on gateways such as LiteLLM to connect applications, users and AI services, these platforms become attractive targets because they sit at the centre of trust.” “For LiteLLM users, the immediate priority is patching and reviewing access controls, but the broader lesson extends beyond a single product,” he added. “Attackers will naturally target the layer that gives them the greatest access with the least resistance.” What defenders should do Check Point recommends that organisations: Upgrade to LiteLLM 1.83.9 or later across every deployment, including instances embedded in other tools Audit gateway user accounts and remove any that are not needed Rotate AI provider API keys if there is any sign of unauthorised access before patching Test that limited roles are enforced in practice, not just on paper Bring LLM gateways into scope for regular security assessments The vulnerabilities were reported to LiteLLM’s maintainers through a coordinated disclosure process that began in October 2025. Full technical write-up: https://research.checkpoint.com/2026/when-llm-gateways-go-wrong-findings-from-litellm/

  • Execute remote code, by registering a “pass-through endpoint” that loads a Python module from an attacker-controlled S3 or GCS bucket, which LiteLLM then downloads and runs

Requests, along with the provider API keys attached to them, would then be sent to the attacker rather than to the AI provider.

Check Point notes that this code path sidestepped restrictions LiteLLM already placed on client-supplied api_base and api_key parameters.

The researchers also found that password hashes were exposed to low-privileged users and were stored without salting, using a single hash iteration. These issues duplicated an existing advisory, GHSA-69×8-hrgq-fjj8.

Old bugs, bigger blast radius

Check Point is clear that none of these are new classes of “AI” vulnerability. Missing authorisation checks, SSRF and unsafe dynamic module loading are all well understood. What raises the stakes is where they sit. An LLM gateway stores provider keys, manages user permissions and routes every prompt and response, making it a single point of compromise for an organisation’s AI estate. And because LiteLLM is embedded in many other AI platforms and internal tools, some organisations may be running it without realising.

“The industry’s focus has largely been on securing AI models, but this research highlights an equally important reality: AI infrastructure is becoming a new critical layer of enterprise security,” said Mateo Rojas-Carulla, Head of Research, AI Agent Security at Check Point Software Technologies. “As organisations increasingly rely on gateways such as LiteLLM to connect applications, users and AI services, these platforms become attractive targets because they sit at the centre of trust.”

“For LiteLLM users, the immediate priority is patching and reviewing access controls, but the broader lesson extends beyond a single product,” he added. “Attackers will naturally target the layer that gives them the greatest access with the least resistance.”

What defenders should do

Check Point recommends that organisations:

  • Upgrade to LiteLLM 1.83.9 or later across every deployment, including instances embedded in other tools
  • Audit gateway user accounts and remove any that are not needed
  • Rotate AI provider API keys if there is any sign of unauthorised access before patching
  • Test that limited roles are enforced in practice, not just on paper
  • Bring LLM gateways into scope for regular security assessments

The vulnerabilities were reported to LiteLLM’s maintainers through a coordinated disclosure process that began in October 2025.

Full technical write-up: https://research.checkpoint.com/2026/when-llm-gateways-go-wrong-findings-from-litellm/

items.title: Releasing the Cobalt Strike Beacon Corpus
items.summary: Authors: Yun Zheng Hu Introduction Today Fox-IT is publicly releasing its full Cobalt Strike Beacon Corpus, containing 56,843 raw beacons and their parsed configurations, from 190,182 sightings collected from 30,604 unique IP addresses running a Team Server (the Cobalt Strike command-and-control server that beacons connect back to) between 4 July 2018 and 29 September 2026, over eight years of beacon data. Eight years of collection captures things that can no longer be observed today, like the waves of cracked 4.0 builds or the adoption of leaked versions. By publishing the raw beacons alongside the parsed data, we keep that record available for anyone to study, long after the servers themselves are gone. What’s in the corpus The corpus is published on Hugging Face as two Parquet files: File Size Rows Contents beacons.parquet 52 MB 190,182 Every sighting of a beacon, with collection metadata, network context and the parsed beacon configuration. payloads.parquet 9.7 GB 56,843 The raw beacon payloads, wrapped in CaRT as an extra safety layer so the samples are neutered until you deliberately unpack them. All beacons were downloaded directly from internet-facing Team Servers, mostly on TCP ports 80 and 443 (HTTP and HTTPS) and UDP port 53 (DNS), with a small number on other ports. We deliberately didn’t include samples from other sources such as VirusTotal, so the corpus reflects the Cobalt Strike landscape as it was visible on the internet. How we collected it The collection method matches our 2022 post. We fingerprint likely Team Servers on the internet, then request a beacon payload from each one using a URI that passes Cobalt Strike’s checksum8 check. Every beacon that comes back is parsed with dissect.cobaltstrike , which decodes the configuration block. The result is stored as a sighting. Discovery : candidate hosts from our own internet-wide scanning. As in 2022, we’re keeping our fingerprints private so they stay effective; writing your own is left as an exercise for the reader. Download : x86 beacons over HTTP(S) and DNS. DNS : for DNS listeners we’re not publishing that fingerprint either, but it’s not rocket science. The beacon is fetched as a series of TXT record lookups sent over UDP port 53 directly to the Team Server’s DNS listener. Parse : Use dissect.cobaltstrike to parse the beacon and export the configuration Enrich : TLS certificate data captured at collection time (where available) and GeoIP/ASN via historical GeoIP databases . Note that there might be some small gaps in the collection due to automation issues that we did not catch in time. Getting started Most research only needs the beacons.parquet dataset. The payloads.parquet dataset containing raw beacon payloads is only required if you want to re-parse the beacons or look into the ones that failed parsing. I’m a big fan of DuckDB (and SQLite), and over time I’ve become fond of SQL for querying data as well. DuckDB is very fast, and AI assistants are very good at writing SQL queries. These days, that beats hand-writing pandas code and the matching matplotlib charts. That’s why I recommend exploring the data with DuckDB, for example in a Jupyter notebook. An example of using DuckDB to query the dataset on Hugging Face directly: SELECT watermark, count(*) AS sightings, count(DISTINCT collected_from_ip) AS servers, min(collected_on) AS first_seen, max(collected_on) AS last_seen FROM 'hf://datasets/fox-srt/cobaltstrike-beacon-corpus/data/beacons.parquet' GROUP BY watermark ORDER BY sightings DESC LIMIT 20; Take a look at our Jupyter notebook in the Hugging Face repository as a starting point. It contains every query and chart from the sections below, so you can rerun them or adapt them to your own research questions. A first look at the data Here are a few quick results to show what the corpus can answer. They’re a starting point, not a full analysis. As with our 2022 post, we invite researchers to explore the data; see also “Research ideas” below. Old versions never die Each Cobalt Strike release takes over from the last, but old versions linger. Cobalt Strike 4.0 dominated most of 2020, 4.1–4.2 drove the early 2021 peak of about 3,000 beacons a month, 4.3–4.4 led from mid-2021 through 2022, and 4.5–4.8 took over in 2023. Since 2024, 4.9 and 4.5–4.8 have shared the lead, while 4.10+ remains a small share. Volume has since dropped to around 200 beacons a month, partly because fewer servers stage their beacon, which brings us to the next graph. No beacon for you Our collection relies on beacon staging, meaning a Team Server can serve its beacon as a downloadable payload to anyone who requests the right URI or DNS record. Operators can turn this off (the host_stage option in the Malleable C2 profile), and disabling it is common OPSEC advice. To measure how much this affects our beacon collection, we counted two numbers per month: The unique Team Servers (ip:port) confirmed by our high-confidence HTTP fingerprint The unique Team Servers (ip:port) that handed out a beacon over HTTP(S) These are monthly totals, not a server-by-server match. On average, the Team Servers that handed out a beacon were only about 32% of those we fingerprinted, and that share has drifted down from around 40% in 2023 to 20–25% in 2026. In other words, because not every server hands out a beacon, the corpus shows only part of the Cobalt Strike landscape, and that part is getting smaller. Disabled beacon staging is the most likely reason, but not the only one. Servers can go offline between fingerprinting and download or block our scanners, and our fingerprint doesn’t catch every Team Server. The dashed sections mark months when beacon collection wasn’t running, because of an automation error that went unnoticed for a while. The short life of a Cobalt Strike Team Server The median Team Server was reachable for 14 days. 35% were seen on a single day only, just 14% were still serving a beacon after three months, and only 2% after a year. We identify a Team Server by its public key and C2 domains from the beacon configuration (or its IP address when the configuration contains no domains), so a server that moves to a new IP is still counted once. This allows us to measure how long a Team Server typically stays online. Identifying servers by public key alone or by ip:port gives almost the same result, a median lifetime of 14–15 days. These are first-to-last-sighting spans, so a server may have been online before our first and after our last sighting. Servers still active in the last 30 days are left out. It’s always DNS Most public scanning focuses only on HTTP(S) beacons, but we’ve also collected DNS beacons since 2020 (apart from the months when our automation broke). DNS beacons have declined much less steeply than HTTP(S) ones, perhaps because they get far less attention in public research and OPSEC advice, so fewer operators think to lock them down. After a peak in 2022, they have mostly hovered around 100 a month since 2024, with a median of 120 over the whole period. Parse me if you can The corpus also includes 128 unique beacons (0.23%) that we downloaded but couldn’t parse. Note that the corpus doesn’t contain HTML pages or other responses that were unlikely to be a beacon. We excluded those before publishing. At first glance, most are beacons with custom modifications that dissect.cobaltstrike can’t parse yet. And some payloads from the early years aren’t Cobalt Strike at all, but Metasploit Meterpreter payloads. We’ve deliberately left them in for researchers to analyse. You can find all unparsed beacons with: WHERE config_json IS NULL The unparsed count used to be higher, but we managed to bring that down. We noticed some operators customised their beacon configs, for example by shuffling the order of the configuration settings or changing their type values, which broke our parser (and probably most others). The corpus helped us find these cases, so we made the config scanning of dissect.cobaltstrike independent of layout and added many other features and fixes along the way. See the dissect.cobaltstrike v1.3.0 release notes . Research ideas Some other research questions that could be answered using the corpus: Clustering : Group operators by config features (watermark, SPAWNTO/PROCINJ hash, C2 profile, certificate, sleep/jitter, specific beacon modifications) Classification : Separate red team from criminal infrastructure. Build and publish labelled subsets. Infrastructure : Top hosting providers that are hosting a Cobalt Strike Team Server. Certificates : Pivot on x509 reuse across servers and time or find how many are running the default Cobalt Strike keystore certificate. Benchmarks : Use the corpus as a shared test set for config extractors and ML models. Parser failures : 128 beacons can’t be parsed by dissect.cobaltstrike . Figure out why. Over to you Eight years of Cobalt Strike beacons are now one download away on Hugging Face . Run your own queries, pick up one of the research ideas above or come up with your own, dig into the beacons we couldn’t parse, and share what you find. Before you start, read the Limitations section on the dataset card. The raw payloads are real Cobalt Strike beacons, so handle them like any other malware sample.
