And here it is, a large, consistent, long-running dataset for the infosec community to build on. The corpus includes the raw beacon payloads, not just our parsed output, so anyone can reproduce our results or improve on them.

We also see publishing this corpus as an act of preservation. C2 infrastructure is short-lived, as the median Team Server is reachable for just 14 days, and the beacons it serves vanish with it. Eight years of collection captures things that can no longer be observed today, like the waves of cracked 4.0 builds or the adoption of leaked versions. By publishing the raw beacons alongside the parsed data, we keep that record available for anyone to study, long after the servers themselves are gone.

What’s in the corpus

The corpus is published on Hugging Face as two Parquet files:

FileSizeRowsContentsbeacons.parquet52 MB190,182Every sighting of a beacon, with collection metadata, network context and the parsed beacon configuration.payloads.parquet9.7 GB56,843The raw beacon payloads, wrapped in CaRT as an extra safety layer so the samples are neutered until you deliberately unpack them.

All beacons were downloaded directly from internet-facing Team Servers, mostly on TCP ports 80 and 443 (HTTP and HTTPS) and UDP port 53 (DNS), with a small number on other ports. We deliberately didn’t include samples from other sources such as VirusTotal, so the corpus reflects the Cobalt Strike landscape as it was visible on the internet.

How we collected it

The collection method matches our 2022 post. We fingerprint likely Team Servers on the internet, then request a beacon payload from each one using a URI that passes Cobalt Strike’s checksum8 check. Every beacon that comes back is parsed with dissect.cobaltstrike, which decodes the configuration block. The result is stored as a sighting.

  • Discovery: candidate hosts from our own internet-wide scanning. As in 2022, we’re keeping our fingerprints private so they stay effective; writing your own is left as an exercise for the reader.
  • Download: x86 beacons over HTTP(S) and DNS.
  • DNS: for DNS listeners we’re not publishing that fingerprint either, but it’s not rocket science. The beacon is fetched as a series of TXT record lookups sent over UDP port 53 directly to the Team Server’s DNS listener.
  • Parse: Use dissect.cobaltstrike to parse the beacon and export the configuration
  • Enrich: TLS certificate data captured at collection time (where available) and GeoIP/ASN via historical GeoIP databases.

Note that there might be some small gaps in the collection due to automation issues that we did not catch in time.

Getting started

Most research only needs the beacons.parquet dataset. The payloads.parquet dataset containing raw beacon payloads is only required if you want to re-parse the beacons or look into the ones that failed parsing.

I’m a big fan of DuckDB (and SQLite), and over time I’ve become fond of SQL for querying data as well. DuckDB is very fast, and AI assistants are very good at writing SQL queries. These days, that beats hand-writing pandas code and the matching matplotlib charts. That’s why I recommend exploring the data with DuckDB, for example in a Jupyter notebook.

An example of using DuckDB to query the dataset on Hugging Face directly:

SELECT watermark,
       count(*)                          AS sightings,
       count(DISTINCT collected_from_ip) AS servers,
       min(collected_on)                 AS first_seen,
       max(collected_on)                 AS last_seen
FROM 'hf://datasets/fox-srt/cobaltstrike-beacon-corpus/data/beacons.parquet'
GROUP BY watermark
ORDER BY sightings DESC
LIMIT 20;

Take a look at our Jupyter notebook in the Hugging Face repository as a starting point. It contains every query and chart from the sections below, so you can rerun them or adapt them to your own research questions.

A first look at the data

Here are a few quick results to show what the corpus can answer. They’re a starting point, not a full analysis. As with our 2022 post, we invite researchers to explore the data; see also “Research ideas” below.

Old versions never die

Each Cobalt Strike release takes over from the last, but old versions linger. Cobalt Strike 4.0 dominated most of 2020, 4.1–4.2 drove the early 2021 peak of about 3,000 beacons a month, 4.3–4.4 led from mid-2021 through 2022, and 4.5–4.8 took over in 2023. Since 2024, 4.9 and 4.5–4.8 have shared the lead, while 4.10+ remains a small share. Volume has since dropped to around 200 beacons a month, partly because fewer servers stage their beacon, which brings us to the next graph.

No beacon for you

Our collection relies on beacon staging, meaning a Team Server can serve its beacon as a downloadable payload to anyone who requests the right URI or DNS record. Operators can turn this off (the host_stage option in the Malleable C2 profile), and disabling it is common OPSEC advice. To measure how much this affects our beacon collection, we counted two numbers per month:

  1. The unique Team Servers (ip:port) confirmed by our high-confidence HTTP fingerprint
  2. The unique Team Servers (ip:port) that handed out a beacon over HTTP(S)

These are monthly totals, not a server-by-server match. On average, the Team Servers that handed out a beacon were only about 32% of those we fingerprinted, and that share has drifted down from around 40% in 2023 to 20–25% in 2026. In other words, because not every server hands out a beacon, the corpus shows only part of the Cobalt Strike landscape, and that part is getting smaller. Disabled beacon staging is the most likely reason, but not the only one. Servers can go offline between fingerprinting and download or block our scanners, and our fingerprint doesn’t catch every Team Server.

The dashed sections mark months when beacon collection wasn’t running, because of an automation error that went unnoticed for a while.

The short life of a Cobalt Strike Team Server

The median Team Server was reachable for 14 days. 35% were seen on a single day only, just 14% were still serving a beacon after three months, and only 2% after a year.

We identify a Team Server by its public key and C2 domains from the beacon configuration (or its IP address when the configuration contains no domains), so a server that moves to a new IP is still counted once. This allows us to measure how long a Team Server typically stays online. Identifying servers by public key alone or by ip:port gives almost the same result, a median lifetime of 14–15 days. These are first-to-last-sighting spans, so a server may have been online before our first and after our last sighting. Servers still active in the last 30 days are left out.

It’s always DNS

Most public scanning focuses only on HTTP(S) beacons, but we’ve also collected DNS beacons since 2020 (apart from the months when our automation broke). DNS beacons have declined much less steeply than HTTP(S) ones, perhaps because they get far less attention in public research and OPSEC advice, so fewer operators think to lock them down. After a peak in 2022, they have mostly hovered around 100 a month since 2024, with a median of 120 over the whole period.

Parse me if you can

The corpus also includes 128 unique beacons (0.23%) that we downloaded but couldn’t parse. Note that the corpus doesn’t contain HTML pages or other responses that were unlikely to be a beacon. We excluded those before publishing. At first glance, most are beacons with custom modifications that dissect.cobaltstrike can’t parse yet. And some payloads from the early years aren’t Cobalt Strike at all, but Metasploit Meterpreter payloads. We’ve deliberately left them in for researchers to analyse. You can find all unparsed beacons with: WHERE config_json IS NULL

The unparsed count used to be higher, but we managed to bring that down. We noticed some operators customised their beacon configs, for example by shuffling the order of the configuration settings or changing their type values, which broke our parser (and probably most others). The corpus helped us find these cases, so we made the config scanning of dissect.cobaltstrike independent of layout and added many other features and fixes along the way. See the dissect.cobaltstrike v1.3.0 release notes.

Research ideas

Some other research questions that could be answered using the corpus:

  • Clustering: Group operators by config features (watermark, SPAWNTO/PROCINJ hash, C2 profile, certificate, sleep/jitter, specific beacon modifications)
  • Classification: Separate red team from criminal infrastructure. Build and publish labelled subsets.
  • Infrastructure: Top hosting providers that are hosting a Cobalt Strike Team Server.
  • Certificates: Pivot on x509 reuse across servers and time or find how many are running the default Cobalt Strike keystore certificate.
  • Benchmarks: Use the corpus as a shared test set for config extractors and ML models.
  • Parser failures: 128 beacons can’t be parsed by dissect.cobaltstrike. Figure out why.
Over to you

Eight years of Cobalt Strike beacons are now one download away on Hugging Face. Run your own queries, pick up one of the research ideas above or come up with your own, dig into the beacons we couldn’t parse, and share what you find.

Before you start, read the Limitations section on the dataset card. The raw payloads are real Cobalt Strike beacons, so handle them like any other malware sample.

items.title: XWorm Malware Can Spy Through Your Microphone and Hijack Logged-In Browser Sessions
items.summary: XWorm malware is moving beyond password theft, giving attackers tools to listen through infected computers, track their location, and control browsers where users are already logged in. Its growing plugin collection turns a compromised Windows device into both a spying tool and a route into online accounts, without requiring attackers to steal passwords first. The browser feature is especially concerning because it uses sessions that have already passed login checks. Instead of signing in from another computer, an attacker operates the victim’s browser directly. This can allow access to authenticated accounts without another multifactor authentication challenge, although it does not mean XWorm can defeat every possible security check. Researchers from Netskope Threat Labs identified four XWorm versions operating in the wild since their July 2025 report. In their latest XWorm research report, they recorded 1,236 detection events across more than 100 customer organizations during Q3 2026, four times the volume recorded in Q3 2025. These figures describe detections, not a confirmed count of unique infected devices. Financial services represented approximately 35% of affected customers, with activity concentrated in India, Brazil, Italy, Panama, and the United States. The findings extend earlier reporting on XWorm Windows script delivery , which showed how scripts and PowerShell helped install the malware while hiding its execution inside legitimate Windows processes. XWorm Malware Can Spy The HBrowser plugin, available since version 6, gives operators an interactive view of a victim’s running browser. An attacker selects a supported browser from the control panel, which sends an OpenBrowser command through XWorm’s command-and-control channel. The infected computer then accepts remote input and sends screenshots back to the operator. Mouse clicks, cursor movements, scrolling, keyboard input, and pasted text travel through the same AES-encrypted channel. This creates a working remote browser session rather than a simple collection of stolen browser files. Authenticated tabs become accessible, allowing attackers to use accounts while the victim’s existing login remains active. The distinction matters: this is not evidence that XWorm breaks MFA itself. It avoids a fresh login by working inside an already authenticated session. Related reporting on GhostProfile browser session hijacking describes another approach to live account access, but GhostProfile copies browser profiles on macOS, whereas Netskope describes XWorm controlling a running browser on Windows. XWorm’s Microphone plugin uses the NAudio library’s WaveInEvent function to capture sound from a recording device selected by the attacker. It first lists available devices through the MICCM command, then records 8 kHz, 16-bit mono audio in 500-millisecond buffers. Each buffer is compressed, encoded, encrypted, and streamed back through the control channel. Netskope reports roughly half a second of audio latency, with recording continuing while the operator keeps the session open. Commands named CLOSEMIC and ENDMIC stop capture or end the session. Webcam capture is also available on demand, widening the risk beyond stolen files to conversations and activity around the infected device. The Maps plugin changes a Windows location-consent registry value to Allow before requesting coordinates. Netskope observed this running without privilege escalation or a visible permission prompt. It calls GeoCoordinateWatcher.TryStart with a 15-second timeout and falls back to IP-based location lookup when GPS is unavailable. IP-derived location should not be confused with precise GPS coordinates. Leaked Builders Drive Continued Development The confirmed plugin count increased from 35 to 46 after Netskope’s July 2025 report. Researchers tracked V6.4, V6.5 “XWorm Reborn,” V7.2, and V7.4, with additions including Rootkit, SteamTokenRecovery, HRDP, Cmstp-Bypass, and ResetSurvival. This growth builds on XWorm defense evasion techniques , previously reported alongside changing loaders, script formats, and attempts to weaken Windows monitoring. A cracked builder appeared publicly in June 2025, followed by modified V6.4 source code in August. Netskope linked these releases to higher detection volumes, which remained above earlier levels through 2026. V7.2 added native-code hiding and six anti-virtual-machine checks, while V7.4 used an XBinder dropper, NTdll unhooking, and LocaltoNet-based control infrastructure. For defenders, the report highlights the need to investigate device compromise alongside account misuse. Earlier XWorm fake receipt campaigns show how ordinary business documents can lead to infection. Browser access, microphone capture, registry changes, and remote-control traffic should be examined together rather than treated as unrelated events. A valid account session does not prove that the person using it is legitimate. Indicators of compromise (IoCs):- Type Source-listed indicator or artifact Context SHA-256 / SHA-1 / MD5 Not provided in the supplied report No campaign hashes could be verified from the linked repository. Branding domain celestialproject[.]org V6.4 PE metadata label; not identified as a C2 domain. Branding domain c3lestial[.]fun V6.5 branding; not identified as a C2 domain. Registry artifact HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\CapabilityAccessManager\ConsentStore\location\Value Maps writes the string Allow to change location consent. Location lookup URL hxxp://ip-api[.]com/csv/?fields=lat,lon Legitimate service used for fallback IP geolocation; not a malicious C2 endpoint. File/path artifact %AppData% and NTdll.dll Associated with V7.4 NTdll unhooking; no complete file path is supplied. Service reference LocaltoNet V7.4 C2 tunneling service; no specific endpoint is supplied. Browser command OpenBrowser chrome Opens browser control. Keyboard command keyboardClick Relays keyboard input. Mouse commands LeftDown , LeftUp , MoveCursor Relays mouse actions. Scroll commands ScrollDown , ScrollUp Controls browser scrolling. Clipboard command paste Sends text for pasting. Browser-close command CloseHBrowser Closes browser control. Location message GMapsapi , Returns location coordinates. Microphone command MICCM Lists available recording devices. Audio message MICGET Carries captured audio. Microphone controls CLOSEMIC , ENDMIC Stops recording or ends the session. Detection names Gen:Variant.Application.Lazy , Trojan.Generic Netskope-listed detection labels. Note: IP addresses and domains are intentionally defanged (e.g., [.] ) to prevent accidental resolution or hyperlinking. Re-fang only within controlled threat intelligence platforms such as MISP, VirusTotal, or your SIEM . Update defenses against new malware as soon as it appears. Integrate TI Feeds with data from 16K SOCs .

Grindr users’ sensitive data shared through ad auctions without valid consent
items.summary: Norway’s privacy regulator Datatilsynet has fined advertising technology company Xandr 92 million Norwegian kroner, approximately $9.6 million, for unlawfully processing and sharing sensitive information about Grindr users. While the decision concerns users in Norway, the data-sharing practices were not confined to Norwegian users. BleepingComputer reports that information about Grindr users in other countries was also exposed through the advertising system. Between July 2018 and April 2020, Xandr handled real-time advertising auctions involving Grindr users. These automated auctions let advertisers bid to display an ad, but also involved circulating information about the person who would see it. Sensitive information revealing sexual orientation could potentially reach thousands of companies. Crucially, users did not have to disclose their sexual orientation in their profiles. Datatilsynet said that simply being identified as a Grindr user was information that indicated sexual orientation. According to the regulator, Xandr relied on Grindr to obtain consent without checking whether that consent was valid. As a company jointly responsible for the processing, Xandr had its own obligations. It was not enough to simply assume the app had obtained the explicit consent required. This was not a case of hackers breaking into a dating app. The information was flowing through an advertising business without a valid legal basis. Privacy group noyb , which filed the complaint in cooperation with the Norwegian Consumer Council, says such systems use tracking identifiers to build profiles of people’s interests, habits, and behavior. Are your details being used by cybercriminals? FIND OUT HERE Although Xandr now belongs to Microsoft, the misconduct predates its acquisition. Microsoft completed its purchase of Xandr from AT&T on June 6, 2022, more than two years after the period covered by the fine. Microsoft told BleepingComputer it was reviewing the decision and assessing its options. How to protect your privacy This is a Norwegian enforcement action, but the data-sharing practices crossed borders. Users in the US and elsewhere shouldn’t assume their information stayed private just because the fine was issued in Norway. You can limit how much additional information you disclose by giving a dating app only what you need to use it. Leave optional profile fields blank when the information feels too personal. Avoid publishing your workplace, home address, regular schedule, or other details that make you easy to locate. Review location permissions and advertising settings and limit them where possible. Think carefully before linking social accounts that reveal more of your identity. Don’t use dating apps on company-issued devices. These precautions cannot guarantee privacy. Responsibility for unlawful sharing lies with the companies involved. This case shows that sensitive information can come from using the service itself, not just from what you write in your bio. Scammers don’t need to hack you. They just need you to click once. Malwarebytes Identity Theft Protection catches suspicious activity before it becomes a problem.

items.title: Sonar joins OpenAI Daybreak Cyber Partner Program, deepening collaboration on agentic security
items.summary: Today Sonar joined the OpenAI Daybreak Cyber Partner Program , gaining governed access to advanced cybersecurity frontier models. The program deepens Sonar’s ongoing collaboration and engagement with OpenAI, following its commitment to OpenAI's call for collective action on cyber defense , and enables evaluation and deployment of Daybreak-class models in its products. Attackers are moving faster than most defenses were built for Frontier AI has changed what attackers can do, not just what defenders can do. Mandiant's M-Trends 2026 puts the mean time to exploit at an estimated -7 days, meaning exploitation routinely begins before a patch even exists. The same report found that the hand-off window between initial access and a second attacker taking over has collapsed from more than 8 hours in 2022 to about 22 seconds today. Whatever angle you look at it from, the time security teams have to find and fix a flaw before it's used against them keeps shrinking, and it's shrinking faster than most review processes were designed to handle. The leverage then moves earlier, to finding flaws before the code ships, and that takes reasoning at the level that attackers are already applying. Security teams have to match that pace, and doing so requires access to the same frontier intelligence reshaping the threat landscape. Bringing Daybreak-class security to SonarQube Hunter Agent SonarQube Hunter Agent is an agentic security researcher that thinks like an attacker and reports like an auditor. It reasons like a senior security researcher, not a model guessing at random: structured playbooks encode deep security domain expertise, paired with guided agentic reasoning. It hunts the logic flaws pattern-based analysis was never designed to catch by orchestrating a swarm of agents that scales to codebases of millions of lines. Every suspected finding is investigated and validated before it's raised. Daybreak brings advanced cybersecurity reasoning into that playbook, including models purpose-built for cybersecurity. As more capable models become available through the program, Hunter Agent runs its existing playbook on top of them: the structure is what makes the output consistent and auditable, the model is what determines how deep and how accurate that reasoning can go. Today, we're excited to announce the availability of GPT-6.1 Sol , the latest Daybreak-class model, inside Hunter Agent, and the difference shows up in the numbers. Across codebases ranging from 17,000 to 1.4 million lines, GPT-6.1 Sol reached 67% complete-finding coverage, 20% more complete findings than Hunter Agent's previous production model. On the largest codebase tested, 94% of its input came from cached context, letting it handle 2.4 times as many input tokens and finish scans up to 43% faster. The deeper reasoning isn't just faster, it catches more: in one test, Hunter Agent flagged a data export feature that correctly checked permissions on paper but still let users reach another team's secrets, exactly the kind of flaw that pattern-matching alone will miss. Bringing Daybreak to Gitar Daybreak access is also extending to Gitar, Sonar's AI code verification agent. It will start with how Gitar reviews AI agent skills, the instructions and tools that direct what an agent can do, including access to credentials and private code. An unsafe change to a skill can quietly remove a required approval step or leak data, and the problem can span both the instruction file and the script it invokes. . Gitar compares versions of an instruction file and catches when an updated summary drops a required sign-off step, exactly the kind of change a pattern match on the publishing command alone would miss. It treats repository instructions as untrusted evidence, inspecting suspicious content without executing it, and validates every candidate issue before it reaches a pull request. Independent verification is the answer to the agentic era As AI agents generate more code faster, the attack surface can grow faster than security teams can defend it. Frontier intelligence makes security teams more capable, but only when it runs inside a harness that makes results precise, repeatable, and auditable. Hunter Agent supplies that structure: Sonar's code security knowledge, structured playbooks, and validation of every suspected finding before it becomes an issue. The agentic era doesn't reward whoever adopts AI fastest. It rewards whoever removes the weaknesses attackers would exploit before software reaches production, and keeps reducing the risk already present in the codebase. That's the standard Sonar is building toward, and Daybreak is how we keep building it at the frontier's pace. As the collaboration with OpenAI deepens and new models become available through the program, Sonar automatically evaluates and integrates them. We expect this same access to extend across more of Sonar's products, bringing the same frontier reasoning to the full path from detection to remediation. Start free trial or contact sales .

items.title: Acting on the AI Shift in Cyber Risk With Prevention at the Codebase Level
items.summary: On June 22, 2026, the heads of the Five Eyes cyber security agencies issued a direct warning to business and technology leaders: AI is rapidly transforming cyber risk , and long-standing assumptions can become outdated in months rather than years. AI is increasing the speed, scale and sophistication of attacks, shrinking the time between vulnerability discovery and exploitation and making foundational controls more urgent. The same shift is reshaping software production. Coding agents generate code, introduce dependencies and complete increasingly complex changes at a pace manual review was not designed to match. Attackers can exploit weaknesses faster at the same time as more code requires assurance. That creates a formal governance problem. A software supply chain policy may define the right intentions, but it cannot by itself show that controls were applied to the changes that shipped. Periodic reviews are equally limited: they capture one moment while developers and agents continue to move changes through development, pull-request and CI/CD workflows. The Five Eyes statement says leaders must be confident that controls will work under pressure, and that secure-by-design and secure-by-default must become standard practice rather than an aspiration. Acting on that direction means moving prevention into the codebase: translating policy into testable standards, verifying every change independently of its origin, enforcing release conditions and producing evidence as those controls operate. What do NIS2 and the EU Cyber Resilience Act require for software security? For organizations in scope, the EU’s NIS2 Directive requires appropriate and proportionate technical, operational and organizational cybersecurity measures. Article 21 specifically includes supply chain security; security in the acquisition, development and maintenance of network and information systems; vulnerability handling and disclosure; and policies and procedures for assessing whether cybersecurity measures are effective. NIS2 operates through national implementing laws, and its precise application depends on an entity’s sector, size, role and jurisdiction. The EU Cyber Resilience Act goes further for manufacturers of covered products with digital elements. It requires cybersecurity to be addressed in product design, development, production, delivery and maintenance. It also requires vulnerability handling, regular security tests and reviews, due diligence when integrating third-party components and a machine-readable software bill of materials covering at least top-level dependencies. The CRA’s reporting obligations have applied since September 11, 2026; most other provisions apply from December 11, 2027. These laws are technology-neutral, but they do make the operating expectation increasingly clear: covered organizations must be able to show how cybersecurity measures are implemented and assessed, not merely that a policy exists. Non-binding government and cyber-agency publications reinforce that direction. Japan’s METI and National Cybersecurity Office connect SBOM use with vulnerability management, supply chain transparency and secure-by-design accountability, while Japan’s 2025 Cybersecurity Strategy identifies SBOMs as part of stronger supply chain risk management. France’s ANSSI supports secure-by-design, auditability, vulnerability management, code review and SBOMs in its open-source policy . CISA and G7 partners have also published non-mandatory minimum SBOM elements for AI systems . These sources do not create a single global rule, but they point toward the same priorities: secure development, component transparency, effective vulnerability handling and evidence that controls operate. A policy proves intent; Operating evidence proves implementation Periodic audits capture a point in time. Between audits, code continues to change across multiple workflows. If standards are checked only at the end, or evidence is reconstructed from spreadsheets and screenshots, the record is fragmented and often stale before an auditor sees it. That creates three practical problems: Standards are applied inconsistently across teams, repositories and delivery paths. Leaders can only show that controls were documented, but can’t prove that they operated on the changes that shipped. Unclear controls for agentic code slow adoption in regulated and risk-sensitive environments. The stronger position is prevention with evidence generated as controls operate. How do you implement continuous security controls in a development pipeline? Sonar describes its broader approach as the Agent Centric Development Cycle, organized around Guide, Verify and Solve. Those stages provide a useful model for continuous code governance. Guide: Establish and Communicate the Standard Guide begins by defining the constraints and standards within which agents operate. SonarQube quality profiles encode the organization’s quality and security standards, while quality gates establish the non-negotiable conditions agentic changes must meet. Sonar Vortex brings those standards and codebase-specific context directly into the agent workflow before work begins. Together, they turn policy into clear, automated boundaries that guide how agents generate and modify code rather than relying on each agent to interpret governance requirements independently. Verify: Analyze Every Change Independently of Its Origin Guidance shapes what an agent produces; verification determines whether the result can be trusted. Sonar provides an independent analysis layer that assesses agentic code and dependencies against the defined standards rather than relying on the agent to review its own output. Verification follows the change through the agentic workflow. Sonar Vortex verifies agent-generated changes within the workflow, while SonarQube independently analyzes the completed change and applies the relevant quality gate. The repository or CI/CD platform can then use that result to block changes that fail to meet the required standard. Configured as a required check, this makes prevention enforceable: agent-produced code cannot progress unless it meets the defined conditions. Solve: Remediate Findings and Verify the Result Findings should move through a governed path from detection to verified remediation. Gitar reviews pull requests and can push fixes for identified problems and CI failures. The SonarQube Remediation Agent addresses eligible issues in technical debt and the backlog, verifies each proposed fix through fresh analysis and returns successful fixes as reviewable pull requests. Hunter Agent strengthens security discovery across the codebase by uncovering access control, business logic and authentication vulnerabilities that conventional analysis may miss. Its findings can then enter the same triage and remediation process as other SonarQube issues. Together, these capabilities turn findings into preventive action, helping organizations identify, remediate and reverify weaknesses before they persist or spread across the codebase. How can organizations prove software security controls are working to auditors? Formal governance requires evidence that controls were established, operated and produced a result. Sonar can provide evidence of: How controls were established: configured quality profiles, analysis rules, quality gates and their assignment to projects. How controls operated: analysis history, issue records and quality-gate decisions showing that code was assessed against the assigned standard. What the controls found and resolved: security findings, dependency and license risks, issue ownership and status, proposed fixes and reanalysis results. What can be extracted as evidence: quality profile and quality gate configurations, dependencies, analysis, issue and remediation data, quality gate results, SBOMs and audit logs. These records show how code-level controls were configured, applied and acted on over time. Who is accountable for software security when using AI in development? Using AI does not transfer accountability. The organization remains responsible for the security of the software it develops, operates or places on the market. Controls must therefore be comprehensive, consistently applied and reliable across every code change. That accountability should translate into clear ownership: Security leaders set secure development, dependency and licensing requirements, including risk thresholds, exceptions and escalation paths. Engineering and platform leaders translate those requirements into automated analysis, repository controls, pipeline checks and release conditions. Product and legal teams determine the regulatory and contractual requirements that apply to each product and market. Compliance and assurance teams define the evidence required, test the controls and connect the resulting records to specific obligations. Begin with the products and applications carrying the greatest regulatory or operational risk, then expand the model across the portfolio. Measure four things: control coverage, exception management, security outcomes and evidence readiness. Useful indicators include the proportion of changes analyzed before merge, repositories with enforced gates, exception age, recurring findings, remediation time, dependency and SBOM coverage and the time needed to retrieve release evidence. How is AI changing cybersecurity risk for software development teams? AI has shortened the distance between software change and cyber risk. Governance must therefore operate where software is created, reviewed and released. Policies and documentation remain essential, but they must be backed by controls that work whenever code changes. A defensible software supply chain connects governance directly to code delivery. Standards guide how agents work, every change undergoes independent verification, release conditions are enforced, findings move through verified remediation and evidence shows how those controls operated. SonarQube provides a core technical control and evidence layer for this model. It helps organizations apply consistent quality and security standards, verify code and dependencies, govern release decisions and trace results over time, creating repeatable evidence across developer- and agent-produced code. Take control of AI-era cyber risk where it enters the software. Explore how SonarQube turns policy into continuous, verifiable controls across every code change.

items.title: SonarQube Cloud now supports bulk import for Azure DevOps and Bitbucket
items.summary: Today, Sonar is announcing bulk import support for Azure DevOps and Bitbucket in SonarQube Cloud . Administrators can now import every repository in an Azure DevOps or Bitbucket organization into SonarQube Cloud in a single action, matching the bulk import experience already available for GitHub and GitLab. With this release, SonarQube Cloud supports bulk import across all four DevOps platforms it integrates with: GitHub , GitLab , Azure DevOps , and Bitbucket . Onboarding an organization's repositories one at a time, or in batches of up to 25, creates a real cost. For an organization with dozens or hundreds of repositories on Azure DevOps or Bitbucket, that repetition adds up to hours of administrative work before analysis runs on a single line of code, and every hour spent importing is an hour that code sits unverified. This release removes that bottleneck. From the Analyze projects page, an administrator of any SonarQube Cloud organization bound to an Azure DevOps or Bitbucket workspace now sees an "Import all repositories" button that brings the entire organization in at once. Bulk import does not leave administrators guessing while it runs. A real-time progress indicator on the Analyze projects page shows the operation's status as SonarQube Cloud works through the repository list, replacing what used to be an opaque, all-or-nothing wait. When the import finishes, SonarQube Cloud generates a downloadable summary report showing exactly which repositories were imported, which were skipped, and which failed, so administrators get a clear, auditable record without cross-checking logs or reimporting to find out what happened. No new permissions are required to use this feature. Administrators need the same Create Projects permission already required to import repositories individually, so anyone with existing import rights can use bulk import immediately. This release matters beyond the time it saves. Verification only works if it covers the whole codebase, and a codebase spread across dozens of unimported repositories is a codebase with blind spots. By closing the last gap in platform coverage, SonarQube Cloud makes it possible for organizations on any of the four major DevOps platforms to get every repository under verification from day one, not after weeks of manual onboarding. For setup instructions, see the Getting started with Azure DevOps and Getting started with Bitbucket documentation.

items.title: Critical Ghostscript Flaw Lets Attackers Use Malicious PDFs to Execute Code
items.summary: A critical vulnerability in Ghostscript could allow attackers to use specially made PDF files to run code on vulnerable servers. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-39919, affects Ghostscript versions before 10.08.0 and has a CVSS severity score of 9.8 out of 10. Ghostscript is widely used to render PDFs, create document thumbnails, and convert PostScript files into images. The issue is especially important for websites and services that accept uploaded PDFs. WordPress sites, document portals, print services, email gateways, invoice platforms, and file-conversion APIs may all call Ghostscript behind the scenes when they process user-supplied files. A malicious PDF can therefore reach the vulnerable component even when the main application has no direct Ghostscript code. Researchers from Wordfence identified the vulnerability during a WordPress 7.1 security assessment using its Argus testing system. This is not a malware campaign, and researchers have not reported active exploitation in the wild. Instead, the finding shows how a crafted PDF can trigger memory corruption and, in certain server builds, lead to unauthenticated remote code execution. Wordfence reported the flaw to Artifex on August 23, and the vendor confirmed it the following day before releasing the fix on September 8. Critical Ghostscript Flaw CVE-2026-39919 is a heap-based buffer overflow in Ghostscript’s JPEG 2000 image decoding path. The issue occurs when Ghostscript processes a PDF containing a JPEG 2000 image with unusual component resolution settings and sub-byte sample values. In simple terms, the program reserves too little memory for image data and then writes more data than the allocated buffer can hold. That extra data can overwrite nearby memory used by Ghostscript. In a controlled WordPress test environment, Wordfence researchers showed that this memory corruption could be developed into remote code execution. The code would run with the permissions assigned to the account that processes the PDF, such as a web server or PHP-FPM user, rather than automatically gaining root access. The public NVD vulnerability record lists the issue as a heap-based buffer overflow and notes that crafted JPEG 2000 content inside a PDF can corrupt memory. The risk starts when an application accepts a PDF and attempts to create a preview or thumbnail. On many WordPress setups, the chain is WordPress, Imagick, ImageMagick, and then Ghostscript. The site may appear to be processing a normal document upload, but Ghostscript is the lower-level tool that reads the file. This is why the issue differs from the earlier WordPress Imagick code-execution flaw , where WordPress upload validation could be bypassed with content disguised as an image. In this case, the memory bug itself sits inside Ghostscript. Affected Versions and Real-World Risk The vulnerable code was introduced in Ghostscript 9.21 and affects upstream versions through 10.07.1. Artifex fixed the issue in Ghostscript 10.08.0, and its official Ghostscript CVE page confirms that CVE-2026-39919 was addressed in that release. However, Linux vendors may backport the fix to an older-looking package version, meaning gs --version alone may not prove whether a server is safe. Wordfence tested ten package environments, including Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, AlmaLinux, Alpine Linux, and an official WordPress Docker image. The researchers found vulnerable builds across those environments during their September 15 tests. Their proof-of-concept files did not work unchanged across all systems, which means there is no evidence of a single universal PDF that compromises every server. Still, a build-specific exploit continued to work on systems sharing the same Ghostscript executable. That result matters for hosting providers and companies that deploy many servers from one container image. A threat actor may not need a PDF that works everywhere if several targets use the same vulnerable build. The concern is similar to the recent malicious HEIC image research , which showed how native media-processing libraries can expose WordPress servers when uploaded files reach vulnerable decoders. Organizations should install the fixed Ghostscript package provided by their operating system vendor or hosting provider. Teams using containers should rebuild images from an updated base image and redeploy them, rather than simply restarting an existing container. Managed WordPress customers should ask their hosting provider whether its Ghostscript package includes the CVE-2026-39919 fix and whether uploaded PDFs are converted into previews. Where updates cannot be installed immediately, administrators should stop untrusted users from uploading PDFs or disable PDF processing through ImageMagick policy settings. Rate limits and upload limits can reduce repeated processing attempts, but they do not remove the underlying flaw. Ghostscript’s -dSAFER mode should also not be treated as a fix because Wordfence reached the vulnerable path while that sandbox setting was enabled. The incident also adds to growing evidence that document and image conversion services need close review. A Discourse image pipeline chain recently showed how Ghostscript and ImageMagick can become part of a wider file-processing risk path. While Claude-assisted decoder exploit research demonstrated how flaws in media libraries can be adapted for real service environments. items.title: SAP Security Update Patches Critical Code Injection and Memory Corruption Vulnerabilities
items.summary: SAP has released its October 2026 security updates, fixing critical code injection, access control, and cloud security flaws alongside a high-severity memory corruption issue. The October 13 release includes 16 new security notes, four GitHub security advisories and two updates to earlier notes. Four entries carry critical ratings, making this patch cycle important for teams running SAP business systems. According to SAP’s October Patch Day bulletin , the fixes cover S/4HANA, NetWeaver, Web Dispatcher, Commerce Cloud and several development libraries. Although the headline highlights critical vulnerabilities, the memory corruption flaw is rated High, not Critical. Its published impact concerns service disruption rather than confirmed code execution or data theft. Across all 22 entries, SAP lists four critical, three high, 14 medium, and one low severity issues, including the two updated notes and four library advisories. SAP Security Vulnerabilities CVE-2026-89107 carries a CVSS score of 9.9 and affects the Manage Substitution/Validation Rules feature in SAP S/4HANA. SAP lists S4CORE versions 105, 106, 107, 108 and 109 as affected, with the correction delivered through Security Note 3805589 . The weakness lies in how the rule definition feature checks input written in a scripting language used for business rules. An authenticated attacker with specific business privileges can submit crafted input that the system treats as executable ABAP code, SAP’s programming language. Successful exploitation could give an attacker broad control over the affected system, with serious effects on data privacy, data accuracy, and service availability. The attack requires an account with suitable business permissions, but the published CVSS vector indicates low attack complexity and no need for another user to interact. CVE-2026-58249 affects the Internet Communication Manager component in SAP NetWeaver and SAP Web Dispatcher. Rated 7.5, the flaw is addressed by Security Note 3765424 . A remote attacker does not need to authenticate before sending a malicious request. The affected software fails to properly check certain fields in crafted requests handled by an internal protocol component. This can trigger a memory handling error and crash the affected process. The published description reports a high impact on availability, with no impact on confidentiality or integrity. SAP’s affected version list spans HDB 2.00, multiple kernel and Web Dispatcher releases, Content Server, XS Advanced Runtime and SAP Extended Application Services. Administrators should compare installed components against the full vendor list rather than assume every deployment needs the same update package. The highest-rated issue is CVE-2026-89111, an OAuth2 server-side request forgery flaw in SAP Cloud SDK for Python, scored 10.0. It affects versions before 0.45.2. In applications serving multiple tenants on SAP Business Technology Platform, an attacker controlling the tenant_subdomain parameter can redirect token requests to an attacker-controlled server and expose client credentials. SAP also fixed CVE-2026-89110, a broken access control flaw in NetWeaver Visual Composer VC70RUNTIME 7.50, rated 9.9. Another critical issue, CVE-2026-89108, concerns a missing authorization check in the Configuration Service of Manufacturing Integration and Intelligence versions 15.4 and 15.5, with a score of 9.1. items.title: Kimsuky Hackers Use Malicious Resume Documents to Deploy Funhouse Ransomware
items.summary: Kimsuky hackers have used a malicious résumé document to deploy Funhouse ransomware through a chain of scripts and remote access tools. The attack begins with a Hangul Word Processor document disguised as a job application, turning a routine work file into an entry point for malware that ultimately encrypts files. The campaign connects document-based deception with tools used in earlier Endpoint ransomware cases. Opening the résumé drops supporting files, but clicking a link inside it triggers the next stage. That distinction matters: the visible document acts as bait, while the link starts the process that leads to remote access and ransomware execution. Researchers from AhnLab Security intelligence Center (ASEC) identified the Funhouse malware delivery case in a report published October 1, 2026. They linked it to earlier Kimsuky activity through shared scripts, Quasar RAT settings, and ransomware traits. The findings show a change in the initial delivery method rather than a completely new toolset. The public report does not establish how many victims. Kimsuky Hackers Use Malicious Resume Documents The malicious file, resume.Hwp , contains embedded Object Linking and Embedding, or OLE, data. When opened, the Hangul process extracts pdf.Exe and pdf.Exe.Manifest into the Windows temporary folder without further user input. The executable is a VbsEdit script executor, while the manifest contains the malicious script used in the following stage. A hyperlink inside the résumé invites the recipient to open a PDF bearing a person’s name. Decoy document (Source – ASEC) Clicking it launches the extracted executable, which runs the manifest script and creates a randomly named batch file. The trigger resembles earlier Kimsuky document tricks: a weaponized HWP research campaign also used embedded files and a clickable link to begin malicious execution. This is not simply a document that encrypts files when opened. ASEC describes several stages between the résumé and the final payload. Batch, VBS, and PowerShell scripts run in sequence, followed by a Python-based backdoor, Quasar RAT installation, and Funhouse execution. Quasar RAT serves as the tool used to deploy the ransomware. The Python stage fits the group’s previous operations. An earlier malicious LNK backdoor campaign used document-themed Windows shortcuts to install a Python backdoor through multiple scripts. In the Funhouse case, ASEC also found batch code resembling earlier Kimsuky samples. The operators periodically updated this batch component, which provided an additional way to maintain access. Quasar RAT Connects the Cases The Quasar RAT sample uses a configuration file with a .dwg extension, storing its command-and-control address, target identifier, and mutex name. A mutex is a named object programs can use to coordinate activity or avoid running duplicate copies. The latest configuration reports version 4.4.3, compared with version 1.1.8 in the earlier cases. Although configuration filenames, server addresses, and target details changed, the Quasar mutex stayed the same across the February, June, and September cases. These matches support ASEC’s assessment of continuity. They also show why investigators should compare settings and code behavior rather than treat each new server or filename as evidence of an unrelated campaign. Similar batch file code (Source – ASEC) ASEC identified Funhouse as a variant of Endpoint ransomware. The June Endpoint and September Funhouse samples share the encryption extension, ransom-note filename, mutex, encryption method, key-generation approach, footer size, and footer marker. The attacker’s contact address changed, but the underlying file-encryption traits remained consistent. Both samples use HC-128 encryption and a 72-byte footer. Their key-generation process combines CryptGenRandom, Curve25519, and SHA-512. By contrast, the February Endpoint sample used ChaCha20 encryption and a different key-generation method. These differences trace changes within the ransomware family; SHA-512 here describes a cryptographic operation, not a published sample hash. ASEC said the shift from recently favored LNK files to HWP documents likely aims to lower suspicion. A résumé is a familiar work item, particularly for staff handling job applications. Earlier Kimsuky recruiter phishing campaigns similarly used fake résumés and business cards, showing how the group shapes lures around a recipient’s normal tasks. Defenders should watch the full sequence, not just the attachment type: Hangul writing executable and manifest files, followed by unusual script activity and remote access tooling. ASEC advises checking document links and sender credibility, avoiding suspicious links, updating Hangul and operating systems, and keeping endpoint protection current. items.summary_html:
Kimsuky hackers have used a malicious résumé document to deploy Funhouse ransomware through a chain of scripts and remote access tools.

The attack begins with a Hangul Word Processor document disguised as a job application, turning a routine work file into an entry point for malware that ultimately encrypts files.

The campaign connects document-based deception with tools used in earlier Endpoint ransomware cases. Opening the résumé drops supporting files, but clicking a link inside it triggers the next stage.

That distinction matters: the visible document acts as bait, while the link starts the process that leads to remote access and ransomware execution.

Researchers from AhnLab Security intelligence Center (ASEC) identified the Funhouse malware delivery case in a report published October 1, 2026. They linked it to earlier Kimsuky activity through shared scripts, Quasar RAT settings, and ransomware traits.

The findings show a change in the initial delivery method rather than a completely new toolset. The public report does not establish how many victims.

Kimsuky Hackers Use Malicious Resume Documents

The malicious file, resume.Hwp, contains embedded Object Linking and Embedding, or OLE, data. When opened, the Hangul process extracts pdf.Exe and pdf.Exe.Manifest into the Windows temporary folder without further user input.

The executable is a VbsEdit script executor, while the manifest contains the malicious script used in the following stage. A hyperlink inside the résumé invites the recipient to open a PDF bearing a person’s name.

Decoy document (Source – ASEC)

Clicking it launches the extracted executable, which runs the manifest script and creates a randomly named batch file. The trigger resembles earlier Kimsuky document tricks: a weaponized HWP research campaign also used embedded files and a clickable link to begin malicious execution.

This is not simply a document that encrypts files when opened. ASEC describes several stages between the résumé and the final payload.

Batch, VBS, and PowerShell scripts run in sequence, followed by a Python-based backdoor, Quasar RAT installation, and Funhouse execution. Quasar RAT serves as the tool used to deploy the ransomware.

The Python stage fits the group’s previous operations. An earlier malicious LNK backdoor campaign used document-themed Windows shortcuts to install a Python backdoor through multiple scripts.

In the Funhouse case, ASEC also found batch code resembling earlier Kimsuky samples. The operators periodically updated this batch component, which provided an additional way to maintain access.

Quasar RAT Connects the Cases

The Quasar RAT sample uses a configuration file with a .dwg extension, storing its command-and-control address, target identifier, and mutex name.

A mutex is a named object programs can use to coordinate activity or avoid running duplicate copies. The latest configuration reports version 4.4.3, compared with version 1.1.8 in the earlier cases.

Although configuration filenames, server addresses, and target details changed, the Quasar mutex stayed the same across the February, June, and September cases.

These matches support ASEC’s assessment of continuity. They also show why investigators should compare settings and code behavior rather than treat each new server or filename as evidence of an unrelated campaign.

Similar batch file code (Source – ASEC)

ASEC identified Funhouse as a variant of Endpoint ransomware. The June Endpoint and September Funhouse samples share the encryption extension, ransom-note filename, mutex, encryption method, key-generation approach, footer size, and footer marker.

The attacker’s contact address changed, but the underlying file-encryption traits remained consistent. Both samples use HC-128 encryption and a 72-byte footer. Their key-generation process combines CryptGenRandom, Curve25519, and SHA-512.

By contrast, the February Endpoint sample used ChaCha20 encryption and a different key-generation method. These differences trace changes within the ransomware family; SHA-512 here describes a cryptographic operation, not a published sample hash.

ASEC said the shift from recently favored LNK files to HWP documents likely aims to lower suspicion. A résumé is a familiar work item, particularly for staff handling job applications.

Earlier Kimsuky recruiter phishing campaigns similarly used fake résumés and business cards, showing how the group shapes lures around a recipient’s normal tasks.

Defenders should watch the full sequence, not just the attachment type: Hangul writing executable and manifest files, followed by unusual script activity and remote access tooling.

ASEC advises checking document links and sender credibility, avoiding suspicious links, updating Hangul and operating systems, and keeping endpoint protection current.

Wishlist inflation is real, but you still need them
items.summary: This is a deep dive into the results of the Steam wishlist and sales data I have been collecting from readers. The survey is still active so if you would like to contribute, please complete this form: Official HTMAG Steam wishlist and sales survey If you want to get a lot of views on YouTube, an easy trick is you take a nugget of common knowledge and say “ doesn’t matter anymore, is the true marker of success.” Boom, instant clicks. The most common form of this is “Wishlists are inflated, velocity is the true indicator of success now” Because of my survey and your generosity in sharing your game’s sales history, I have data from 160 games and I can actually test this hypothesis. Part 1: Is Wishlist inflation real? Wishlist inflation is the theory that games these days are earning more and more wishlists because more and more developers are “wishlist maxxing.” (also known as doing marketing.) Maybe even some developers are using underhanded ways to get those wishlists. The side effect of all these efforts (both honest and not so honest) is that wishlists are “worth less” so they convert worse. The survey has data spanning several years, so I can test how well a wishlist converted then vs. now and see if there is “inflation.” I broke the period in half: 2020-2022 is the first modern wishlist maxxing era. The early pandemic era is when virtual festivals became a thing. The birth of Steam Next Fest and 3rd Party virtual festivals showed developers that they could earn thousands of wishlists in a week. A few enterprising developers knew about festivals, demos, and running sustained content creator campaigns. The second era: 2023-2025 is when festivals really matured so far that Valve started to take a more selective approach to festival featuring on the front page of Steam. I didn’t include 2026 data in this analysis because we are still living through it and I can’t provide as many months of sales to compare. Comparing the two eras, you can see that it is true. There is wishlist inflation. Stats and Sample size In the survey I have 160 games that were released in the 2020-2025 period (34 in 2020–22 and 126 in 2023–25). So how well do wishlists convert? You can see the difference in the chart below. In the first month of release, a game in the 2023-2025 era sold about half (give or take because the range is wide) as many units per wishlist at launch as a game in the 2020-2022 era. There is definitely wishlist inflation. It is real. Theories? I think there might be a few causes: Valve made wishlisting easier Valve worked with developers to make it easier to get wishlists. This chart comes from a 2021 Steamworks blog post. During the early era, Valve was touting how many wishlists they were pushing to games. They too were wishlist maxxing. For instance, they started adding little stars on hover tooltips (see screenshot below) so you could wishlist a game without even going to the Steam page. The wishlist became more of a “bookmark.” Adding a game to a wishlist used to be more cumbersome so people only did it when they truly liked a game. Democratized visibility via festivals In a previous blog post I looked at how many festivals Valve has run since they introduced the “make an event” tooling back in 2020. As you can see in the following chart, the number of games getting featured has exploded. We have suspected for a while that festival wishlists don’t convert as well. So more games have been getting more wishlists that don’t convert very well. More developers are learning how important it is to get wishlists There is better marketing information out there now, and more and more people know the importance of wishlists. So they are working hard to get them. There is nothing wrong with trying. People know about Steam Next Fest. If you look at the rough number of games releasing every year and compare it to the number of games appearing in Steam Next Fest, you would see that for many years developers just skipped Steam Next Fest for some reason (probably naivety). With better information now, people are learning to do the basics like opt in to free wishlists earned from this event. This will lead to more wishlists with worse conversion. Part 2: So Wishlist don’t matter anymore, right? Again, this is where you can farm free engagement on YouTube. Just post a video of you scowling with your arms crossed with a label: “Wishlists don’t matter anymore, here is one weird trick.” TL;DR – nope, wrong. Wishlists are still key to predicting how well a game will do at launch. Let’s look at the real data. We can use correlation between two numbers to measure predictive power. So first let’s determine if the first part is true. Is it true that “wishlists don’t matter anymore?” This chart is a statistical analysis of how much the number of wishlists at launch correlates to units sold in the first month. A value of 1.0 for Spearman correlation means if we made 2 columns that ranked the top wishlisted games and then ranked games that sold the most units, the order of the two lists would be identical. R-squared means how closely games follow the trend line (a R2 of 1.0 would mean every dot is on the line). Measure 2020–2022 2023–2025 R², log-log 0.77 0.72 Spearman correlation 0.89 0.87 Here is a scatter chart of the games analyzed, with a “best fit” line for each era. I like the lines because they make clear what the table can’t. Each line represents a different era. The lines are nearly parallel, so wishlists scale with sales the same way in both eras. The later line sits lower, which is the inflation I pointed out earlier. Wishlists aren’t perfect, but they do predict how many units a game will sell. But what about velocity If you want to sound smart, you can post on Reddit “actually I think we are moving into a world where wishlist velocity is a more important indicator instead of raw wishlist counts.” In this case I define velocity as the number of wishlists earned in the 30 days before the game launches. A game with “high velocity” gets a ton of wishlists right before launch. A game with low velocity gets a few. Wishlist–sales fit (R², log-log) by launch era Measure 2020–22 2023–25 Total wishlists 0.77 0.72 Wishlist adds, last 30 days (velocity) 0.77 0.70 As you can see, in the more recent era, velocity is not any better than total wishlists in correlation to unit sales. (Side note, yes velocity is 0.07 points lower in 2023-2025 but difference is statistical noise, considering there were far fewer games in the survey for the 2020-2022 era.) BUT, if we look at all games smooshed together across all eras, we can improve the units sold prediction a bit more if we look at both total wishlists AND velocity. Measure R² log-log Total wishlists at launch 0.73 Adds in the last 30 days 0.72 Adds in the last 7 days 0.68 Total + last-30-day adds together 0.75 Wishlists are still king It is hard to wrap your mind around it… but both things are true: wishlist counts have inflated (each wishlist sells fewer units), but wishlists predict sales just as well as they did 3 years ago (the 0.05 difference is within the noise for this sample size.) As an analogy to the real world… just because the cost of living is going up doesn’t mean we don’t have to pay rent. Unfortunately, we still need to count, collect, and talk about wishlists. Sorry, you can’t make any cool viral YouTube videos about wishlists not mattering. Life is boring. Prove me wrong I am still trying to collect more data from more games. So if you have launched a Steam game in the last 6 years, please submit your data. Official HTMAG Steam wishlist and sales survey
items.summary_html:
This is a deep dive into the results of the Steam wishlist and sales data I have been collecting from readers. The survey is still active so if you would like to contribute, please complete this form:

Official HTMAG Steam wishlist and sales survey 

If you want to get a lot of views on YouTube, an easy trick is you take a nugget of common knowledge and say “ doesn’t matter anymore, is the true marker of success.” Boom, instant clicks. 

The most common form of this is “Wishlists are inflated, velocity is the true indicator of success now”

Because of my survey and your generosity in sharing your game’s sales history, I have data from 160 games and I can actually test this hypothesis. 

Part 1: Is Wishlist inflation real?

Wishlist inflation is the theory that games these days are earning more and more wishlists because more and more developers are “wishlist maxxing.” (also known as doing marketing.) Maybe even some developers are using underhanded ways to get those wishlists.

The side effect of all these efforts (both honest and not so honest) is that wishlists are “worth less” so they convert worse. 

The survey has data spanning several years, so I can test how well a wishlist converted then vs. now and see if there is “inflation.”

I broke the period in half: 2020-2022 is the first modern wishlist maxxing era. The early pandemic era is when virtual festivals became a thing. The birth of Steam Next Fest and 3rd Party virtual festivals showed developers that they could earn thousands of wishlists in a week. A few enterprising developers knew about festivals, demos, and running sustained content creator campaigns.

The second era: 2023-2025 is when festivals really matured so far that Valve started to take a more selective approach to festival featuring on the front page of Steam. I didn’t include 2026 data in this analysis because we are still living through it and I can’t provide as many months of sales to compare. 

Comparing the two eras, you can see that it is true. There is wishlist inflation. 

Stats and Sample size

In the survey I have 160 games that were released in the 2020-2025 period (34 in 2020–22 and 126 in 2023–25).

So how well do wishlists convert? You can see the difference in the chart below. In the first month of release, a game in the 2023-2025 era sold about half (give or take because the range is wide) as many units per wishlist at launch as a game in the 2020-2022 era.

There is definitely wishlist inflation. It is real.

Theories?

I think there might be a few causes:

Valve made wishlisting easier

Valve worked with developers to make it easier to get wishlists. This chart comes from a 2021 Steamworks blog post. During the early era, Valve was touting how many wishlists they were pushing to games. They too were wishlist maxxing. 

For instance, they started adding little stars on hover tooltips (see screenshot below) so you could wishlist a game without even going to the Steam page. The wishlist became more of a “bookmark.” Adding a game to a wishlist used to be more cumbersome so people only did it when they truly liked a game.  

Democratized visibility via festivals 

In a previous blog post I looked at how many festivals Valve has run since they introduced the “make an event” tooling back in 2020. As you can see in the following chart, the number of games getting featured has exploded. 

We have suspected for a while that festival wishlists don’t convert as well. So more games have been getting more wishlists that don’t convert very well.

More developers are learning how important it is to get wishlists

There is better marketing information out there now, and more and more people know the importance of wishlists. So they are working hard to get them. There is nothing wrong with trying.

People know about Steam Next Fest. If you look at the rough number of games releasing every year and compare it to the number of games appearing in Steam Next Fest, you would see that for many years developers just skipped Steam Next Fest for some reason (probably naivety). With better information now, people are learning to do the basics like opt in to free wishlists earned from this event. This will lead to more wishlists with worse conversion.

Part 2: So Wishlist don’t matter anymore, right?

Again, this is where you can farm free engagement on YouTube. Just post a video of you scowling with your arms crossed with a label: “Wishlists don’t matter anymore, here is one weird trick.” 

TL;DR – nope, wrong. Wishlists are still key to predicting how well a game will do at launch. 

Let’s look at the real data. 

We can use correlation between two numbers to measure predictive power.

So first let’s determine if the first part is true. Is it true that “wishlists don’t matter anymore?”

This chart is a statistical analysis of how much the number of wishlists at launch correlates to units sold in the first month. A value of 1.0 for Spearman correlation means if we made 2 columns that ranked the top wishlisted games and then ranked games that sold the most units, the order of the two lists would be identical. R-squared means how closely games follow the trend line (a R2 of 1.0 would mean every dot is on the line).

Measure2020–20222023–2025R², log-log0.770.72Spearman correlation0.890.87

Here is a scatter chart of the games analyzed, with a “best fit” line for each era. 

I like the lines because they make clear what the table can’t. Each line represents a different era. The lines are nearly parallel, so wishlists scale with sales the same way in both eras. The later line sits lower, which is the inflation I pointed out earlier.

Wishlists aren’t perfect, but they do predict how many units a game will sell.

But what about velocity

If you want to sound smart, you can post on Reddit “actually I think we are moving into a world where wishlist velocity is a more important indicator instead of raw wishlist counts.”

In this case I define velocity as the number of wishlists earned in the 30 days before the game launches. A game with “high velocity” gets a ton of wishlists right before launch. A game with low velocity gets a few.

Wishlist–sales fit (R², log-log) by launch era Measure2020–222023–25Total wishlists0.770.72Wishlist adds, last 30 days (velocity)0.770.70

As you can see, in the more recent era, velocity is not any better than total wishlists in correlation to unit sales. (Side note, yes velocity is 0.07 points lower in 2023-2025 but difference is statistical noise, considering there were far fewer games in the survey for the 2020-2022 era.)

BUT, if we look at all games smooshed together across all eras, we can improve the units sold prediction a bit more if we look at both total wishlists AND velocity. 

MeasureR² log-logTotal wishlists at launch0.73Adds in the last 30 days0.72Adds in the last 7 days0.68Total + last-30-day adds together0.75 Wishlists are still king

It is hard to wrap your mind around it… but both things are true: wishlist counts have inflated (each wishlist sells fewer units), but wishlists predict sales just as well as they did 3 years ago (the 0.05 difference is within the noise for this sample size.)

As an analogy to the real world… just because the cost of living is going up doesn’t mean we don’t have to pay rent.

Unfortunately, we still need to count, collect, and talk about wishlists. Sorry, you can’t make any cool viral YouTube videos about wishlists not mattering. Life is boring. 

Prove me wrong

I am still trying to collect more data from more games. So if you have launched a Steam game in the last 6 years, please submit your data. 

Official HTMAG Steam wishlist and sales survey

items.title: Fake Web3 Accelerator Uses Malicious npm Packages to Target Crypto Founders
items.summary: A fake Web3 accelerator called Apex has been using malicious npm packages to target cryptocurrency start-ups and founders with what appeared to be free AI credits, coding tools, smart-contract audits, investment access, and invitations to in-person events. Behind the polished Web3 pitch, the operation delivered malware for macOS and Windows, exposed AI-agent data to attacker-run systems, and provided false security results that could mislead teams into trusting unsafe code. The campaign used two npm packages, @apexacc/cli and @apexacc/audit , presented as an AI coding agent and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) security-audit tool. Users who ran the packages through npm or npx could trigger a multistage infection chain. The operation is especially concerning because crypto founders often handle wallet keys, source code, cloud credentials, investor data, and smart-contract material on the same developer systems. Analysts at Elastic Security Labs identified the malicious @apexacc/cli package after a supply-chain monitor flagged suspicious behavior. Their investigation linked it to a broader operation posing as the Apex accelerator and later found @apexacc/audit , another malicious package from the same publisher. The packages were malicious when published rather than being legitimate projects that were later compromised. Fake Web3 Accelerator Uses Malicious npm Packages Apex presented its main service as “Apex Arena,” a private workspace for Web3 founders. The site claimed more than 200 portfolio projects and more than $124 million raised. It promoted smart-contract reviews, founder messaging, a directory of vetted talent, investment scoring, free Claude and Gemini credits, and the Apex Copilot coding tool. The group also used fake reviews and advertised a physical event connected to TOKEN2049 in Singapore, a tactic designed to make the operation look like a real startup programme. Fake reviews (Source – Elastic) This mix of AI services, crypto branding, public repositories, and live-event activity shows how modern social-engineering campaigns can move beyond a simple phishing page. Similar risks were seen in a malicious npm campaign targeting Web3 developers , where poisoned packages sought wallet phrases, API tokens, SSH keys, and cloud credentials. Apex Copilot largely copied the legitimate open-source Oh My Pi coding agent. Elastic found that 1,351 of 1,363 compared source files matched the original project. The altered code added a bootstrap component that could receive commands from Apex-controlled infrastructure, change AI service routing, and add an attacker-controlled MCP server to the victim’s configuration. Malware Delivery on Windows and macOS The npm package launchers used apex.cjs and audit.cjs to download platform-specific files from GitHub releases. On Windows, the code contacted vrf.apexaccs[.]org and received server-selected commands. It then created PowerShell and VBScript staging files before launching wscript.exe , PowerShell, and later malware stages. The Windows chain led to a custom information stealer through bludness.exe , install.exe or exegis.exe , and updater_loader.exe . The final payload collected system details, clipboard data, screenshots, browser information, Wi-Fi profile names, files, and data from wallet, VPN, remote-access, messaging, and AI-client applications. Auth dialog pop-up (Source – Elastic) It also targeted Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Yandex browser data, including saved credentials and cookies, before archiving collected material and sending it through Telegram. On macOS, a Rust helper requested a command from the same verification service. The command fetched a script that delivered CloudSyncD, a backdoor which requested the user’s administrator password through a fake prompt and then collected host information before contacting its command-and-control server. The CloudSyncD delivery method overlaps with the earlier fake Zoom installer CloudSyncD campaign , which also used a counterfeit installer and password prompt to run a privileged backdoor on macOS devices.
