items.title: Legacy refrigeration controllers exploited in OT attack on hundreds of French supermarkets
items.summary: A coordinated attack on the operational technology (OT) behind supermarket refrigeration has hit hundreds of stores across France, in what security experts are calling one of the clearest examples yet of cyber sabotage with physical consequences. Retailers confirmed the attack on Monday 12 October, with disruption reportedly beginning on Sunday night. Intermarché and its Netto brand said at least 300 shops were affected, Coopérative U more than 100 and Carrefour 80, with Monoprix, E.Leclerc and Auchan also reporting impacted stores. According to BFM TV, attackers remotely forced refrigeration units into continuous defrost cycles, driving temperatures up to 50°C. Paris prosecutors said the attack also caused fires. “This incident is not surprising. A supermarket refrigerator is no longer just an electrical appliance. It is a computerized system connected to a network, enabling remote monitoring and control. While this connectivity allows refrigeration systems to be managed efficiently, it also exposes them to cyber security risks, particularly when operational equipment runs for years on outdated software, without regular security updates, and with management interfaces accessible from the internet,” said Oded Vanunu, Head of Vulnerability Research at Check Point . Unpatched, internet-facing and end of life The affected equipment has been traced to refrigeration management systems from Danish manufacturer Danfoss. A source close to Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said France’s National Cybersecurity Agency (ANSSI) had identified a vulnerability in Danfoss software, and the agency has been ordered to investigate. Danfoss said most of the compromised units were “legacy” products that no longer receive software or security updates, singling out its AK-SM800 and AK-SC355 controllers, and noted that an affected version of the AK-SM800 was running outdated firmware. The company said it had long advised customers to upgrade or replace these models. Known vulnerabilities in the control software date back to 2023, some rated critical, with patches available. In August, OT security firm Claroty published research describing flaws in Danfoss systems that could allow attackers to bypass authentication. Reports suggest attackers may have used the Shodan search engine to locate exposed devices, some of which are connected via 3G cards for remote monitoring. “One of the significant aspects of this incident is that the attackers did not necessarily need sophisticated cyber capabilities. Refrigeration systems have legitimate operational functions, such as defrost cycles, and when an unauthorized party gains access to the system, those same functions can be exploited to disrupt operations. Unlike attacks aimed at stealing data or encrypting files, the impact here is on the physical operation of the equipment itself, with direct consequences such as food inventory losses and potential safety hazards.” Vanunu continued. “In previous research conducted by Check Point on smart devices, including LG products, we demonstrated how a vulnerability in a centralised management platform could allow attackers to gain control of connected devices. However, in the current incident, it is still unclear exactly how the attackers gained access to the systems.” OT in the crosshairs No group has claimed responsibility, and there is no evidence of a ransom demand or data theft. The Paris prosecutor’s cybercrime unit has opened an investigation into what it described as a “large-scale” attack on connected refrigerators at several major food retailers, while ANSSI is coordinating with European counterparts. Sekoia analyst Felix Aime said stores in Spain, Portugal, Poland, Germany and Belgium were also affected. “The refrigeration systems in supermarkets are operational technology. Building management controls, HVAC, cold chain infrastructure. These are the same category of systems that the security industry has been warning about as the next frontier for sabotage attacks, and they’ve now been weaponised against food retail infrastructure in one of Europe’s largest economies,” said Muhammad Yahya Patel, vCISO and cybersecurity advisor for EMEA at Huntress . ANSSI had already listed sabotage of industrial control systems among the main threats facing France in its most recent threat report. “Heating fridges to 50 degrees for six hours is not data theft; it is physical sabotage executed through software, and that is the lesson for every sector. Refrigeration controllers, building systems and point-of-sale equipment are now connected and remotely managed, often through a handful of suppliers, so one weak link scales to hundreds of stores overnight,” said Samuel Hassine, CEO and co-founder of Filigran . “The problem extends beyond a single refrigeration system or an isolated security vulnerability. Operational equipment is often designed to remain in service for 15 years or more, while cyber threats and technologies evolve at a much faster pace. In addition, the same controllers and management systems are deployed across retail chains worldwide, meaning that a compromise affecting widely used technology could potentially impact a large number of locations,” added Check Point’s Vanunu. Counting the cost Intermarché chief executive Thierry Cotillard told BFM TV that losses could run to “tens of millions of euros nationwide in a single day”, while Coopérative U’s Dominique Schelcher said larger stores could each lose up to €180,000–200,000 in stock. France’s retail federation, the FCD, has called on Danfoss to provide “full transparency”. “The immediate financial consequences are significant and visible. Failures at the stores means total write-off of perishable stock across every affected location simultaneously. The operational disruption compounds quickly. Staff cannot trade normally without functioning refrigeration. Products cannot be restocked until systems are restored and verified safe. The food retail sector across Europe should be treating this as a signal that they are being actively targeted,” Huntress’ Patel warned. “The cyberattack on French supermarkets is a stark reminder that cyber threats extend far beyond stolen data and financial losses. Hackers reportedly manipulated refrigeration systems, raising temperatures to 50°C, causing fires and forcing retailers to dispose of large quantities of food. With hundreds of stores affected, the incident highlights how vulnerabilities in connected systems can have serious real-world consequences, disrupting operations, damaging equipment and potentially putting public safety at risk,” said Jamie Akhtar, CEO and Co-founder of CyberSmart . Mitigation: find the exposure first Experts agree that defenders’ first priority should be identifying which OT assets are reachable from the internet, and who holds remote access to them. “To reduce these risks, the first step is to identify which controllers and management interfaces are directly exposed to the internet and eliminate any unnecessary exposure. It is also important to keep systems updated, replace default passwords, restrict remote access, and enable multi-factor authentication wherever supported. Separating operational control networks from other networks and monitoring unusual changes in system behaviour are also essential measures. These recommendations apply not only to refrigeration systems, but also to HVAC, building management systems, and other operational infrastructure.” said Vanunu. “It also demonstrates how increasingly interconnected technology can create new opportunities for cybercriminals. For businesses, this reinforces the importance of securing all connected devices and systems, not just traditional IT infrastructure. Organisations should prioritise regular software and firmware updates, strong access controls, multi-factor authentication where supported and network segmentation to prevent attackers moving between systems. Regular security assessments and employee cybersecurity awareness training are also essential for identifying vulnerabilities before they can be exploited. Ultimately, businesses must recognise that cybersecurity is no longer just about protecting data, but also about safeguarding physical operations, customers and business continuity.” said CyberSmart’s Akhtar. Filigran’s Hassine urged security leaders to put the issue in front of the board: “Boards should ask three questions this week. Which connected equipment could cause physical or financial damage if someone changed a setting, and who can reach it from outside. Which third parties hold remote access, and how that access is monitored and segmented. And has anyone tested that the response works, from detection to switching to manual operation. Resilience in retail now means knowing your exposure before an attacker maps it for you.”

No group has claimed responsibility, and there is no evidence of a ransom demand or data theft. The Paris prosecutor’s cybercrime unit has opened an investigation into what it described as a “large-scale” attack on connected refrigerators at several major food retailers, while ANSSI is coordinating with European counterparts. Sekoia analyst Felix Aime said stores in Spain, Portugal, Poland, Germany and Belgium were also affected.

“The refrigeration systems in supermarkets are operational technology. Building management controls, HVAC, cold chain infrastructure. These are the same category of systems that the security industry has been warning about as the next frontier for sabotage attacks, and they’ve now been weaponised against food retail infrastructure in one of Europe’s largest economies,” said Muhammad Yahya Patel, vCISO and cybersecurity advisor for EMEA at Huntress.

ANSSI had already listed sabotage of industrial control systems among the main threats facing France in its most recent threat report.

“Heating fridges to 50 degrees for six hours is not data theft; it is physical sabotage executed through software, and that is the lesson for every sector. Refrigeration controllers, building systems and point-of-sale equipment are now connected and remotely managed, often through a handful of suppliers, so one weak link scales to hundreds of stores overnight,” said Samuel Hassine, CEO and co-founder of Filigran.

“The problem extends beyond a single refrigeration system or an isolated security vulnerability. Operational equipment is often designed to remain in service for 15 years or more, while cyber threats and technologies evolve at a much faster pace. In addition, the same controllers and management systems are deployed across retail chains worldwide, meaning that a compromise affecting widely used technology could potentially impact a large number of locations,” added Check Point’s Vanunu.

Counting the cost

Intermarché chief executive Thierry Cotillard told BFM TV that losses could run to “tens of millions of euros nationwide in a single day”, while Coopérative U’s Dominique Schelcher said larger stores could each lose up to €180,000–200,000 in stock. France’s retail federation, the FCD, has called on Danfoss to provide “full transparency”.

“The immediate financial consequences are significant and visible. Failures at the stores means total write-off of perishable stock across every affected location simultaneously. The operational disruption compounds quickly. Staff cannot trade normally without functioning refrigeration. Products cannot be restocked until systems are restored and verified safe. The food retail sector across Europe should be treating this as a signal that they are being actively targeted,” Huntress’ Patel warned.

“The cyberattack on French supermarkets is a stark reminder that cyber threats extend far beyond stolen data and financial losses. Hackers reportedly manipulated refrigeration systems, raising temperatures to 50°C, causing fires and forcing retailers to dispose of large quantities of food. With hundreds of stores affected, the incident highlights how vulnerabilities in connected systems can have serious real-world consequences, disrupting operations, damaging equipment and potentially putting public safety at risk,” said Jamie Akhtar, CEO and Co-founder of CyberSmart.

Mitigation: find the exposure first

Experts agree that defenders’ first priority should be identifying which OT assets are reachable from the internet, and who holds remote access to them.

“To reduce these risks, the first step is to identify which controllers and management interfaces are directly exposed to the internet and eliminate any unnecessary exposure. It is also important to keep systems updated, replace default passwords, restrict remote access, and enable multi-factor authentication wherever supported. Separating operational control networks from other networks and monitoring unusual changes in system behaviour are also essential measures. These recommendations apply not only to refrigeration systems, but also to HVAC, building management systems, and other operational infrastructure.” said Vanunu.

“It also demonstrates how increasingly interconnected technology can create new opportunities for cybercriminals. For businesses, this reinforces the importance of securing all connected devices and systems, not just traditional IT infrastructure. Organisations should prioritise regular software and firmware updates, strong access controls, multi-factor authentication where supported and network segmentation to prevent attackers moving between systems. Regular security assessments and employee cybersecurity awareness training are also essential for identifying vulnerabilities before they can be exploited. Ultimately, businesses must recognise that cybersecurity is no longer just about protecting data, but also about safeguarding physical operations, customers and business continuity.” said CyberSmart’s Akhtar.

Filigran’s Hassine urged security leaders to put the issue in front of the board: “Boards should ask three questions this week. Which connected equipment could cause physical or financial damage if someone changed a setting, and who can reach it from outside. Which third parties hold remote access, and how that access is monitored and segmented. And has anyone tested that the response works, from detection to switching to manual operation. Resilience in retail now means knowing your exposure before an attacker maps it for you.”

items.title: Introducing the Agentic Skills Marketplace: Curated AI Capabilities for the Modern SOC
items.summary: For years, SOC Prime has focused on one core problem: curating behavioral detection rules that cover both the threats that never go away and the new ones that emerge every day. As agentic AI changes how security teams work, we see the same opportunity opening up in a new area — and we’re expanding our curation approach to meet it. Meet the Agentic Skills Marketplace , available inside Prime Architect’s Agentic Threat Research. The Problem: Capability Isn’t the Bar Agentic AI is giving security teams more skills and agents to choose from than ever. But in cybersecurity, capability alone was never the bar. Before a skill earns a place in a SOC workflow, teams need to know what it does, what it can access, how it operates, and whether it can be trusted. That’s the gap the Agentic Skills Marketplace is built to close — curation, applied to a new kind of asset. Built on Infrastructure We Already Trust This isn’t a new direction so much as the next step on one SOC Prime is already on. Prime Architect’s Agentic Threat Research already lets analysts take a raw threat report and, with one click, turn it into structured, actionable intelligence and environment-tuned detections — without the data ever leaving SOC Prime infrastructure. That capability is backed by ongoing R&D across bare-metal and cloud architectures, using multiple open-weight models deployed on infrastructure SOC Prime owns. Owning that infrastructure means control over data sovereignty and performance, and it reflects a broader belief: when the people building the AI are also the security experts, security becomes a design principle from the start, not a feature bolted on later. The Agentic Skills Marketplace is built on that same thinking. What’s Inside the Marketplace The marketplace launches with more than 1,000 open-source skills, organized around the functions defined in the NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0 — Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover — so teams explore skills in the context of the work they’re already doing, rather than starting from scratch. Contact Sales That means real, ready-to-use skills for the workflows that eat up analyst time: Detection engineering — Turn raw log samples, detection ideas, or descriptions of attacker behavior into detection content. Skills can guide the agent through analyzing relevant fields and producing detection logic tailored to the target environment. CTI analysis — Process unstructured threat reports and extract useful intelligence, including hashes, domains, IP addresses, URLs, malware names, techniques, and affected technologies. An extraction pipeline can define what to look for and how to organize the results. Threat hunting — Turn a hunting hypothesis into a query designed for a specific data plane and its available data sources. Skills provide the workflow needed to move from what to investigate to a runnable hunt. Adversary emulation — Structure attacker behavior for emulation and testing. Skills can help identify relevant techniques, translate adversary behavior into actionable steps, and support workflows based on mapping techniques within MITRE ATT&CK and MITRE Attack Flow. These are exactly the kinds of repeatable, judgment-heavy workflows Agentic Skills is built for. Instead of a one-off prompt that may or may not capture the nuance of the task, you get a curated, reviewed, versioned instruction set the agent follows every time — built by the SOC Prime team, by trusted publishers, or by you. And if a workflow is unique to your team, you’re not limited to what’s in the marketplace — you can create your own personal skills from scratch, with your own instructions, and use them exactly like any marketplace skill. Know Exactly What Skills You’re Using Before installing any skill, its details page gives you everything you need to evaluate it — no black box, no guesswork: Security score — an at-a-glance indication of the skill’s overall safety Vetting details — how the skill was assessed before being listed Operation flow chart — a visual walkthrough of what the skill does and how it works Use cases — real examples of where the skill applies Prerequisites — what needs to be in place before you run it Compatibility — which environments, agents, and tools it works with Putting Skills into Practice Discover. Go to Prime Architect > Agentic Threat Research > Agentic Skills . Browse the library by NIST Cybersecurity Framework, or check “For You” and “New” for recommendations and recent releases. Evaluate. Open a skill’s details page for its flow diagram, when-to-use guidance, prerequisites, a worked example, security score, and compatibility. Not ready to use? Bookmark it for later. Install. One click adds it to your skills, ready to use in your workflow. Installed skills auto-update, so you always run the latest, most accurate version with zero manual maintenance. Take it with you. Generate a ZIP package containing the skill’s SKILL.md file — useful for storing it locally or running it with a compatible external agent or platform. Use it. In Prime Architect chat, add the installed skill to your message any of three ways: Click the + icon and select Add Skills , then pick a skill Type / to search by skill name or description and select the skill from the list Click the Agentic Skills button above the chat input, then pick a skill Pair it with your own prompt, a file, or a detection for context, then send — the agent follows the skill’s instructions to produce the output. The marketplace doesn’t sit in isolation — it’s also connected directly to Active Threats in Prime Core . When you’re exploring a specific threat, relevant agentic skills surface automatically, right alongside the investigation. Instead of leaving your threat research to go hunt for the right skill, the skill finds you at the moment you need it — keeping analysis and action in the same flow. Experience the Marketplace This isn’t meant to be another catalog layered onto an already crowded security stack. It’s built to make it easier to find useful skills, understand what they actually do before adopting them, and bring them into existing workflows with real confidence instead of guesswork.

items.title: CVE-2026-97229: Critical GitLab RCE Flaw Enables Unauthenticated Code Execution
items.summary: GitLab has released emergency security updates addressing CVE-2026-97229, a maximum-severity remote code execution vulnerability affecting GitLab Community Edition (CE) and Enterprise Edition (EE). The flaw has a CVSS score of 10.0 and could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary code on a vulnerable GitLab server under certain conditions. The vulnerability resides in GitLab’s CI/CD Regular Expression Compiler and results from insufficient validation of specially crafted regular expressions. Successful exploitation could compromise the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of a GitLab environment without requiring authentication or user interaction. GitLab released patched versions 19.2.8, 19.3.4, and 19.4.2 on October 12, 2026, strongly urging administrators of self-managed installations to upgrade immediately. GitLab.com already runs the fixed release, while GitLab Dedicated customers do not need to take additional action. With source-code management and CI/CD infrastructure containing sensitive repositories, credentials, deployment secrets, and access to production environments, vulnerabilities in GitLab can create significant risks for modern software supply chains. Security teams can strengthen their defenses against emerging vulnerability exploitation with SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform, accelerating threat hunting and detection engineering while adapting detection logic to their organization’s security telemetry. Contact Sales CVE-2026-97229 Analysis CVE-2026-97229 affects GitLab CE and EE installations across three currently vulnerable release branches: GitLab 19.2 before 19.2.8 GitLab 19.3 before 19.3.4 GitLab 19.4 before 19.4.2 The vulnerability is caused by an integer overflow in the CI/CD Regular Expression Compiler. This component processes regular expressions used within project pipeline configurations. According to GitLab, insufficient regular expression validation can allow an unauthenticated attacker to supply a specially crafted expression that ultimately results in arbitrary code execution on the GitLab server. GitLab assigned the vulnerability the maximum CVSS 3.1 score of 10.0, with the vector AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H. This reflects the severity of a network-accessible vulnerability that requires neither authentication nor user interaction and can potentially have a high impact on confidentiality, integrity, and availability. The flaw is particularly dangerous because GitLab servers commonly occupy a highly privileged position within development infrastructure. They can host proprietary source code, CI/CD variables, deployment credentials, access tokens, configuration files, and integrations with cloud and production environments. Arbitrary code execution on the underlying GitLab server could therefore provide attackers with opportunities to access sensitive repositories, extract secrets, manipulate source code, interfere with pipelines, establish persistence, or use compromised infrastructure as a stepping stone toward additional systems. The vulnerability was reported to GitLab through its HackerOne bug bounty program by security researcher joaxcar. GitLab has not publicly specified the exact date on which the issue was initially discovered or privately reported. It was publicly disclosed with the October 12, 2026 critical patch release. The disclosure follows other recent vulnerabilities affecting GitLab’s regular expression processing components. The flaw has a CVSS score of 10.0 and could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary code on a vulnerable GitLab server under certain conditions.

The vulnerability resides in GitLab’s CI/CD Regular Expression Compiler and results from insufficient validation of specially crafted regular expressions. Successful exploitation could compromise the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of a GitLab environment without requiring authentication or user interaction.

GitLab released patched versions 19.2.8, 19.3.4, and 19.4.2 on October 12, 2026, strongly urging administrators of self-managed installations to upgrade immediately. GitLab.com already runs the fixed release, while GitLab Dedicated customers do not need to take additional action.

items.title: Scammers know your name, and they’re counting on you to reply
items.summary: Scammers are finding different ways to use personal details exposed in data breaches to lure people into conversations. Last week , we showed how a Facebook Marketplace listing used the recipient’s name to make a text asking “Is this still available?” more convincing. The one we got this week was a lot simpler. No suspicious link. No overdue payment. No warning that your account is about to be closed. No fake images. Just your name, followed by a question mark. It’s a remarkably small opening for what could become a much bigger problem. A message like this invites an almost automatic response: “Yes?” Or perhaps, “Who’s this?” That’s because a scammer needs to get you to engage before they can persuade you to hand over money or personal information . Sometimes, the first thing they ask you to give them is simply a reply. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) has warned about similarly brief, apparently harmless messages that scammers use to start conversations. The text in our example gives the recipient very little information, but leaves an obvious question unanswered: Who wants to know? Using the correct name makes that question more compelling. This is not just a generic “Hello” that could have gone to anyone. It looks as though the sender is trying to reach you specifically. It’s tempting to think, “They have my name and number, so this must be someone I know.” But having those details is not evidence they know you. As we discussed in the Marketplace article, name-and-phone-number combinations can come from breached data traded by cybercriminals. What follows depends on the scheme. The first message doesn’t tell us which route this scammer planned to take. But documented scams show how an innocuous introduction can develop: A supposed wrong-number exchange becomes a friendly conversation. The sender builds a relationship rather than immediately asking for money. An investment opportunity eventually enters the discussion. The victim is encouraged to send money to a fraudulent investment scheme. The FBI describes how cryptocurrency investment scammers build trust before introducing fake investments, and identifies unsolicited texts as one way they approach victims. Even if the conversation goes no further, your reply can still be useful to the scammer. As we explained in our earlier article on wrong-number texts , it shows that you are willing to engage. Your number can then be reused or sold for other scam campaigns. How to stay safe A scam doesn’t have to begin with an outrageous promise or an urgent threat. Sometimes it begins with something much more ordinary: your name, a question mark, and the expectation that you will be polite enough to answer. Don’t reply. Even “Who’s this?” or “Wrong number” tells the scammer you are willing to respond. If you think it might be someone you know, contact them through a number or channel you already trust. Report before you block. Use your messaging app’s reporting option, then block the sender. If you have already replied, stop engaging. Make yourself harder to profile. Review privacy settings on messaging apps and social media. Limit who can see your profile photo, status, last seen, and phone number. Run a Malwarebytes Digital Footprint Scan to check for personal information exposed in known breaches and on the dark web. It helps to be aware of what can be used to target you. Use Malwarebytes Scam Number Check to see whether the sender’s number has been flagged for scams or spam. What do cybercriminals know about you? Use Malwarebytes’ free Digital Footprint scan to see whether your personal information has been exposed online. SCAN NOW

items.title: RSVP to Disaster: How One Click Installs a RAT
items.summary: By: Willmar Cheng, Cofense Phishing Defense Center Imagine receiving a digital invite from a friend or relative. The message looks legitimate; the timing feels believable, and curiosity naturally takes over. This sense of curiosity and trust is exactly what cybercriminals are exploiting. The Cofense Phishing Defense Center (PDC) has recently intercepted a malicious email disguised by an online event invitation. Choosing to RSVP through the attached URLs leads users to a fake event page containing malware that grants threat actors remote access to systems. This attack is notable because the email looks harmless, and these emails are more common as the holiday season begins. The campaign demonstrates how attackers can turn everyday social events into convincing malware lures. Figure 1: Email Body Phishing emails such as this sample are effective at targeting a larger scope of users as the vague wording can be applied to a variety of situations. The generic subject line, event title, and lack of organizers or details is not just an oversight – it is the strategy. Vague messages create curiosity; curiosity overrides caution, and one click later you're downloading malware or handing over your credentials. Breaking it down piece by piece, the manipulation gets even clearer. The subject line, "You are cordially invited," and "Join Us for a Special Gathering, Let Us Celebrate a Milestone," is engineered to feel personal without saying anything too specific. It uses the language of weddings and galas to trigger a curious reaction from the user, but the invite names no one, and no specific details are present. That's not sloppy writing; it's scaled: a generic line can be blasted to thousands of inboxes while still feeling individually addressed. Then comes the button, "Click Here to Download the Invite," where the email capitalizes on all that setup. The threat actor utilizes a forced download in this case to hide the destination of the malicious file that the user unknowingly downloads once the button is clicked. Figure 2: CAPTCHA Verification After clicking the download button, users are redirected to a CAPTCHA verification page. CAPTCHAs, as seen in Figure 2, are often used by threat actors to create a false sense of security for the user, making the page feel more legitimate. That illusion falls apart on closer inspection, though: the CAPTCHA is hosted on a generic, unbranded domain that's less than a month old, a strong instant indicator that the CAPTCHA and the generic URL together form a two-step confirmation that this "invite" was never legitimate to begin with. Figure 3: Malware Download Page After passing the CAPTCHA, the user lands on a second fake invitation page shown in Figure 3. Once again, the design is deliberately generic: there's no date, venue, time, or any of the specific details a real invitation would naturally include. The only detail that screams to the victim is to click the "eInvite" button. Figure 4: Malware Extracted Clicking the “eInvite” button begins the download of a zipped folder labeled “ViewDePartyyinvites”. Inside is an executable named ScreenConnect.exe, This is a legitimate ConnectWise Screen Connect installer that is being abused by threat actors as a remote access trojan, The RAT, remote access trojan that abuses trusted remote-support software to avoid antivirus detection. Once executed, the malware grants the threat actor full remote access to the user’s device, effectively handing over control without the user realizing what they've installed. Figure 5: Malware Executed Finally, once the executable runs, a small icon quietly appears in the taskbar, easy to miss if you're not looking for it. Clicking it reveals a chat box along with a connection status, showing the RAT actively linking up with the host machine as seen in Figure 5. This is the moment the compromise becomes fully operational. The attacker now has a live channel into the device, and from the user’s side the only visible trace is a small, unassuming icon that gives no indication of what's happening behind it. Campaigns like this are unique because they do not use sophisticated techniques but rather use the user's own curiosity to successfully accomplish the attack. From the vague subject, email content, webpage, all push the user to click a button. This campaign illustrates the importance of training employees to spot and report these unique attacks. Cofense is uniquely positioned to spot these attacks and also catch these types of attacks that have turned up in environments protected by SEGs. With Cofense Managed Phishing and Defense, provided through our Phishing Defense Center (PDC), enterprises benefit from our complete view of real phishing and malware threats. items.title: Massive DDoS Attack Disrupts Ubuntu’s Canonical Websites and Security APIs
items.summary: Canonical, the company behind Ubuntu Linux, suffered a sustained distributed denial-of-service attack on October 8, 2026, disrupting its main websites and security information services. The outage lasted four hours and 12 minutes, according to OMG! Ubuntu. It was Canonical’s second major DDoS incident this year, following a broader disruption in late April. Canonical confirmed the incident through Ubuntu Discourse, warning that some services could become intermittently unavailable. “Canonical’s websites are under a sustained distributed denial of service attack,” the company stated. Its engineers worked to restore access, and an October 9 update said most affected services were available again while recovery work continued. Ubuntu Websites and Security APIs Affected The affected services included ubuntu.com, canonical.com, the Ubuntu blog, the developer portal, and Ubuntu’s security advisory pages and API. These resources provide product information, developer guidance, and vulnerability details. Their disruption left users unable to reliably reach parts of Ubuntu’s public web infrastructure, even though several software delivery services continued operating. items.title: Yandex Data Center Outage Disrupts Access to Cloud Files Following Drone Attack
items.summary: Yandex has confirmed a major service outage after drone attacks damaged three data centers in Russia, leaving some users unable to access cloud files. Two facilities stopped operating, while a third lost part of its infrastructure. The disruption affected Yandex Disk users and businesses running services on Yandex Cloud across the platform. The first attack hit the Sasovo data center during the night of October 7 to 8, 2026. Yandex said the site suffered serious damage and stopped operating completely. Another attack struck its Kaluga facility on October 9, disabling part of the infrastructure. A third attack hit Vladimir overnight on October 11 and halted operations there. Yandex reported no injuries across the three incidents. Emergency teams and company specialists were working at the damaged sites. In its statement , the company said engineers were working day and night to keep services running, but assessing the equipment remained difficult. It could not provide a reliable restoration timeline. Cloud Files Become Unavailable The outage has exposed problems beyond simply opening an application. That one Yandex Disk customer experienced missing thumbnails and failed downloads of previously uploaded files, with problems beginning on October 8. The customer also reported HTTP 302 redirects, HTTP 504 Gateway Timeout errors, and HTTP 500 errors while accessing files. These reports show that some stored content could not be retrieved through normal service requests. However, failed downloads do not establish that files have been deleted. Whether any customer data has been permanently lost remains unclear, and Yandex had not addressed that question in the status updates cited by BleepingComputer. The impact also extended to business cloud tools. The report said Yandex Cloud’s console, API, identity management, container registry, databases, S3 storage, and Kubernetes were available with some performance or availability issues. Compute, AI Studio, and security services were only partly available, while Monium remained offline. Those conditions reflected the latest update cited in the October 12 report, not a guarantee of current availability. Yandex described its remaining cloud resources as unstable and said the platform was operating in emergency mode. It urged customers to use alternative disaster recovery plans and warned that technical support channels could also be unstable. The incident concerns physical damage to hosting infrastructure. The available reporting does not establish a malware infection, stolen credentials, or unauthorized access to customer files. Related coverage of a Microsoft data center power outage and the AWS outage linked to DNS problems shows how infrastructure failures can interrupt services far beyond the original fault. For affected organizations, Yandex’s warning makes recovery planning urgent. Access to another working environment matters while damaged facilities remain offline. The immediate unanswered questions are when full service will return and whether all affected files can be recovered. Cut every SOC alert investigation by 21 min. items.title: WordPress Plugin Vulnerability Exploited in Attacks to Upload and eEecute Arbitrary PHP code
items.summary: Attackers are targeting a critical security flaw in the Bricksforge WordPress plugin that lets them upload and run arbitrary PHP code without logging in. Tracked as CVE-2026-85097, the vulnerability carries a maximum CVSS score of 10.0 and can lead to remote code execution on affected websites. Patchstack first observed exploitation attempts on October 7, 2026, at 21:47:17 UTC. The flaw affects Bricksforge versions up to and including 3.1.8.9. Patchstack identifies version 3.1.8.10 as the fixed release. Bricksforge extends Bricks Builder with advanced forms, animations, dynamic data tools, and site controls. Its form upload process is at the center of this attack. According to Patchstack’s technical report , Bricksforge checks a file’s MIME type during the initial upload. This check helps identify whether the submitted file is an allowed image. However, when a form is submitted later, the plugin trusts the visitor-supplied file details without properly checking the URL field inside temporaryFileUploads. Attackers exploit this gap by uploading a file that looks like a GIF but also contains PHP code. The image passes the first check and enters the temporary upload directory. A crafted form submission then pairs the image’s server path with a destination URL ending in a PHP extension. Bricksforge accepts those details and places the file contents at the PHP destination. Requesting that file causes the server to execute the hidden code. Attackers can then install web shells, change website content, read sensitive data, or maintain access. The attack also uses the publicly accessible bricksforge_regenerate_nonce AJAX action to obtain a valid request token. WordPress Plugin Vulnerability Exploited This is separate from the earlier Bricks Builder remote code execution vulnerability . It also highlights risks seen in other WordPress plugin file upload flaws , where unsafe file handling can turn an upload feature into a code execution path. Almost every captured attempt targeted /wp-json/bricksforge/v1/form_submit. One used /wp-admin/admin-ajax.php with the bricksforge_form_submit action. In 95% of requests, the server path ended in .gif or .png, often paired with a PHP destination URL. Attackers tested extensions including .php5, .php8, and .phtml, alongside mixed capitalization and encoded filenames. Some attempted to place login_admin_*.php files outside the temporary directory, in regular WordPress upload folders. Patchstack recorded 63 source IP addresses. One cluster involved 44 IPs sending 56 identical requests within seconds. Another involved three IPs testing 25 extension and encoding variations. These patterns suggest automated activity using distributed infrastructure, but they do not establish a single attacker’s identity. Administrators should update affected installations to version 3.1.8.10 or later. The vendor changelog also lists a Pro Forms upload security fix in version 4.0.1, released October 8, and urges updates even when active forms have no upload fields. Review logs for crafted temporaryFileUploads submissions and inspect /wp-content/uploads/bricksforge/tmp/ and other upload directories for unexpected PHP files. Check for requests to newly created scripts and unauthorized changes. Patchstack says its RapidMitigate rule blocks exploitation attempts, offering temporary protection when immediate updates are not possible. Sites previously exposed should still undergo a compromise review. Stops threats before impact with 21 min faster MTTR. Integrate ANYRUN’s Sandbox in your SOC

items.title: LG webOS Flaws Let Remote Attackers Execute Commands as Root Without Authentication
items.summary: Security researchers have disclosed four serious vulnerabilities in LG webOS smart TVs that could allow an attacker to bypass authentication, create a privileged account, and ultimately execute commands with root-level access. The flaws, tracked as CVE-2023-6317 through CVE-2023-6320, affect selected LG TV models running webOS versions 4 through 7. Bitdefender researchers said the issue could give an attacker full control of a vulnerable television if it is reachable on the same local network. In some cases, the risk could extend beyond the home network because researchers found more than 91,000 exposed devices through Shodan. This search engine indexes internet-connected services. Bitdefender said LG fixed the reported issues before it publicly released the research in April 2024. The most important flaw, CVE-2023-6317, affects the pairing process used by the LG ThinQ mobile app. Normally, when setting up the app, a user must enter a PIN displayed on the TV before the app can gain access. LG webOS Flaws Bitdefender found that a weakness in the webOS account-registration process could let an attacker skip that PIN verification and create a user profile with elevated permissions. The problem involved how the system handled client-key and companion-client-key values. An attacker could first request a low-permission account, obtain its client key, and then reuse that key while requesting another account with higher permissions. The TV verified that the key existed but did not properly confirm that it belonged to the account being created. That allowed the request to avoid the on-screen PIN prompt. Once the attacker created a privileged account, they could access services unavailable to normal unauthenticated users. This is where the remaining flaws become important. CVE-2023-6318 and CVE-2023-6319 are command-injection vulnerabilities that can be used to run operating system commands. CVE-2023-6320 affects a network configuration endpoint and can run commands under the dbus account, which researchers said has permissions close to root. For readers following smart-TV security issues, Cyber Security News previously reported that more than 90,000 LG TVs were exposed to authorization bypass risks , highlighting how internet exposure can turn a local-network weakness into a wider concern. Bitdefender confirmed the flaws on several webOS builds, including webOS 4.9.7, 5.5.0, 6.3.3-442, and 7.3.1-43. The tested devices included the LG43UM7000PLA, OLED55CXPUA, OLED48C1PUB, and OLED55A23LA. CVE-2023-6317 affected all four tested webOS versions and enabled the authentication bypass. CVE-2023-6318 was confirmed on webOS 5.5.0, 6.3.3-442, and 7.3.1-43. CVE-2023-6319 affected all tested versions, while CVE-2023-6320 affected webOS 5.5.0 and 6.3.3-442. The full chain is particularly concerning because it combines a simple authorization bypass with command execution. A threat actor would not need a TV owner to approve a pairing request or enter a PIN. After obtaining elevated access, they could change settings, install unwanted software, access connected services, or use the TV as a foothold inside a home network. LG’s Product Security Response Center publishes security bulletins for product issues, and the company says smart TVs receive software and security updates at least once a year for at least two years after launch. LG also says its security update period lasts five years from the webOS platform launch date. Owners should turn on automatic software updates and manually check the TV’s firmware version through the device settings. Updating is especially important after unboxing a TV that may have sat in storage for months before you connect it to the internet. Users should also avoid exposing smart TVs directly to the internet through router port forwarding, keep home routers patched, and, where possible, place IoT devices on a separate guest or IoT network. These steps reduce the chance that an outside attacker can reach a vulnerable TV or use it to move deeper into a home network. Stops threats before impact with 21 min faster MTTR.
